MADAME ROBIN'S AFTERNOON TEA. - Cue afternoon -464 In the heart of June— The very brightest, bluest weather— Some of the song-birds came together. They met at Madame Robin's, you see, In the top of a breezy maple-tree, For she'd asked them in to an "early.tea." All were dressed In their very best; . • ide. Jay wore an azure vest; Mistress Sparrow and Lady Wren, The one in brown and the one in yellow, Fluttered merrily in, and then Came Sir Bobolink—jollyifellow! Timid Miss Phcebe and pert Miss Thrush Followed Lord Oriole, spick and sprightly; ' Next the Finches with rustle and rush, And Parson Blackbird beaming brightly. And there were others, a score' - Or more— All in the very merriest mood, too; And there arose such a patter, • And clatter, and chatter, That those not invited Were soon quite affrighted,' . For nobody knew what on earth was the matter, Or what such a babel of talk could elude to. But nothing alarming Heard thoFe overhead, so They found it quite charming, And each of them said so; For they'd all been south, and they hadn't met Since the autumn time with its chill, a9d wet. So this was all that the babel meant; They were asking each other with rapt intent, "Where and how was your winter spent?" ....Harper's Young People.

In apple-pie order: Cheese. Moderation makes a throne stand sure. Never hit a man when he has got you down. If a man "stands to win," will he lose if he sits down That man has got a long way on the road towards truth who doesn't call his adversary's firmness "obstinacy." A seho)l teacher asked an Irish boy to describe an island. "Sure, ma'am," said Pat., "it's a place you can't lave without a boat." • He: "I believe in calling things by their proper name,." She (who teaches a grammar class) ; "But things don't have proper none 3, you know.", "Faint heart never won fair lady," or conquered diffi- culties, or achieved glory; but insolent assumption is more'contemptible than a lack of moral courage. Po'ite Passenger: "Pardon me, sir, can I sit down in this seat ?" Old Sourboy : "Well, I presume you can if you try hard enough. I didn't have any trouble." When Dir. Sme h scat asked for his "Christian name in full" he replied: "My Christian name is Zerubbabel. When full, this becomes Zrubble as near as I can figure it out." Wit loses its respect with the good when seen in com- pany with malice, and to smile at the jest which plants a thorn in anothees breast is to become a principal in the mischief. He who, when called upon to speak a disagreeable truth, tees it boldly and has done, is both bolder and milder than he who nibbles in a low voice, and never ceases nibbling. It is the perfection of friendship to be able to receive unpleasant truths without offence. But in all personal criticism let us remember that "a great hand is careful lest it crush." The more people do the more they can do; he who does nothing renders himself incapable of doing anything; whilst we are executing one work we are preparing our- selves for undertaking another. Widow: "Now, my dear sir, promise me your vote on this bill." Congressman: "but, my dear madam, I—" Widow: "Now look me in the eyes and promise." Con- gressman: "Madam, the eves have it." So mixed it is, a body hardly knows If fame is manufactured goods, or grows. Douce man is he whose sense the point imparts Where advertising ends and glory starts. Miss Prim (to her little nephew) : You should not ; say that water is unhealthy,-but unhealthful. ' How can water be unhealthy?" Nephew: "I don't know, auntie, but you often hear of well water," Artist: " oh ! so you think the background's 'beastly,' do you? Perhaps the cattle are beastly,' too, thougu I flatter myself—." Friendly Critic: "Oh, no, my dear fellow, that's just what they are not." "Ah !love, I should like to listen to you all night," said Clarence, as he rose to go. Six months after they were married he chanced to stop out fifteen minutes after his hour, and he had his desire gratieed. Stranger: "Do the cars run to the park all the time?" Conductor: "No, sir; only half the time." Stranger: "That's funny. How does it happen?" Conductor: "It takes the other half for them to run back." "Have you seen Cleopatra's mummy ?" "Yes." "Is it really beautiful?" "Well, that depends on what you call beautiful. Did you ever see a dried apple ?" "Yes." "Well, that's Cleopatra's mummy on a small scale." Harry: "She has jilted me, and I know I shall die. The disappeintmentwill kill me." Aunt Hannah: "I know how disappointments affect one, Harry. But you'll get over it. I felt just as you do now when I set that yeller hen on 13 eggs and only got just one poor chick out ot the lot." A married, lady, alluding in conversation to the 148th Psalm, observed that while "young men and maidens, old men and children" were expressly mentioned,enot a word was said about married women. An old clergy- man venom she was addressing assured her that they had not been omitted, and that she would flnd them in- cluded in one of the prece ling verses, under the descrip- tion of vapours and storms. Lord Campbell tells this story about Henry Erskine : I Having been speaking in the Outer House, at the bar of Lord Swinton, a very 'good, but a very slow and deaf judge, Erskine was called away to the bar of Lord Brax- field, who was Lord Ordmary for the week. On his com- ing up Lrrd Praxfield said to him "Well, Dean, what is this you've been talking so loudly about to my Lord Swinton I'" About a cask of whisky, my lord," replied Harry • "but I found it no easy matter to make it run in hie lordship's bead." An Aberdeen widew, who called upon the minister, Seemed desirous of relieving her mind of something which oppressed her, at which the reverend gentleman, wishing to hurry mat terseexclaimed, "My good woman, you see I can be of no service to you till you tell me what it is that troubles you." " Well, sir, I'm thinkin' 'o gettin' married again." "Oh, that is it ! Let me see; that is pretty frequent, surely. How many husbands have you had ?" " Well, sir," she replied, in a tone less of so:row than of bitterness, "this is the fourth ; I'm sure there's nae wumman been sae tormented wi' a set o' deein' men." The Brazilian rabob, Berm Fereau, who died not long since, was as miserly in trifles as he was extravagant in ether respects. It was ens of his peculiarities never to fee servants, and the waiters of the various hail; at which lie sojourned were for that reason not partial to bin:. One morning, while staving at the magnificent Maux Hotel, in Ito ate Janeiro, he came down to break- fast and ordered a cutlet. Alter he bad eaten it he ordered a second. "Baron," said the head waiter, maliciously, it's a custom with us never to serve the same course twice at a meal." "Is that so ?" said Tereau ; and rising from his &at he left the room. In ten minutes he came back into the dining-MM. "Waiter," said he, :" I have just boug.eit this hotel, ilea am master now. As you will not tee ewe to get accus- tomed to my plan of serving ttiti pests according to " their wishes, you are dismissed ett once." Thereupon he took up his napkin again, and called te another 'waiter : eel Now bring me another outlet" i ATER! LXACT INDENP,—ID, One 6° .• f f t e c,evefea.t . mouern Frence —.esque9 the author describes a battie-field on which a young soldier is mourning over the corpse of his comrade. when a grim old sergeant says, sternly, "Leave off blubbering, you fool. What are you making all this noise about?" "Poor Pierre Lafleur is dead, sergeant." "Dead, do you say? Young ma". remember for the futhre that no soldier is to be considered dead until he has been entered as such upon the official list of killed and wounded." A gentleman a such rigid accuracy might fairly have claimed kindred with the scrupulous Quaker who always spoke of a pew-tree as a thou-tree; but even this exactness has been rivalled elsewhere, as may be seen by the following story, which, if not literally true, certainly deserves to be so. Shortly after the publication of Tennyson's famous poem, "A Vision of Sin," the Laureate was some- what startled to receive from Mr. Babbasee, the renowned arithmetician, a letter which ran as follows: "Dear Sir, —I rind in a recently published poem from your pen, entitled A Vision of Sin,' the following unwarrantable statement :

," Every moment dies a maq. Every moment one is born.' I need hardly polnt out to you that this calculation. if Correct, would tend to keep the sum total of the world's population in a state of perpetual equipoise, whereas it is a well-known fact that the said sum total is constantly on the increase. I would therefore take the liberty of suggesting that in the next edition of your excellent poem the erroneous calculation to which I refer should be corrected as follows: "'Every moment dies a man, And one and a sixteenth Is born.' I may add that the exact figures are 1'167; but some- thing must of course be conceded to the laws of meter. have the honour to be, sir, yours sincerely, C. Emmet's." David Ker, in Harper's Magazine. The latest instalment of Joseph Jefferson's auto- biography in the " Century " magazine contains a touching story of the relations between Tom Robert- son, the author of "Caste," and poor Artemus Ward, then rapidly dying :—A strong attachment had sprung4ip between them, and the devotion of his new-found English friend was touching in the ex- treme and characteristic of Robertson's noble nature. Just before Ward's death, Robertson poured out some medicine in a glass and offered it to his friend. Ward said, "My dear Tom, I can't take that dreadful stuff." "Come, come," said RobeTtson, urging him to swallow the nauseous drug: "there's a dear fellow. Do now for my sake; you know I would do anything for you." " Would you ?" said Ward, feebly stretching out his hand to grasp his friend's perhaps for the last time. "I would, indeed," said Robertson. "Then you take it," said, Ward. The humorist passed away but a few hours afterwards. -

Cur advanc3d guard had been skirmishing with the enemy for five days, and with empty stomachs. The commissary of the division had either missed us in his march with the provisions, for Which he had been dispatched to the rear, or else had not been successful in procuring a supply. But what- ever might have been the cause, the consequence was trying to us; for the men, officers and all, were wholly without provisions for three days. At the time the commissary went to the rear, two pounds of biscuit, one pound of meat, and a pint of wino were served out to each individual; and upon this quantity we were forced to exist for five days; for nothing was to be bought. If we had been loaded with gold, we could not have purchased a morsel of any sort of food. Most of the men, from having been accustomed to disappointment of supplies of rations, managed their little stock of provisions so economically, that it lasted nearly three days, but the greater part finished it in half the time. As the men grew

weaker, the work grew heavier; and as hunger in- creased, so did the necessity for physical exertion. The enemy were constantly annoying us, and every hour of the day brought a skirmish, either with their little squads of cavalry, their riflemen, or their voltigeurs. The latter were troops of very short stature and strong make, very much esteemed by Napoleon. They wore short breeches and half gaiters, and none of the men were more than five feet three inches high. The rifles would advance by the cover of a hedge, or hill perhaps, while the voltigeurs would suddenly 'dart out from a ditch, into whick they had crept under cover of the weeds, and fall upon our picquets with the ferocity of bull- dogs; and when they were mastered, would (if not killed, wounded, or held fast) scamper off like kan- garoos. In like manner the cavalry would try to surprise us; or, if they could steal upon us' would dash up, fire their pistols, and, if well opposed, gallop off again. On the fifth morning after the commissary had delivered the rations above mentioned, we had a

very sharp brush with the enemy. A company of infantry and a few dragoons were ordered to dislodge the French from a house in which they had a party, and which was necessary to the security of our position; for, from this house, they used to sally upon our picquets in a most annoying manner. The French, not more than fifty in num- ber, made a considerable resistance ; they received the English with a volley from the windows, and immediately retreated to a high bank behind the house. From this point they continued to fire until their flank was threatened by our dragoons, when they retreated in double-quick disorder, leaving about fifteen killed and wounded. -

Our men were then starving. The poor fellows, although they had forgotten their animal wants in the execution of their duty, plainly displayed in their faces the weakness of their bodies. Islvery man of the crowded encampment looked wan and melancholy; and all kept up their flagging spirits by resolution and patience. Many a manly fellow felt in silence the bitterness of his situation. There were no upbraidings, far all were sufferers alike. In about an hour after taking of the old house in front, I went out from our huts in a crowd to see the place of action. I met some of our men wounded, led and carried by their comrades. The officer commanding the party now joined me, and walked. back to the house, to give farther direc- tions regarding other wounded men not yet re- moved. When we had gone about fifty yards, we met a wounded soldier carried very slowly in a blanket by four men. As soon as he,saw the officer who was along with me, he cried out in a feeble but forced voice, "Stop I stop I—lay me down— let me speak to the captain.' The surgeon, who was along with him, had no objection, for, in my opinion, he thought the man beyond the power of his skill, and the sufferer was laid gently down upon the turf, under the shade of a projecting rock. I knew the wounded man's face in a moment, for I had often remarked him as being a steady, well-con- ducted soldier; his age was about forty-one or two, and he had a wife and two children in England.

. saw death in the poor fellow's face. He wa'S shot in the throat, or rather between the shoulder and khe throat; the ball passed apparently downwards, probably from having been fired from the little hill on which the French posted themselves when they left the house. The blood gurgled from the wound at every exertion he made to speak. I asked the surgeon what he thought of the man, and that gen- tleman whispered, "It is all over with him." He said he had done everything he could to stop the blood, but found, from the situation of the wound, that it was impossible to succeed. The dying soldier, on being laid down, held oat his hand to my friend the Captain, which was not only cordially received, but pressed with pity and tenderness by that officer. "Sir," said the unhappy man, gazing upon his Captain with a look such as I shall never forget—" Sir, you have been my best friend ever since I entered the regiment—you have been every man's friend in the company, and a good officer.—God bless you I You saved me once from punishment, which you and all knew afterwards that I was unjustly sentenced to. God bless you r Here the tears came from his eyes, and neither the Captain, nor any one around, could conceal their kindred sensation. The poor sufferer resumed—" I have only to beg, sir, you will take care that my dear wife and little ones shall have my back pay as soon as possible ; lam not many hours for this world." The Captain pressed his hand, but could not speak. He hid his face in his handkerchief. "I have done my duty, Captain—have I not, Sir r " You have, Tom, you have, and nobly clone it," replied the Captain, with great emotion. " God bless youl—l have only one thing more to say." Then addressing one of his comrades, he asked for his ,haversack, which was immediately handed to him. "I have only one thing to say, Captain," said the, "I have not been very well this week, Sir, and did not eat all my rations. I have one biscuit—it is all I possess. You, as well as others, Sir, are-without bread; take it for the sake of a poor grateful soldier—take it—take it, Sir, and God be with you I" The poor good-natured creature was totally ex- hausted as he concluded; he leaned back—his eyes grew a dull glassy colour—his face still paler, and he expired in about ten minutes after on the spots The Captain wept like a child. Few words were spoken. The body was borne along with us to the wood where the division was bivouacked, and the whole of the company to which the man belonged attended his interment, which took place in about two hours after. He was wrapped in his blanket, just as he was, and laid in the earth. The Captain himself read a prayer over his grave, and pronounced a short but Impressive eulogy on the merits of the departed. lie showed the men the biscuit, as he related to them the manner in which it had been given to him, and he declared he would never taste it, but keep the token in remembrance of the good soldier, even though he starved. The commissary, how- ever, arrived that night, and prevented the neces- sity of trial to the Captain's amiable resolution. At the same time, I do believe that nothing would have made bins eat the biscuit. This is no tale of fiction: the fact occurred before the author's before the author's eyes. Let no man, then, in his ignorance, throw taunts upon the soldier, and tell him that his gay apparel and his daily bread are paid for out of the citizen's pocket. Rather let him think on this biscuit, and reflect, that the soldier earns his crust as well as he, and when the day of trial comes, will bear the worst and most appalling privations, to keep the enemy from snatching the last biscuit out of the citizen's mouth. It is for his countrymen at home that he starves—it is for them he dies.

div.head: ABOUT HELIGOLAND
div.p: ABOUT HELIGOLAND

BY WALTER ARMSTRONG. In the "English Illustrated Magazine," for August, price sixpence, there is a capital article on Heligoland, from the pen of Mr. Walter Armstrong. It is admirably illustrated 'by Mr. Hamilton Macallum ; and, as the subject is of special interest at the Present moment, we append a number of extracts. Heligoland was taken from the Danes in 1807; when Napoleon's "Continental system "was in force, It lies about twenty-five miles from Cuxhaven, in a direction north-west-by-west. The colony consists of two islands once united by a bank of sand and gypsum. The larger, or residential island, as I may call it, is about a mile long, by a quarter of a mile wide at its widest part. In superficial shape it is a triangle, with one short side and two long ones. The northern extremity is almost a point, and the total area is less than a quarter of a square mile. It is built—as I feel inclined to put it—of a loosely compacted red rock, and the slightly undulating plateau which forms its summit varies from about one hundred and sixty to more than two hundred feet above the sea-level. On.ts south-eastern coast —if one may use such a woa of Bitch a scrap of land—there lies at the foot of the' otherwise un- broken cliff, a small ledge of sand on which the lower town is built. This acts as an apology for a port. A mile away stretches the long low bank of white sand which the Germans and the Heligo- lenders know as the Dune, and the English as the Sandy Island. Here the water shoals very gradually, and affords perhaps the best seabathing in Europe As for statistics, the population live on fishing and the profits made from the summer visitors. These swarm in to the number of from tweive to fifteen thousand 'every season. The average yield of the fisheries is about £7,000 annually, lobsters, of which about 30,000 are taken. each year, counting for a considerable share of the total. The average dura- tion of life in Heligoland is said to be over sixty- three years, and there can be no question of its mar- vellous salubrity. The permanent population num- bers about 2,200, and the revenue touches the respectable sum of .Cll, 715, ,or considerably more than £5 per head. The fascination of Heligoland lies in what is done for it by the sea and by its own isolation. No one should go there who cannot be content with the charms of brilliant light, of ever-changing atmos- pheric effects, of a land free from the 'countless discomforts of a large and busy population, of a life almost childlike in its simplicity, and of an air which tastes like draughts of life itself. Heligoland was a British possession for eighty- three years, but few English went there. When its cession was announced the other day, the chief person to feel aggrieved should have been Mr. Ham- ilton Macallum, for whom the island had been a storehouse of subjects for some years. The B.eligo- lenders talk an unwritten language of their own, a sort of Frisian, which some linguists declare to be neither more nor less than Anglo-Saxon. The annual influx of German bathers has compelled. them to add German to their repertoire. Had the example of Mr. Macallura been more largely follow- ed or anticipated, they might have learnt English instead. Life at Heligoland is like nothing so much as life on board an enormous but motionless ship. Prac- tically everything in the place is brought from the mainland. In an ill-lighted byre seven or eight cows are kept, about the same number as might be stowed away en an Atlantic liner. On the Oberland a flock of about 150 sheep exist on the scanty herbage and on imported food. The ewes provide a certain amount of milk, and one of the quaintest sights of the place is that of a girl acting as dairymaid, while her grandfather, or some other antique male, stands at the animal's head and holds its ears to keep it quiet! Not long ago the surreptitious milk- ing of a sheep by a jady who was not its owner caused a great sensation in the island. The daring thief was brought up before Captain Campbell, the "H. M.," and in spite of a pathetic and public offer qi twenty-five shillings, not as compensation but as a bribe, was sentenced to six weeks of prison ! Like a ship the island has to be provisioned; like a ship it is kept serupulously, clean. There is a tra- dition that an English smuggler once rode urthe " treppe " on horseback and frightened an old woman to death, but no horse has been there in historic times. The main street has 'a brilliant cleanliness that not even Broeck can rival, for in the North sea there is no dust. Within the last year or two a lift has been contrived, and is a boon to those to whom the steep climb to the Oberland was too much. Otherwise all locomotion must be done on the feet or in boats. The national costume of Heligoland is very pic- turesque. The women wear a red petticoat with a border of yellow silk, a bodies, and apron of brocaded silk, a gay kerchief folded across the breast and a jaunty little silk cap with a border of old Flemish lace and long brocaded silk ribbons hanging down almost to the foot of the petticoat. Many costumes like this are still worn, especially among the middle- aged and elderly women. The younger ones are unfortunately beginning to prefer bad imitations of Hamburg fashions. The men's national dress is now very rarely to be seen. It consists of a ribbed velvet coattee With square tabs round the skirt, breeches oi the same material, stockings, and buckled shoes. The men are very handsome and tall ; the women are pleasant-looking, of medium height, and grace- ful both in shape and movement. The life led by summer visitors to Heligoland is eminently one of routine, one day repeating another, with the exception of stets er two, when a special programme' is gone through. The German who comes for hi cure rises early, has coffee and rolls in his lodgings, and then sallies out to buy his bathing ticket, which also franks him for the ferry-over:to Sandy Island. Ticket in hand, he makes his way to the pier and there embarks in a boat. These boats , are allowed to carry eighteen people under sail and twenty-two when rowed. They have each a crew of six men, and so well built and well managed are they that no serious accident has ever been known to happen to them. The mile of sea is soon negotiated. A landing is effected by means of a sett of jetty on wheels, and then the passengers divide according to sex, the females turning to the left and the males to the right. The bathing takes place from movable machines, very small, very green, and mounted on the largest of wheels. These are run down into the water and dragged up out of it by women, sturdy girls in a loose white costume which is allowed to lt aarkgee i wt hciht ea nhcoeowd si t hi nts ht eeawd a vofe s .d oTohres mo ancthhi en es isdlei etc:. wards the sea. The separation between the sexes is not conducive to any such display of pretty cos- tumes de baits as one sees at a • French or Belgian watering place, but brilliant colours are so popular that the crowd at a distance looks like a bank of flowers. One curious feature of bathing at Heligo- land has now become much less common than it was. The ladies from the more remote parts of Germany used at one time to have a curious preju- dice against bathing othersvise than in the costume of their mother Eve! According to the "Vossische Zeitung," when Heligoland has become German it is intended by German naturalists to use it more than hitherto for scientific examination, as it offers considerable opportunity for studying special problems, especi- ally in minute life in the sea, now so important to biology. Zoology, and particularly the knowledge of bird-life, will be much furthered by study in Heligoland. Then the island is regarded as an important meteorological station, and as likely to assist medical inquiries regarding climate.

London and Paris will soon be on speaking terms. There has been talk for several years of establishing telephonic communication bebween the two cities, and now the work is in hand. A new cable is being laid between Dover and Calais for the purpose. It is about time that the two greatest capitals of the world were united. It is long since Paris spoke with Brussels, and Lyons, and other towns twice as far away as London. ft was not the distance that caused the delay, but the Post Office which raised difficulties. Had our Govern- ment owned the telephones, London and Paris would have been connected long ago.

Are the white gloves ',which it is customary to present to our judges on the maiden assize intended to be worn, and, if so, is any care taken to provide their lordships with a reasonably good fit? Lord Coleridge's observation at Mold, "I am much obliged to you, ram sure, and I will make it a point of wearing them—if I can," may have referred to the fact that white kid gloves are not much in fashion now. On the other hand, it may be that the High Sheriff has taken a hint from that contractor tor police boots in a provincial borough who chose for his standing model the biggest foot in the force, so as to make sure at least that "they could all get 'em on."

Queer tales are being told about the cause of the revolution in the Argentine Republic. Itis •alleged that the head of the Government has during his administration "made "five million pounds sterling besides his salary, and his subordinate 91inisters have had their pickings in proportion. British capital has been poured into the country like water. Trade has been stimulated, and a condition of arti- ficial prosperity excited, of which the present bloodshed is the ultimate result. Much of the capital sent to the Argentine has been judiciously invested. But I imagine it will be found that a great deal haS "stuck " to the itching palms of politicians, and that many worthy people will wait for dividends in vain.

When the Emperor William was in Norway re- cently, and when the Germans were reading, the official intelligence that he was directing the naval roanceuvres, it now appears that for four nights he was salmon fishing with an Englishman named Byron, who has the fishing rights on a Norwegian river. William was only:accompanied by his valet. It would be inconvenient to have a crowd around when salmon fishing, but think of the danger of the great young man in going out unprotected ! Why, the Englishman might have pushed him into the river, or he might have slipped on a atone and fallen in himself ; although this latter danger was very improbable, as emperors, just as kings can do no wrong, can never make a slip.

It is no secret that the Queen would gladly have dispensed with the Emperor William's visit, which happens, for many reasons, to be peculiarly incon- venient. The Emperor is to arrive at Cowes next Monday afternoon, and he will dine with the Queen at Osborne, where there is to be a "family dinner" to welcome him. There is no fleet now at Spithead for the Emperor to inspect, but he is to spend a day at Portsmouth Dockyard, and the squadron regattas will occupy another day, and it is probable that he will visit the fortifications at the needles. The Emperor is to leave on Friday morning for Wilhelm- shafen, unless he reverts to his original plan, and goes to Edinburgh to see the Forth Bridge, in which case he would embark at Leith on the Hohenzol- lern.

Lord Jersey, who has been finally fixed upon as the new Governor of New South Wales, is a War- wickshire landowner and the senior partner in Child's Bank. He is also the proprietor of 43sterley-park, a stately suburban residence close to Southall, famous for its trees and garddn parties, which take place regularly every Saturday during the season, and whereat many social lions do congregate. Osterley came to Lord Jersey through his grandmother, who was a daughter of Lord Westmoreland and grand- daughter and heiress of Mr. Robert Child. A torrespondent writes apropos of the Rol/ad statue :—ln the travels of Thomas Watkins, A.% F.R.S., I have come across proof which you may like to record, that the great philanthropist, John Howard, was both a vegetarian and a teetotaller. Dating 28 July, 1788, from the Greek island of Zante, Mr. Watkins says at page 169 of letter xxxi.: "We were visited by Mr. Serjeant, the English consul. From him I learnt that the last of our countrymen who visited this island was the great philanthropist, Mr. Howard, whose simplicity of manners and extreme abstinence (for he subsisted on bread, fruits, and tea) astonished all who knew him. They were surprised that a man of his fortune should come in a merchant ship without even a servant to attend him."

There is a great deal of interesting anecdote and just a touch of Carlylean frankness in Mr. Edward Marston's article, "How Stanley wrote his Book," in the August" Scribner." The page boy, for ex- ample, who handed in a telegram was in danger, we are told, of having an inkstand thrown at his head; and Mr. Joseph Bell, who illustrated the book, is accused of "excessive verbosity." Of the any good letters sent to Stanley on his return perhaps this is the neatest :—" Right glad am I that you are once more in a civilized country. I have care- fully watched your proceedings from the time you discovered Livingstone. You are a brick! Now, if you are inclined to sell the cap you wore through Africa, I am prepared to give you a fancy price for it to add to my collection of curiosities; it shall he preserved in a glass case with your name on same."

Wz must now leave the troopsTbefcre Delhi and come hack to Bombay, where all was bustle and confusion. Any reader can imagine for himself or read the journals of the period if he wishes to picture the state of things in ;;India;at that time. Our way is over the sea. A fine " troopship " was making her way to England with invalids, civilians, wom,en, and children. The dreadful massacre, but alas only the beginning of it, which had already taken place had induced all who could do so to send their near and dear ones home. But though many devoted English women elected to remain and share their hushand'i lot for better or for worse; though many with true self-sacrifice waited to hear news of the loved ones,

tidings which never came to some of them; ladies with children who had arranged to leave India betare the mutiny actually broke out, left for England in the first available vesEel. The _Durham Castle was a fine specimen of her class, and she made her way bravely homewards, dashing the salt spray from her handsome bows, and leaving a long white track behind her in the heaving sea. . . _ _

All:the conversation l turned upon thClate out- break. Would England ever be able to send out troops in time? Was the Peninsula for over lost tb us? Could we conquer the Sepoys ? Some croakers said not. But then they were civilians as a rule, and did not all appreciate the eirctunstances nor the tenacity of the British soldier. Amongst the passengers in the cabin was a lady who attracted considerable attention. Her husband was known to be engaged against the rebels in a superior command, and hcr opinion was listened to when she could be induced to join in the convera- tion at table. 2. She was tall, with fine features and aristocratic bearing and manners. But she was evi- dently in a very delicate condition, and nailing but sheer necessity, she declared, would have induced her to undertake the voyage at that time of year, and in her then condition, for she was expecting a baby to be born by the time the vessel reached England. As the voyage proceeded, the doctor begin to eet very anxious concerning her. The trial of leaving her husband in danger and the uncertainty of the voyage, the chances of storm and tempest, all weighed with him as likely to affect the sensitive mind of his patient, for she had been particularly committed to his care. "Do you think I shall be ill before we" reach England, doctor ?" she inquired anxiously, one lovely evening, as she sat upon deck beside her friend. "I have no maid, and am terribly anxious." "My dear madam," replied the doctor, "we must not permit ourselves to have fancies; it is very wrong, and, believe me, unnecessary. But even if the un- expected were to happen, I can promise you an ex- cellent nurse." " Really !" exclaimed the lady, as if a load' had been removed from her mind. " Yes ;" he replied, "so you need be under no apprehension., I must myself leave the ship at the Cape. I regret to say, but I will take care that all arrangements shall be made for your comfort, and my successor is a very competent practitioner." But the services of the successor were not so greatly required. It fell out that a bad storm came on, and the Durham Castle was in considerable danger for some time. Nothing but the steadiness of the crew and the marvellous self-possession of the captain prevented a panic. The wind lulled, and subsided to a moderate breeze, and the proverbial calm succeeded the storm. How beautiful it was! Scarce a ripple upon the rolling ocean, whose great hunch-backed " swell " pitched and rolled the fine ship like an immense cork upon the glassy surface. Everyone, including Mrs. Deane, came upon deck and enjoyed the freshness of the evening after the confinement of the cabins, which, with the scarce appreciable change from the state,room, had for three days been the sole retege of the passengers. What has happened? There is a movement for- ward.. The mate dives suddenly into the second-class cabin,, and then hurries up—the boatswain pipes a peculiar call—the crew hurry up with consternation visible in their faces. Some make for the boats and unloose the tackling; others drag an indiarubber tube across the deck and man the pumps. The ship must have sprung a leak. The passengers crowd together upon the quarter- deck. Those from forward—soldiers' wives and invalids—mingle freely and unreproved with the wives, and widows of officers. One poor woman, with a tiny new-born babe at her breast, excites much sympathy, and Mrs. Deane endeavours, to comfort her, but the young woman is not very responsive. Have we sprung a leak P Is there dangerr." "Is there land near?" "Shall we be saved, sir ?" "All is lost, all is lost! Lord, have mercy, on These were some of Uwe exclamations which rose as the crew were passing and repassing, but no answer was returned except to the last observation made by a young man. Ile was told in very decided. if not profane, terms to hold his tongue, or he would be " chucked " overboard to the sharks for,a lubber This gentle hint had the desired effect, fOr he, sub-!: sided and was heard no more. No; it was not a leak: The ship was on fire ! How, no one knew,,and no one could imagine. Whose fault it was will-never be lenovvind suppose, for the unhappy men wha were suspected ,of having caused the tire by rank disobedience have passed away, and will never be arraigned before any earthly judge or commissioner. The smoke which came driving up tlfe fore hatch. way now rendered aU concealment useless as well'ae dangerous. Death faced the passengers -by fire or water. How could they hope to reach land so manse., many miles away ?•f How could all r attempt to, escape in the boats?, It certainly appears every eurioueefact that chips, upon whose boats so-many hundreds, of -'lives- :mem e- times depend, should' be so ill-furnished with means of safety. A few life-buoys and a- few beasts- capable of holding; perhaps, on-half 'of the re- gistered complement of passengers,- are the only , provision made fen succouring life at sea if accidents , happen. Besides these: inadequate applittnees thu piCaid is I generally enhanced by the unprepared condition off even the few boat; fit for service,. That they eshouillh be required suddenly is apparently the.vary Last 1 notion that enters the sailor mind. Neatecoveringa I and webbieg; everything fixed securely initas plane.; ' probably one pair of oars to a.boat requiring sin; te, propel it, will be found with ae very nciacellarneolae collection of things (fowls amd sheep) in, the. boats intendechfor usa in sudden and terrible-emergency. The Durham Castle was certainly amexcepeione in some respects-4e the far too general rule of unre-adi- Mess of the beats. She had not sufficient Reconvene- datiomfor all her crew and passengers, but hen-'boats were not encumbered with odds and ends, amd the oars were forthcoming.. AA/or and, a- ve* 'trying time was occupied in castieg them Those' arid had not the see,been fortunately smooth. on the. murface, much doss of life would have oceuered. The fire had broken oat in the foro part of the shipeand; the captain's first care wasth sat the vessel before the wind, a coLese which, not only bad the advantage of putting her head to land,,huh,the gentle breeze drove the fire away from the qmarter-deck where all the affrighted passengers luta tgathered. Darkness had rapidly fallen upon thee sea, and the passe.2gers strained their eyes in oreCkavoming to. pierce the gloom beyond the- glare which was now becdming stronger.. The heat, too, began to be. inconvenient, and the terrified W 0 314al and children were huddled together while the men endeavoureelts assist the crew. .e P The boats were at length launched, and the sailors answered to their names. The:- was no confusion —no crowding. The women were put into. the boats first, and Mrs. Deane, with seem of the second tabin passengers were pat snider the champ Of the doctor and the clergyman en board. But while this was being done, and while the crew were working with a will to subdue the flames, the foremast and rigging had caught Ere, and all was burning fiercely. To make mat tern worse, the wind gave notice of again shifting, and also of rising to a strong breeze, so before .the Durham, Castro could be got round, the llamas-came leaping aft, and the terrified passengers, who, remained on deck, were huddled together likeeheep. It was a grand yet fearful sight, this great burae in ship—a beacon upon th e w'a sto of waters, dying as it were at sea. Her living freight as helpless almost at the time as the ship herself there was little chance of escape unless the sea remained calm, and of- that there was not much probability. At length the foremast fell with s tremendous crash, and, a cry of anguish lose ifkudly as it was

Sir Charles Russell has been haymaking at Tad- worth Court as well asother courts. The other day he might have been seen in his shirt sleeves and sombrero, perched on the iron Seat of the cutting machine, gathering in the crop one Sunday morning, resolved to make his hay while the sun shone. ' '

The Duke and; Duchess of Connaught and their children have gone down to Osborne to relieve Princess Christian in her attendance on the Queen. The Duke and Duchess are, it is said, writing an account of their Indian experiences, taken from the long weekly letters they wrote to the Queen. The book is td be illustrated by the Duchess, who took many hundred sketches during her stay there. She is a very good artist.

It is officially announced that the Duchess of Fife is " quite convalescent," but I am sorry to hear that she looks wretchedly ill, and people who saw her last week were painfully struck by, her wan and delicate appearance. The ,hurried departure of the Duke and Duchess for Scotland was due to medical advice, and it may be hoped that the highly bracing air of Braemar will soon restore the Duchess to her former health and strength.

I remember finding myself seated for several days at a table d'hôte by the side of a very agreeable German. I took it into my head that he was the head-waiter of some hotels on his travels. When he was leaving he told me he inhabited some town (I forget now its name) and invited me, if ever I came there, to look him up. "Certainly," I said, What is the name ,Of the hotel where you are ?" Ido not live in an hotel," he replied. I live in 'the palace, for I am sovereign of the country.

perceived to lean backwards. It fell a mass of flame upon the ,smoking deck, dashing sparks in all direc- tions, and worse than that, bu ying in its fiery • embrace some of the passengers and crew. The shrieks and cries were awful, and horror set. on every face. " Same them—oh, save them !" screamed the poor affrighted women. But no one could do anything then, and the captain, still unin- i-ured, gave instructions for the boats *, already loaded to steer off and keep aivay, ;for there was danger of the powder on board. , The boats pulled away from the ship, and we shall follow the fortunes of, but one of them. By a curious coincidence it ontained! the doctor and his most in- teresting patient. for whom he now experienced the greatest anxiety, • There was another woman who , also craved his attention—a pretty fee() with a some- what fierce and defiant expression; a face with firm. - nese and passion curiously,blencted. determination, Yet softness. This young woman carried a tiny baby in her arms asnd appeared listless and lost in thought. She was sitting next the lady We have men- tioned, and observed her closely. With a woman's quickness she divined the situation, and said some sympathising words,, which were kindly and .gra- ciously responded to. -Each of their natures went out to the other for a moment, but only for a , moment in one case. . .

The doctor addressed the lady in whom he took such an interest with professional courtesy, and, we may add, with professional anxiety. "We are sure to gain land soon, Mrs. Deane; somewhere about Natal, I' suppose. The second mate tells me that in three days—"

"Three days! Shall we have to remain in the boat three plays ?" exclaimed the poor womanu ",Oh, doctor, I shall never survive it ! ' "Three days!" murmured the you mother. "What may not happen in three days "441 wonder what is happening in India?" she continued. "Is ,your husband in the service, madam?" .
"Yes," replied Mrs. Deane. "He commands the fort at Komptor. Are you the wife of a soldier,
" Lwas," replied the woman. "My husband is dead. And yours— Pardon me. Is be the Celonel Deane who executed the rebel: Sepoy by blowing him from the .gun, about which we all heard so much?"
"Yes, Colonel Deane' had condemned the poor wretches to hanging, but the authorities altered the sentence."

'Serve them right," broke in the doctor. "There • is no language too strong for them. So your husband was killed by them too ?" he added, sympathetically, to the young woman with the baby. "No," she replied. 'He was murdered by his friends—shot—by, order of a court - martial for coming away-from his regiment without leave, and ' But never mind me," she added, "I shall be revenged. God'knows howl pray for it!" Mrs. Deane, perceiving how affected she was, said no more. Few had heard her speech, or noticed the • sudden change in her manner; but there was -a wildness in her )demeanour that gave/ one the im- pression of incipient insanity, and her thoughts just then were anything but good.' Mrs. Deane, the wife of the detested officer, who had scorned i her, was here in the boat. Now was- the time for vengeance. As night gave way to morning the woman nursed : her child, planning how she might best achieve her object. Under the silent stars, with only a narrow plank between her end eternity, this " warped" • nature could only think of venseanee, forgetting Hini who, has declared " 'V engeance is mine."

A ,man, had Lifson bathe hexed the boat, and was extendieg his,b,andi.. He bad perceived something—wasdt land? He was too exhausted to articulate freely- His dry and painful throat and tongue =fused to =ewer to, his will; but ,he pointedeend the haggard faces looked gaunter veld cadre terrible in their expeetancy than ever they ,had in the lethargy. But it 3V3S hind—the low shore couldhe seeneanti ceinfortecl the unfortunate sufferers. If the wind held they woul,dedoubtless, seem reach the longed-for:shore, and some of theaess exhausted in the boat made feeble efforts to row. That they helped a little was evident, and ell the castaways now plucked up courage and eat up. The land was near but locked forbidding 4 Still it was land, andianyone,ethelaa been. away fromshoreflongwillunderstanCltb.e delig ht in again. touching ground which the occupants of the boatse experienced after all the dangers they had escapeek All these were now forgotten. in the delirium of i treading upon terra fiima, The steonge t of the parts itumediately went, along the coast in search of food. Others, and: amongst them Mrs. ,Deane .an& Mrs. Layton, wile, remained to comfort each othez a little if the word; can be-used to describe suckietercourse where there was no sympathy, There was no water left, on board, and in the little rtieelett the poor thirsty, famishing creatures, bathed their faces and drank luxuriously. Some crabs were found, and eaten raw and: alive, devoured without; a thought of cooking, When several of the largest had been thus disposed of, languor again, asserted its sway, and sleep came creeping upon. all. But the doctor and the state, with some of the most willing of the. sailors, managed to haul the boat up and turn, it over against a rock, tinder this temporary shelter the womeaa were accommodated for the, night, and it is woncieeful to remember how they bore the perils and sustained their courage amid the strange and 'terrible sur- roundings. The zeeollection of these few days appear now like a chapter of the Family Robinson snore than the sober reality I know it bo, have been. Poor Mrs. Deane Isere up wondeefally, but a sad time fox-her was at hand. OeA A- Lucy Layton, appeared strangely absorbed. She was at one time in boisterous spirits, and as active as a man. At ether times she wouldesit nursing her babyeboy, and crooning over it like .an old womens rather than a young one. Again, she appeared thoughtful and calculating, and would converse, at tines with Mrs. Deane, but, never mentioned her husband. When he was spoken of, her eyes flashed au4 her hands clenched; even in her misery she was nursing her revenge. On the second day Mrs. Deane was taken Rh It was a terrible time for her. But enmity was en- tirely 'mit aside in Mrs. Layton's breast, and she tended the poor lady tenderly. The doctor,' was so prostrate he could scarcely do anything, but his ad- vice was followed, and the anxious day passed away. 14 The little child was born, and cried and mingled ita tiny treblewithtliebassof the breakers on the beach, end Mrs. Layton saw the child—a pretty little girl— and tended it. The poor razther was in a very ill plight. She was max her death: so near one day

tints even the rough sailors left old play and qu ,rrel —to thent much the same--to ask how Madam was, and how the child was getting on. Mrs. Deane was very ill—delirious—and lamy tended her for very shamerbut plotting in her heart. In the delirious ravings of the apparently dying mother many things were said, and revealed to the unscrupulous nurse a way to have revenge. The property would all descend to an heir; the child, as yet unrecognised by its mother, was a girl. The. temptation came, and was admitted. Lees* change the children. My boy shall be the heir of all the proud estates—the girl shall be .my charge instead, and I shall then, through him, control the fortunes of the future Deartes ; aye, better still, shall stab the father in a tender place, when all his
love is centred on his heir! This- whisper came to her at night—almost audilly it seemed to her-Las she sat gazing on the moonlit beach and scanning the sea, whose never-eeming surf

keep booming on the shore. But how to effect the exchange? Her own child would' never pass as Mrs. Deane's while on that shore. The doctor would know them even. No; the doctor, had been there but once, and never inquired for the child. He was ill, poor man, and, some said,. dying. The clergyman was asked, and had been put aside at ence. Nothing easier should the mother not yet recover: and if a ship would only come how well it might be done! • And so she thought and planned all night, and nursed the children underneath the boat turned bottom upward on the beach. Two pretty mites they were, these babes—both very small and fair, with dark and dark-blue eyes and dimpled arms and rounded cheeks, though pare just then—bnother and sister they might be as yet; and so Lucy' pondered even as she nursed the heivess, and, watched her ,baby sleeping.. The morning dawned, and still she sat and gazed in dreamy lUngi.'ng o'er the sea. Of a sudden she started , up, and. with :a piercing scream roused the sailors and the other men at once. The doctor, rushing from his-hut of boughs, was running head.. 'Ong to the sea • He was mad—the.fever had, seized him in its full embrace—and; ho • was mad! Ere they could stop him he had rushed to the rocks, which were high above the swirling sea. Throwing his arms aloft, ha cried, out t " Help ! 'help/ sail r. ai sail t Hurrah!" He leaped into theefeaming breakers and was seen no more alive. For one brief second his head was visible in the foam and then he sank to be torn in pieces -bythe shirks which crowded round the ; LueyLaytoro heaved m deep sigh. "Poor man!" she said, despite herself, and 'then a rushing flood of thought came fultupon har.braim. The last objec- tion to herplais had been 'removed. The doctor dead she had nothing more to feart The children would be . chinged,land her revenge-would he accomplished. But the.poor maniac's cries had directed attention to the sea; and yonder, hearing dawn with sails all set,' her sang at full froire, truck- to taffrail, comes a full-rigged ship,. the Brltleh ensign streaming from the peak. They came nearer and nearer. A yell; of joy and weltome went up from all assembled on the shore. Hands were waved, oars . were,' spliced and lifted up with handkerchiefs for • flags,-,and ;cheer after cheerwas given for the ship. The clelrgymave amongst the rest was wild as any ,- schoolboy, and ran up and down upon the shore ; within a,smal/ space as if he had hit a succession of ; sixes at, a cricket match and was running them all out at once. The noise and cheering- lad long ere this . awakenediMrs. Deane, who feebly inquired the cause otall the uproar. She had then recovered her faculties, and Lucy noticed her collected manner mid her lowing gaze as /frosted on the child. "Give.. nue my baby,, muse," cried the poor mother, "-How can I' ever repay you—tell me. Yes; there then, my darling. Come, give it to me-- quickti.lS itt a boy or gisl.?-,;1 hopo--- But which is, it P—tell me. ' Lucy pretended not IQ hear, but the question could not, be ignored. Now or never was the time. A sigh escaped her, buteshe rose, and taking up the A spletalid boy—an heir for the colonel, worthy. 'of 'his-parents, I'll be bound ! " "A\ bey! Oh, ',nurse, lam so glad. Colonel 'Deane will be delighted. My boy, my beryl," And; the poor lady,,clasping the baby.boY, fell,; .backwards on the rough. couch which ,had been ex- temporised for her use. In at few hours afterwards the survivors of the Durham Casa, were taken on board the homeward- hound! ship which had pic,ited up another boat, and came oruising on the. chance so near the shore on whichithe rescued people had gained a footing. Thus Lucy Laytonthad succeeded in her plan,seel, clasping the little girl in her arms, Om went ,on board the ship defiant and expectant. Perks, tht hon. secretary of the Privileges -Committee of the Wesleyan Conference. . A number of,. leading mem- bers of the Wesleyan community werednviteek to meet the ra4) hon. gentleman there being:present, Mr. Isaac Holden. M.P., Mr. A.W.L-irAhur,M.P.,Mr. S. Di. Mr. Gladstone,, on rising at twentv-five rainutes past nine o'clock to, reply, was receivail with loud cheers. In responding to the toast o`a his ktalth the right hon.. gentleman spoke at some length. CO Sir Lintern Simmon'S. mission to the Vatican. Ha-said that though the Year,' was probab.-^yi too far gone for vex), effective discussion of the Maltese question at present, yet in the comi* session in alh probability the matter would call for a good deal of attention. He thought he had got a glimpse la the papers which had been pubrashed of the reasons toF the arrangement which had been made with the Vati- can. The Papal Rescript against the Irish Nationalista demand a return, and we had now got the retort! before us., The Irish members felt that Ireland. was- being Oven up as against Malta fox the purpose of ginbaS the Court of Rome an equivalent for the favour it did. to Her Majesty's Ministers la months ago. Referring to the remarkable charge of Mr. Justice Harrison, Gladstone said he did not believe that a search througll the Irish newspapers: for 13 years could producea declar- ation that had passed the lips of any Nationalist one" tenth as dangerous. as the words which had fallen from ths.lips of this judge.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mosmer. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a *, quarter past four. Thu LIVERPOOL BILL.--This Bill was read a third time,

and passed. LORD SALISBURY'S DUAL CAPACITL—Lord STRATMEDEN • and CAMPBELL called attention to the result which has followed the connection of the duties belonging to the First Minister with those belonging to the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, .and moved for precedents, but the Marquis of Salisbury having given an explanation, the motion was withdrawn. trzB ApveNcsn.--Several Bills were advanoed. The House adjourned at 6.30. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. BUBNOS AYRES.—Sir J. FEW:MESON told Mr. Maclean ' that the, Government had received a telegram from Buenos Ayres stating that the revolution was proceeding ' nthat place on Sunday, but owing to an armistice hay- ' Mg been subsequently agreed to till the following morn- ' lug, the town was then tolerably quiet. '''lFavain BERMITDA.—Mr. BROUWER informed Mr. Banbury that six men had been in hospital in Bermuda, suffering from enteric fever, but that every precaution 'would be taken as to the health of the Grenadier Guards. 'THE CONSTABLESHIP OF CARNARVON, CA—Mr.. W. SMITH informed Mr. D. Thomas that the appointment `414 Sir J:. Puleston as Constable of Carnarvon Castle was fanade by the Queen, on the recommendation of the Prime Mirdster. Sir Joim PULESTON, in answer to another question by the same hon. gentleman, said there was no truth in. the statement that he had appointed the ,Con- servative agent for Carne.rvon Boroughs his deputy con- - -stable. .

House Bracernee.—Mr. JACKSON told Mr. H. Pewee That the Government did not intend to give effect to the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Horse Breeding that the sum disposable for Queen's premiums should be increased from £5,000 to £lO,OOO. . James Ilanarsoe's CHARGE.—Mr. Balfour read another letter. from Judge Harrison, in which his lordilepetated that no member, neither of the bench or the bar, would , for retirement entertain the belief that he had., directly or 'indirectly, defended the use of illegal methods for the re- dressof privatowrmes, however intolerable these wrongs might-beeble.'W. H. Sures declined to give Mr. Dillon an opportunity to further discuss the subject. Pastitehr, or Terrors. —Mr. SMITH told Mr. S. Leighton 'that there had been no organized resistance blithe pay- 'tient of tithes in Montgomeryshire for the last three ' Years. Trut-AvetteGenrese Biree—The Anglo-German Agree- 's:trent-Bill, after some discussion, passed through, Corn- mittee, -was reported, and read a third time. -Sovety.—TheHouse then went into Committee out the -Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Duties Bill, and :111r. CkmpNrEeL BANNERMAN moved that £90,000 be -devoted to the relief of fees in,„Scotch elementary schools., 'instead of tlete£4oooo set apart for that purpose in the Bill. Th(ediecussion was continued until twelve o'clock, When according to the rules of the House the debate was adjourned. The House adjourreel at 12.16. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUBSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at half-past five. , BILLS ADxmccup..—The. Elementary Education (Blind and'Deal) Billepassed through Committee. The Settled Land-Bill and the Court of Judicature Bill were readathird time. The-Statute Law Revision (No. 2) all•was read a.seconcl time. Ammar, cotoree'e Deverserox.—Lord SMILEY asked Her Majesty's Government whether Admiral Colomb had accepted the £2,4100 which Lord Elphinstone, on behalf of the Admiraltyesaid recently had been granted him for his .invention. Lord ELPHINSTONE said he was un- able to reply to the question, as there was some cones- Pondence now passingon the subject. The'House adjourned at five minutes to six. HOUSE GF COMMONS.—TIIESDAY. The (Speaker tookthenhair shortly after three o'clock.: Quectereess.—Mr. :John Barry was the cause of the only little stir that relieved the heaviness of the ques- tions. He called upon the Home Secretary to allow two membetenf Parliament' tog° down to Chatham for the Purpose eif receiving from the convict James Egan a statement upon .a matter of "life and death." Mr. Matthews calmly mentioned many ways in which pri- soners cottld make their-complaints, and laid down the rule that "wither members of Parliament nor other" out Riders" entald be alloweddo investigate matters of prison discipline. There was a little laughter when Sir Jorns GORGE, answering Sir Wilfrid Lawson as to the fate of a deceit leader, calmly observed that the statements of the ." Times' " correspondent at Rangoon did not " generally commend themselves for accuracy to the Secretary of State." Mr. Atkinson was sadly disappointing, for although lie endeavoured to promote the encouragement of butter-makine in this country .and to secure religious liberty in Tonza he failed to raise even a smile. SCOTCH EDUCATION, &C. Even the telegrams from 13ueuos Ayres were unin- teresting, and the possibility ef agreeable agitation on _any topic, had become extremely doubtful when Mr. '.llaartioeuisexii urged the Government to reconsider their eettitude towards the scheme foa,applying the new duties to free education in Scotland, in view of the fact that 42 Scotch members had voted for the proposal, and only 14 against it. The Opposition rousectup and cheered men- tally, but Mr. Serra frigidly replied that the Govern- Inent could not change their views. A minute or two having been bestowed upon a certain Foreign Jurisdiction (Censolidation) Bill, sent down from the Lords, which nobody cared for or understood, and for which the Attorney General easily obtained a second reading. Committee was resumed upon the Local Taxation BIS' and the battle began again over Mr. Parker's attempt to Prevent the £40,000 applied by the Bill to the relief of , school fees from being limited to the compulsory stand- ards of the Scotch Code. It became by degrees a very spirited contest, the Chancellear of the Exche- quer tageng the place of the Lord Advocate in resist- Thg of ScOtland, and Me. Buxton and Memdella striving to assist the Scottish zepreseutatives from the English point of view. Sir GecrgecCampbell highly resented the indifference of ' the leader.ef the House to Scotch appeals, and moved to report progaw for the express purpose of bringing him 'back again. Mr. Smith, however, came in •at the last :moment, foNewed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, 'and was greeted with a burst of derisive cheering which 'Considerably astonished him. His presence being secured, 'the division was not taken, but Sir L. Playfeir and Sir iWilliam Harcoret successively applied their arts of per- -"suasion to the rigirt hon. gentleman. The controversy was 'renewed, but without effect, for in the end the amend- Stent was negatived by 132 against 97. Later eflorts to beitag Ministers to-season were equally futile, for, As Mr. hunter said on their refusing further amendmente, the 'Government, Bettina up what they thought was a stiff- baels. Sevcral amendments were 'leak with, and ,Sir WILLIAM fIARCOURT complained Zronglv of theconduct of the Government in the matter wards Scotland and its representatives. On the appli- Zion ef the closure 6Ra/A of the Government proposals agreed to without a division. The discussion was v4l-inued on other point st and at five o'clock progress teported. t,.II4I€4CELLARRO^S.—The 2/11CS Publication Bill, which for committee, was withdrawn.—The order for p"e gecood reading of the ltlaintenance of Destitute alents Rill was discharged, and the Bill was Withdrawn. exslr. Jackson brought in a bill to continue varioUs wPiring laws, and it was read a fast time.—Baron H. de orms laid on the table the report of the committee on "17 ..Merchandise Marks Actsb -the House adjourned to twenty minutes to six o'clock. The HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. Lord Chancellor took his teat on the woolsack it ft minutes past four o'clock.

itiCELLANEOUS. —The Earl Of MEATTI gave notice of a question with refeience to an -explrcted influx of Jews into this country. The report of thb amend- ',writ to the Companies (Winding Up) Bill was received, as also was the report of amendment to ,the Elementary Education (Blind and Deaf) Bill. The Earl of Mani moved the second reading of the Physical Education in Elementary Schoola Bill, which proposed that no school should received a grant unless 'physical education was carried out to the satisfaction of the inspector. The bill was withdrawn on Lord CROSS stating thatAhere was no possibility pf passing it this -session. The Shrewsbury and 'Holyhead ..taglesey and 'Carnarvon) Bill passed through committee. The House adjourned at tens minutes past five 'o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. . .

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clook. QuEmma, &c.—Mr. SEXTON asked the Chief Secretary for Ireland whether he would introduce a Bill allowing lappeals by persons sentenced by Irish courts of summary jurisdiction to terms of imprisonment of one month and I under. Mr. BaLroun replied that legislation was im- possible usder existing circumstances, and denied that he had ever given instructions to magistrates in the exercise of their duties. Mr. CHAPLIN, replying to Mr. Howell, said the Board of Trade was considering regula- tions to prevent the suffering of cattle in the passage from America. Mr. Sartrumade a statementon the order of business and the intentions of the Government. Tax GOVERNMENT AND THE VATICAN.—A series of questions arose out of missions to the Vatican, and Mr. GLADSTONE complained strongly of Mr. T. Russell not having given him notice of a question addressed to the First Lord cf the Treasury respecting Sir George ,Errington's mission in the time of his (Mr. Gladstone's) Government. The difference between Sir George Errington's case, said Mr. GLA.DSTONE, and that of Sir Liatorn Simmons was that the former had no power to commit the Government upon any subject, or to receive requests or demands from the Vatican.—Mr. CAVENDISH-BENTICK followed with a question based on a reference to the Papal receipt against Nationalists in a speech made by Mr. Gladstone eighteen months ago; but the SPEAKER said the question was one I which the:Under Foreign Secretary ought not to be called upon to answer. , POST OFFICE, &C.—Other questions had reference to the speed of the new cruisers and .the precedence of Cardinal Manning, after which the House went into com- mittee on the Local Taxation Bill, which passed through committee after a number of amendments had been dealt with. The House afterwards weht into Cenamittee of Supply on the Post Office estimates. In the course of the discussion Mr. Samuel Smith made tin appeal to the Postmaster-General on behalf of a new Zest Office ;forLiverpciol, and referred to the manner in which Post dilffice . employes were frequently overworked. Mr. RAIKBS replied on the various points raised, and, refer- rim, to Mr. Smith's appeal, did not deny that the Post Ogee at Liverpool was inconveniently situated, or that the buildings were badly adapted for the purpose. He should be glad if he could see his way to find a better site and provide better buildings. An amendment moiled by Mr. A. Connor to reduce the vote by £lOO, as aprotest ,against the actiori of Sit A. Blackwood at a meeting at Exeter Hall, was negatived by 185 votes against 64. Just before midnight the vote was agreed tor as was another for the Post Office Packet Service. At midnight progress was reported, and the remaining Orders having been disposed of, the House adjourned at five minutes past Ofle.

div.p: MOCKING iDEATIf OF A CARTES.

THE INQUEST.—" GROSS INHUMANITY:" At an early hour on Saturday morning, Thomas Moran, employed by Mr. Ramsden, butcher, Knotty Aah, was found to have met his death under shook- ing• circumstances. Moran, and another man itamed John Mercer, in charge of a two-horse lurry, set out from one of Mr. William Bennett's farms at Padget°, oviththe .carcases of seven cows which had ibeeu slaughtered owing to pleuro-pneumonia having Ap- peared among the stock. ,On Saturday morning. at au early hour, the lurry wascliscovered at Bold with the shafts'broken and tied together with rope, and. ! Moran in &dying state from exhaustion, consequent ' upon loss of !blood., It appeared that both of his legs had seen broken by the wheels of the harry passing over them. The only account Mercer could give of the affair was that be remembered Moran falliag,out of the lurry.soinewhere between Mar- -1 rington Bridge And Sankey Bridge, and saying, something like,'" Oh, I'm hurt; take me to the Royal Infirmary." Moran's age was ,obout thirty-six, and he resided at Bilch-lane,Knotty Ash. On Tuesday morning Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy t coroner, 'held an inquest at the Black Horse Inn, Farn-! ' worth, tenchingthe death of Moran. John Mercer said he was a farm labourer, and lived at Rainhill. On Friday night they were removing some carcases of cows to Liverpool from Padgate. They left Padgate at 10.30 p.m„ and went by way of Bold. On the way, they called at the King and Queen Inn, and had some drink, 'but they were both sober when they left the house. 'Deceased got on to the wagon, and witness walked withthe horses. It was dark andraining heavily, but he could see the deceased wii6i3 he looked back. When in Liverpool-road, Warrington, he heard a shout, land on looking back, he saw the deceased lying on the road. Witness went back to him, and the deceased said "Take me to the Royal Irrfirmary, Jack.' Witness got help, and placed the deceased on the wagon, and continued his journey. The next time he saw the deceased was when the shafts of the wagon broke, and Moran again said "Take me to the Royal Infirmary." The shafts broke when he was coming down the hill at Sankey. When he arrived at Bold Heath, at about 4.45 am., he got a young man to pull deceased higher up the wagon. The young man said it would be better to get some one to see the deceased, and suggested that he should call on the policeman, who lived close by. He (witness) did not do so, but kept going ahead, and, when at Lunt's Heath he got the wagon into a hedge. When he got it out, a man named Houghton, who had helped him, looked at the deceased, and finding him dead, sent fir the police. Abraham Bates, 17, Wright-st., Sankey, said on Saturday morning, about 1.15 a.m., he was going to- wards home when he saw a body lying on the Liverpool- road, Warrington. He touched it with his foot., and found it was the body of a man. When witness touched him, Moran said, "Oh, is that Jack?" About two yards further en, there was a lurry and two horses standing, and a man came up to him from the lurry and said, "Mate, will you give me a lift with this man on the lurry, as he is drunk, and the wheels have gone over his legs ?" He helped to put the deceased on thelurry,and the innired man said, "Oh, Jack, send for a doctor, my leg is broken." Witness went along the road with the driver, and the deceased continually asked for a doctor. When witness left them, Mercer seemed capable of what he was doing, and was sober. He told him to go back to the Infirmary, and offered to take or direct him to the place. William Prescott deposed that he lived at Bold, and while at Bold Smithies on Saturday morning, about five o'clock, he saw John Mercer coming from the direction of Warrington with a lurry drawn by two horses. The driver said, "Get on the wagon, Walter, and pull that man into the middle of the wagon, for he is fast asleep." Witness did so, and noticed that Moran appeared to be asleep. He saw a cut on Moran's hand, and asked Mercer whether or not the deceased had fallen off the lurry, and Mercer replied do not know." Witness told him he had better go and fetch a policeman, as he thought the man was very near dead. Mercer said" I will go and knock up the blacksmith, and get plates on the broken shaft." Wit- ness left them to go to his work. Mercer complained to witness of his ankle. He was Clo.lo to where a policeman lived, and the officer had only just gone down the lane. Merser seemed perfectly sober. George Goddard, Lunt's Heath Farm, said on Saturday morning, about 6.15, Mercer came to him for a horn. On going outside, he noticed something was wrong, and Mercer, in reply to his questions, said the deceased had fallen off the waggon and got run over. Witnes3 glt on the wagon, and examined the man and found him dead. He at ante sent for the police. Mercer was sober, but walked lame. The Coroner, in summing up, said that Mercer's story was correct to a certain extent, as there was no direct evidence to the contrary. Bates tried to persuade him to take Moran to the Infirmary or the sergeants'; notwith- standing this Mercer took the deceased on the lorry and paid no further attention to him until he ran the waggon into a ditch or hedge and broke the shafts. Even when told by Preserrtt to take the dying man to a neighbouring constable, Mercer 'did not do so, but drove on for another two miles until he met Goddard. It was for the jury to say whether this abominable conduct, this most gross cruelty and inhumanity on the part of Mercer in omit- ting to get aid when it was at hand, was tantamount to manslaughter. Mercer, recalled, said he did not know they were near the Warrington Infirmary, and on Bates' evidence being read over to him he said he did not remember being told where the sergeant lived, although he admitted having told Prescott that he did not know if Moran had fallen from the waggon. After some further remarks from the coroner, the jury returned a verdict that death resulted from the fall, ac- celerated by exposure consequent on the grossest inhu- manity on the part of Mercer.

Cholera has been declared epidemic in Mecca, eighty deaths ow:wring daily. - The Duke of Cambridge left London,on Thursday morn- ing. for the Continent, proceeding first to Bonn and Coblentz, where he will inspect the 28th Regiment of the German Army, of which he is honorary Colonel.
