div.head: EXAMINER, SATIJRDAN, AUGITST 2, 1800
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATIJRDAN, AUGITST 2, 1800
THE CRESdIRE POLICE INQtIRY:
THE CHIEF CONSTABLE EXAMINED.

The public inquiry into the charges made against the administration of the Cheshire Police by Mr. Slater Lewis, was resumed at Chester Castle on Saturday, before his Honour Judge Sir Horatio Lloyd and the othpr members of the Special uom- mittee. Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, appeared for the police, and Mr. Lewis had the legal assistance of Mr. E. Brassey.

Sergeant John Gosling, who was stationed at Runcorn in September, 1889, deposed that on the night of the 24th of that month he took three men from Runcorn to Norton to assist inintercepting a gang of men who were seen in that locality. Four constables and Inspector O'Donnell were left on duty in Runcorn. Inspector O'Donnell came out to Norton later on, and found witness and his men in the road with gamekeepers. O'Donnell pro- posed to, goon the land and drive the gang off. Wit- ness protested against going, and took is men back to Runcorn, telling O'Donnell that he would not go on the land for anyone. Witness had taken part in intercept- ing poachers on several occasions. The only time wit- ness had gone on land was at Bostock, in 1382, when he apprehended one of a gang of poachers who assaulted a constable who was standing on the road. Witness had been warned by his superiors against going on private land after poachers. Cross-examined by Mr. Lewis.—He entered the duty he referred to:as.ratchingJor;suspicious characters, and not for poachers. He did so by orders he received 16 years ago, and he had always done so since. When they were watchingSor prizefighters, which they had to do often at that time, he also entered that as watching for suspicious characters. Mr. Lewis again appealed to the committee to allow the letters which had been written by Superintendent Egerton to ex4nspector O'Donnell to be put in as evi- dence. If he had gathered. from the committee that Superintendent Egerton's letters would not be allowed to be put in as evidence he should certainly have with- drawn from the.case._ . . . .
Mr. Fletcher strongly objected to the admission of the letters. ' .

The Chairman, after consulting with the other mem- bers of the committee, said they would allow them to be read, or such portions as Mr. Fletcher and Mr. Lewis might think necessary. The Hon. Cecil T. Parker, agent to the Duke of West- minster, appeared to contradict statements that had been made in reference to the police watching for poachers on the Eaton estate. One of the witnesses said the spot where the police were watch* with the keepers at Platt's Rough was three quarters of a mile from the pub- lic road; whereas as was shown on the map, they were on a public footpath. Instead of police being there thir- teen nights they were not there more than three nights, and they never watched on the land at all. They were always on the highway. There was only one occasion on which the police and keepers joined forces, and that was by accident. Neither the Duke of Westminster, himself, nor the head keeper, had the slightest idea of r this taking place. Sergeant Morgan was so thoroughly ashamed of not haying taken the poachers when they passed close to him, that he made a compact with the keepers to keep the affair secret, and it led been most religiously kept secret until this inquiry, With regard to leepers and police matching together, if it ever had been done, it had been without the sanction of the Duke, himself, or the tkaddreeper. By Mr. Fletcher: The Duke of Westminster pays for three constables, two for night duty round the house, and one for day duty in the park. Henry Garland, head-gamekeeper on the Eaton estate for 17 years, said he could not regall a single occasion when the police had been matching with him for poach- ers on private land. He was never with Sergeant Morgan at Platt's Rough, and be never saw Sergeant Morgan in the night. He was not out with policemen for thirteen or fourteen nights. He did not-supply hay bags for the officers. _ . . . . _

By Mr. Tomkinson : Eft had noknocvledge that Police- -constable Metcalf had been watching with the keepers tor' a month. The Chairman! You swear -solemnly that you never heard of this until you saw it in the newspapers the other day P--Witness : No I never heard a word of it. 'Wm. Morgan, assistant keeper, said he did nbt know of any arrangement between the keepers and the police for watching at Platt's Rougis. Crocs-examined : He remembered the policemen watch- Mg, part of a week there, but they were-on the footpath. It wastrue that Constable Meisalf one night was lying agaiust.a tree with a hay bag on his feet. He got the hay bagfrom witnesses' house. Witness neVer heard of rugsnbeirg provided for the keepers or the police. He never heard of this watching with Morgan and others being kept secret, except on the occasion when the poachers appeared on the scene. That was kept qUiet because Sergeant Morgan and a keeper Named Shave were too faint-hearted to catch them. (Laughter.) , By Mr. Temkinson : He did not think POlice-sonstable Metcalf was watching for morg, than two nights. He certainly was not there for a ibonth together. Robert Youd also deposed to Sergeant Morgan and Shave letting-the poachers pass without attempting to arrest them, because, as Morgan said, they were armed with a pikel, and he thought about his wife and family. (Laughter.) 'lt was untrue that Metcalf watched with witness night after night for a month at Platt's Rough. , The Han. Cecil Parker said in another anonsunous letter put in byleir, Lewis it was said that •the :police were supplied with cottages on the Eaton estate. That looked as if they got the cottages rent free, but the 'fact

was that the policemen employed by the Duke paid rent • for the cottages. By Mr. Lewis: The Duke of Westminster paid £l7 10s. a quarter for each of the coxstables he employed. • Police-constable John Hulse deposed that he and three other constxbles were on duty in Runcorn on the night of 4he24th September,lBB9, when thepolice were called out to watch at Ntktonk Police-constable George Carrington corroborated, and i said on one occasion O'Donnell, n the coupe of a con- versation with him before he left the force, said he would trouble the chief-constable as long as he could hold a

pen. Superintendent Large, who was under examination when the committee adjourned at the last sitting, was further examined. He said when he handed ex-Inspector O'Donnell a general order regarding Inspector Walker being promoted to Superintendent, O'Donnell stepped back from the office desk and said the Chief Constable was a—fool for promoting old Walker over him. Witness intended reporting that to the Chief Constable, but he was away from home at the time. O'Donnell gave out an order amongst the men that everything that occurred was to be reported to him before it was report- ed to the Superintendent, and said if that was not done he would report the men for neglect of duty. O'Donnell did that in consequence of witness having detected a robbery which O'Donnell ought to have detected. He was present at the inquiry which was made on the re- port of Constable Bullock, and O'Donnell told hint that in future he would not obey any orders given by witness. Whenever O'Donnell spoke to the constables he always cursed, Since O'Donnell left the force the magistrates had convicted on the evidence of two constables, while previously they would not convict on the evidence of five or six eonstables. During the thirteen months witness had been in Runcorn twenty-three informations were laid against publicans. Ten cases were dismissed, and in seven of these the informations were laid by O'Donnell. During that time there was no undue drunk- enness amongst the police. The men in every respect discharged their duties satisfactorily. There was no ground for saying that there were any irregularities existing among the police. On the night the constables were at Norton there were four constables left on duty at Runcorn. He re- mained on duty himself. He did not sanction O'Don- nell's going to Norton. The entry in the policeman's journal "watching for suspicious characters was not intended to mislead the Government inspector. He knew no reason why the word "poachers" should be left out. He instructed the men not to go on private land, and to keep away from gamekeepers. The Clair of the County Council (Mr. R. Potts) here read a letter written by O'Donnell to the Chief Constable after his dismissal, giving notice that he intended appeal- ing to the Joint Committee against the chiet's decision, complaining of the treatment he had received at Run- corn, pointing out that he could not help his religion or nationality, and alleging that the cause of the superin- dent, magistrates' clerk's assistants, and some of the men under him wishing to ruin him was that he was a total abstainer. Mr. Large, he further alleged,,could be found many evenings after nine playing billiards in the Devonshire Hotel. Superintendent Large said with regard to the accusa- tion that he was to be found at the hotel mentioned, it wasa tissue of falsehoods, and he was prepared to call a switness to show that. The Chairman said the committee accepted his ex- planation en the matter. Cross-exinnined.—Mr. Ashton told him the magis- trates had lest all confidence in O'Donnell. The magis- trates used to impose fines of Ms. and costs in cases of drunkenness before O'Donnell came to Runcorn but while he was there they reduced ,the fine to 2s. eci. and costs. Since O'Donnell left they had returned to the old fine of 10s and costs. Witness reported to the chief constable that O'Donnell never addressed the men with- out using oaths, and the chief reduced him. Superintendent Large said he should like Mr. Lewd' to ask him a question with reference to the allegation that he paid 8100 for his promotion. He did not pay one penny, but got his promotion through hard work. Mr. S. IT. Sandbach said Police Constable Metcalf had said that :he had been watching for a whole week at Handley covers. He was prepared to prove that that was not the case. William Jackson, keeper to Mr. Sandbach, was then called and denied that Metcalf had ever watched for even an hour with him. ' Thomas Clarke. keeper, and William Oakrey, butler to Mr. Aldersen also dewed the truth .of Metcalf's evi- dence. Superinteadent John Plant, who has served for twenty- one and a!half years an the Cheshire police, was next called, and asserted that he was never applied to by the Duke of Westminster or any other person in the Broxton 1 Division for men to watch for poachers, nor had the gamekeepers asked the police to assist them. When the police were watching for poachers they. were really pro- tecting the property of the inhabitants m the district, as poachers were notorious thieves. Supte. Leightomof Altrincham, andelindley, of Wirral, gave evidence of a similar nature, the latter stating that it would be impossible to carry out the poaching preven- tion act without massingStbe constables. The committee retitled at this point to consult together, and on their return to the room, The Chairman saidthey had come to the .unanimous decision that they did not require to hear any further evidence. if Mr. Lewis desired to put any question to 1 Colonel Haniersley, the thief constable, he might do so. After that Mr. Lewis could address the committee on the whole case. He could also make use of Superin- tendent Egerton's letters in examining the chid con- stable.
CHARLOTTE'

Colonel flamersley was then examined by Mr. Lewis. He said O'Donnell—if he might use the expression— poisoned his mind against Superintendent worth. Be made accusations and innuendoes, but never lodged any absolute charge against him. The innuen- does were to the effect that Hollingsworth was not a sober man, and he did not doubt O'Donnell's word at the time. He placed implicit trust in him, and in fact it was mainly upon his word that the case went against Hol- lingsworth. Witness was called to Runcorn continually during the time O'Donnell was there, as the place was in a turmoil. He was not prepared to say that O'Donnell would have got on better with a strictly sober superin- tendent, because he quarrelled with Superintendent Large, who was a man of very equitable temper. Further, when O'Donnell was at Birkenhead he told his superior, Superintendent Hindley, that he did not care a— for him or any other superintendent, as there was no one between him (O'Donnell) and the Chief-con- stable. 'That was not reported to witness until a con- siderable time after it occurred, else he would have instantly reduced O'Donnell. Witness sent O'Donnell ts Runcorn not because the town was in a disorderly state, but because he considered O'Donnell a more active officer than Millington, whom he succeeded. He looked upon Superintendent lollingsworth as ;a very good su- perintendent, and he had come to the conclusion now that all the squabbling at Runcorn was caused by O'Donnell. - Addressing the committee,ColonelHamersley said it had i been stated n that room that a letter had been written by one of the superintendents who was afraid to take any action in the proceedings. He had had an assurance from all tha 'superintendents that not one of them had written a letter of the kind. Mr. Lewis also said he was very glad that some of the constables had clean sheets. He had had the records of the whole 387 men examined, and out of that number 212 had not a single report of any sort against them. That was a very high per centage. The examination of the records also showed that for being under the influence of drink on or off duty 20 men were reported in 1887, 29 in 1888, and 20 in 1886, making a total of 69 reports against 60 constables. Of these 21 had been discharged, which showed that drunkenness was not tolerated in the Cheshire constabulary.
The inquiry was further adjourned until August 26th.
ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday morning,. a middle-aged woman named Louisa Mainwaring, of Rodney-street, wife of a 'bus pro- prietor, was brought up in custody on a charge of having tried to take her life by drinking a quan- tity of laudanum. She appeared to be in a dazed condition on taking her place in the dock. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt), in telling the particu- lars of the affair to the magistrates, said that the prisoner had for some time been addicted to drink. On Monday afternoon she sent one of her children for two penny*orth of laudanum from a druggist's shop, and sent another child for a similar quantity from the shop of another druggist. Soon after- wards she was found to be in an unconscious state, and was taken to the Infirmary, where she was attended to by the doctors. He (Mr. Hunt) was of i the opinion that the woman was scarcely n a fit state to plead. Her husband, however, was anxious that she should not be locked up any longer. The prisoner had been drinking heavily, and what she had done seemed to be due to her mind having been upset. When asked to say what explanation she had to give for her conduct, prisoner said that she lived very unhappily with her husband, and would be better in her grave. The magistrates, consider- ing her condition, remanded the poor woman to the Workhouse fora week. THE BOROUGH JUSTICES' LAW QUESTIONED. I At the meeting of Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, Mr. Ward, the workhouse master, reported that he did not know under what law the order com- mitting Louisa Mainwaring was given, and he should be glad to know if be could legally detain the woman under such an order. The order was signed by two of the borough justices—Mr.E. M.Crosfield and Mr. R. Garnett —and ran as follows—" We,the undersigned, two of Her Majesty's justices of the Peace for the borough of War- rington, do hereby order Louisa Mainwaring, of 25, Rodney-st., Warrington, to be detained in the Warrington Union Workhouse hospital for a space of seven days." The The CLERK could not say under what law the order was made, and be pointed out that in a case of this sort the workhouse master must act on his own responsibility. If he detained a person on such an order as that brought under their notice and the order turned out not to be legal the workhouse master would not escape liability.— Mr. SHEARER (relieving officer) said the order was not a proper one.—Mr. WARD said if the woman had not been admitted before he saw the order he should not have accepted it, and be should now tell the woman that she was at liberty to leave if she desired, and he should also inform the chief constable of the view he took of the order.—This course of action seemed to meet with the approval of the Guardiar, and the matter then dropped. Louisa Mainwaring was again brought up yesterday on the charge of having attempted to commit suicide. The Chief Constable said that the woman was now much better, and her husband was wishful that she should be released. The magistrates admonished her, and then allowed her to go. She left the court with her husband.

PETITION TO THE WATCH COMMITTEE. The members of the Warrington police force, or a large proportion of them, are asking the Watch 1 Committee of the Town Council for a re-adjustment of their hours of duty. With the object of drawing the attention of the Committee to what they con- sider to be in the way of grievances, the men drew up and signed a petition that was, on Monday after- noon, considered by a special meeting of the Watch Committee. The petition was as follows "Police Station, Warrington, July, 1890.—T0 his Worshipful the Mayor and gentlemen of the Watch Com- mittee. Sirs,—We, the undersigned constables of the Warrington Borough Force, beg most respectfplly to lay before your worships, for your consideration, the follow- ing proposals with respect to the arduous and tedious duties we now have to perform, and trust that your worships will be able to learn from the same that a r3vision of ourduties is most anxiously needed cad required, viz. : First, that a day's duty consist of eight hours, instead of nine hours as at present, viz. : First relief, 6 a.m. to 10 a.m., and 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. ; second relief, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., and 6 p.m. to 10 p.m., thus allowing us to finish duty one day at six p.m., another at ten p.m:, the present system being first relief six a.m. to nine a.m., one p.m. to five p.m., and six p.m. to eight p.m.; second relief nine a.m. to one p.m.' and five p.m. to ten p.m., thus allowing us not the least opportunity of the slightest enjoyment and recreation, especially so in the case of not a few of us, who live a distance away. Second, that we be allowed one day's leave of absence per month, in addition to seven days' annual leave, as in the case in all the neighbouring boroughs and cities, namely, Liverpool, Manchester, Wigan, St. Helens, Chester, Birkenhead, Southport, and many other borough towns. Third, that we be Rllowed time off when attending Court, as formerly, when on night duty, being often detained there for two or three, and sometimes four, hours, no time being allowed except in cases of felony, when one hour only is allowed. Fourth, that Park and Cemetery duty be done by day duty men, or the full time allowed off night duty for the actual duty done on Sunday afternoons. Fifth, that market duty be treated the same as Park and Cemetery duty on Saturdays and Wednesdays, namely, the full time allowed off for the actual duty done, instead of the present system, namely, three hours allowed off night duty for four hours' duty done in markets; also two hours off night duty for three hours done on Cemetery and Park duty. We, the undersigned, earnestly entreat your worships to give the above petition your full con- sideration, and anxiously hope that you may see the need and aLso see your way to giving us the same.—We are, sirs, your obedient servants." [Here follosr the signa- tures.] The chair was occupied by Alderman Harrison, the deputy-chairman, the other members of the Committee present being Aldermen Chandlev and Sutton, Council- lors W. Pierpoint, W. Bolton, and Edward Greenall, with the Town Clerk (Mr. J. L. Whittle). The Chief Constable (Mr. S. Hunt) was also present, and as any of the men who chose to do so were allowed to go to the Town Hall, whether off duty or on, some twenty-five constables had assembled in the vestibule of the Town Hall, ready to lay their case before the Committee. To shorten the proceedings it was intimated that a deputation of three or four of the men would be received to speak on behalf of the other signatories to the petition, and Constables Hollingsworth, Evans, and Robinson, having been se- lected by the others, were admitted tothe meeting, and presented the memorial, of which a copy is given above. After the memorial had been read, the Chairman cora- -1 mented on the impropriety of theway in whichit had been presented. He thought that it should have come through the Chief Constable to the Watch Committee. In the labsence of satisfactory explanation, he must say that he could only regard it as an act of insubordination, and an insult to their chief. Before hearing them, he must re- quest them to inform the Committee why the usual course was departed from in this instance. It was thereupon stated that the police had presented a similar memorial before through Mr. Hunt, but nothing came of it, and they supposed no notice had been taken of it; but they did not mean any disrespect whatever to Mr. Hunt. Indeed, they much regretted that that gentleman should think disrespect had been intended. On reference to Mr. Hunt's report book it was found that he had made a note of the previous memorial, and had presented it to the Watch Committee, who had decided not to interfere with the existing arrangements. The explanation of the men was deemed satisfactory, although it was pointed out to them that they were clearly mistaken as to the disposal, of the previous memorial. The Chairman then pointed out that the Committee regarded the publication of the memorial, before it had been presented to the Watch Committee, as highly objectionable, and in vain endeavoured to elicit from the deputation who was responsible for the pro- ceeding. He asked the denotation whether they pre- sented their memorial in the nature of a grievance from which they were suffering, because if they did he had no hesitation in telling them that they were out of court and had no case whatever,inasmuch as they had no com- plaint to make. He would ask if the Committee had, either by themselves or through the Chief Constable, departed in the slightest degree from the contract into which they entered with the men when they sought and obtained their respective appointments? Had the Watch Committee or Mr. Hunt sought to impose upon them any additional duties to those they contracted to discharge when they were appointed? The deputation replied in the negative, and in answer to further questions put by the chairman said that they attended to ask forsfavourable consideration of the sug- gestion for some modification of the contract with the Committee as to the terms of service. The men would be perfectly satisfied with the decision of the Committee, whatever it might be. Councillor Pierpoint and Alderman Chandley expressed their satisfaction at the replies, and thought, they were very creditable to the good sense and discretion of the deputation. After the Committee had conferred in private, the chait man told the deputation that the Committee had passed a resolution to the effect that they would confer with the Chief Constable for the purpose of taking his opinion upon the questions which were raised in the memorial, and authorize him to obtain such further information from other sources as might enable the Committee to arrive at a just and equitable conclusion. He also intimated that they must not be surprised if the Committee declined altogether to re-opeo the question, which they had previously considered, and decided ad- versely to their memorial, because if they vséii marleyed they had their remedy. If they were not satisfied' thej' could determine their connection with the Corporation' by peaceghly and quietly giving the legal notice to leave, and acting upon it. The deputation then ret:red. A VIEW OF THE SITUATION.

The terms of the petition, and the summary of the transactions at the meeting of the Watch Committee, pretty accurately describe the state of affairs, so that comment is scarcely necessary. The men have certain requests for an alteration of the hours on duty, and thus approach the Committee, and they emphatically deny the statement that was put on record that they had made up their minds to come out on strike if their demands were not complied with. The idea of a strike, they say, never entered their minds. The alterations they ask for, which include an eight hours working day and the conces- sion of other privileges, are matters that have to be con- sidered by the Committee, but we believe that the Chief Constable, notwithstanding that he complains of the action of the men in not first addressing themselves to him, will be inclined to advise the Committee to grant some portion of their request. Those who signed the petition appear to be in earnest about the matter, but it is a question whether the agitation, if such it may be called, is so deep-seated as some would have it appear. Certainly, they ask for less hours and other privileges, which they have a perfect right to do, but to judge by the answers of the deputation they are perfectly prepared to abide by the decision of the Committee, whether favour- able or not. In this connection, it may be mentioned that the superior officers and older hands in the force have been doing the same duty for years, and that before the appointment of Mr. Hunt in 1866 the force did nine hours duty at night as well as during the day. Soon after his appointment the time-list was revised, and since then the night duty has only been eight hours. The Chief Constable has written to various towns for copies of the time arrangements in force in such towns, and it is probable that the Committee will base a decision in ' aCCOrdallee with the conclusions arrived at aftei a careful persual of these arrangeinen,tstri a comparison tu„e•m• with the regulations eXistieg in ibis borough. In any case, the public May be assured that the matter will receive very caret u 1 attention, the Chief Constable and Committee having an earnest desire that the members of the force shall have no valid cause of complaint in regard to their duties. It may be mentioned that the wages of the police are 255. a week at the commence- ment, and 28s. a week after two years' good conduct.

div.head: WHAT THE "CHIEF" SAYS:
div.p: WHAT THE "CHIEF" SAYS:

_ Mr. Hunt has given us full particulars with regard to the previous petition drawn up by the men. A story having been pretty freely circulated that the reason of the present petition having been addressed directly to the Watch Committee was that a previous one had been ignored, an " Examiner " reporter thought it worth while to inquire more closely into the matter as one hav- ing an important bearing on the propriety or otherwise of the petitioners in not making their wants known to the Committee through the medium of the Chief Con- stable. Waited upon, Mr. Hunt willingly gave particu- lars, substantiated in black and white. The petition was dated October 29, 1889, and, put generally, asked for lan eight hours' working day. It was not signed by any of the inspectors and sergeants, and several constables did not sign. On the receipt of the petition, Mr. Hunt I wrote to Southport and Coventry to obtain particulars as to the system adopted in those towns. The Committee did not sit until the 14th November following, after the I new Mayor had been elected, and at that meeting, accor- ding to the Chief Constable's diary, which is signed by Mr. Francomb as Mayor, Mr. Hunt reported that he had found in his letter box a petition from the constables, asking for a revision of the time of day duty, and he

laid it before the Committee, together with the Warring- ton time lists and those reed'. ed iron'. Southport and Coventry. Following this entry was another to the effect that thi Watch Committee had gone into the mat- ter, and had left the matter to be arranged by the Chief Constable at some future time if it would benefit the public and the police. They thought, however, that the Warrington time was really good. and tha`, the constables suould let well atone, This atter memoran•l' dum was read to the men ou die 15th November, 1560, when on parade. Mr. Hunt added; and proved it by reference to his books, that it lathe custom to ask the men if they have any grievances to complain of when paraded on a Friday, and that these had been no coins plaints. Mr. Hunt says that the men on the whole are very well treated, anddhat they have no cause for com- plaint. He believes that the old policemen are con- tented with their lot, and it is only the recent impor- tations who are the instigators of the agitation. The Chief Constable also explained that the rule in regard to leave of absence from the borough was used as a means of convenience, as it was advisable to know when a constable was out of town. The utmost latitude, however, was allowed, and as a rule all that a constable had to do was to intimate that he was leaving the town for a place specified, and he would be allowed to do so without let or hindrance. In regard to this, Mr. Hunt said, any respectable ratepayer was at liberty to see the leave of absence book, Mad information would be will- ingly given. Any constable desirous of attendii g a place of worship on a Sunday was allowed an hour's time off on intimating in writing that he was going to service.

div.head: 'STRENGTH OF THE FORCE,
div.p: 'STRENGTH OF THE FORCE,
The full strength of the force is 48, made up of a Chief Constable, three inspectors, four sergeants, and 40 constables.
ADJOURNED MEETING OF THE WATCH COMMITTEE.

On Thursday there was a meeting of the Watch Com- mittee to take various matters in connection with the police force into consideration. Alderman Harrison pre.. sided and amongst those present were Councillors Tinsley, Platt, Pierpoint, Bolton and Greenall. The chief matter dealt with by the Committee was the misconduct of several police officers, and after the charges and evidence had been very carefully gone into, and the defence of the inculpated men heard, it was decided to dismiss three constables, suspend one, and fine three others. We understand that the charges had no direct reference to the recent agitation. Chief Constable Hunt had, as requested by the Committee on Monday, obtained a considerable amount of information as to the hours and duties of the police in various boroughs similar to Warrington. He was prepared to lay the information before the Committee, but as the Committee had already sat a considerable time, and as it was deemed desirable that the details should be tabulated, it was decided to leave any decision upon the subject over till the next .meeting of the Watch Committee. We learn that, speaking broadly, it is the opinion of the Chief Cpstable, after seeing what is done in other towns, that the police of Warrington are in as good a position in regard to hours and duties as the police in most otker towns, but it is not unlikely that some modification of duties would be made in order to meet the men's wishes. _

It may be mentioned that indirectly two of the police —Constables Hughes and Bracewell—were discharged in consequence of the agitation, as the Committee dispensed with their services on the ground that they had used improper language to one or more constables who had refused to sign the petition. The other officer, Constable Halstead, was dismissed because of complaints having ro reference at all to the present movement among the men.

div.head: EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.
div.p: EXECUTION AT WANDSWORTH.

George Bowling, 57, labourer, was hanged at Wands- worth Gaol, on Tuesday, for the murder of a woman named Eliza Nightingale, with whom he cohabited at Mitcham, Surrey. They both were addicted to drink, and after a quarrel one nightßowling killed his paramour with a hammer. He has since admitted his guilt. He was allowed a drop of over five feet by Berry, the exe- cutioner. He appeared to die in an instant,

div.head: LIVERPOOL CADET BATTALION..
div.p: A LIVERPOOL CADET BATTALION..

The Queen has approved, through the Secretary of State for War, of a cadet battalion being formed under the provisions of paragraphs 1,082 and 1,093 of the' Volunteer regulations in connection with the Gordon Institute for Working Lads at Liverpool. The battalion will be known as the Ist Cadet Battalion Liverpool Regiment. Its headquarters will be at the Gordon In- stitute in Stanley-rd. The cadet Battalion will be an establishment of four companies of not less than 60 rank and file each, the uniform to be as at present, worn with the addition of an Austrian knot of white, the colour of its facings.

div.head: QUESTION OF PRECEDENCE.
div.p: THE QUESTION OF PRECEDENCE.
LETTER FROM THE PRINCE OF WALES.

The Rev. Dr. Preston, of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, has received the following letter from the Prince of Wales, in reply to a letter respecting Cardinal Manning's precedence :—Marlhorough House, Pall Mall, S.W., 22nd July, 1890. Sir.-1 am desired by the Prince of Wales to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 20th inst., and to inform you in reply that it is quite correct that on being consulted as to the precedency which Cardinal Manning should occupy on the Royal Commission of the Work- ing Classes,his Royal Highness expressed an opinion that, as a matter of courtesy, the name of the Cardinal should appear immediately after his own I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient ser- vant, FRANCIS KNOLLYS. The Rev. Dr. Preston."

div.head: LORD DITLO FAILS TO GET A DIVORCE.
div.p: LORD DITLO FAILS TO GET A DIVORCE.

The respondent and co-respondent in the Dunlo case were examined at great length on Tuesday in the Divorce Court. They severally denied the charges against them, and the case was adjourned at the con- clusion of the evidence for the defence. The suit was concluded on Wednesday, before Sir James Hannen and a special jury. Mr. Lockwood, Mr. Gill and Sir Charles Russell having replied on behalf of their respective clients, Sir James Hamann, in summing up, said the trip which the respondent and Wertheimer took to the Continent would under ordinary conditions point to the relation- ship of protector and mistress, but the difficulty of the present case was that it gave a glimpse into the life of a class of people quite foreign to ordinary knowledge. He did not think it fair to assume that every woman on the music hall stage or who had given birth to an illegiti- mate child was purchasable. Looking at the case as a whole, it was one which under ordinary circumstances would-point to improper relations. But could the jury place reliance on the evidence? The case did not de- pend on what Lord Dunlo said, or thought, or did. He was a mere puppet in the hands of his father and the gentlemen he employed. The result must depend, not on Lord Dunlo's conduct, but on the impression the jury had of the evidence. The jury, after consulting for fif- teen minutes, found that the respondent an,u eo-respon- dent had not committed adultery. rtig lordship there- upon dismissed the oetitir)ns Tfil4 &Sets for Lady Dunlo and tt; When Lady Dunlo, accompanied by her sister and brother-in-law, appeared at the main entrance of the Law Courts in the Strand, she received quite an ovation. There was considerable cheering, with cries of "Bravo. Belle," and "Well done, Flo." The crowd was so great that the cabman who was hailed by the party had :great difficulty in getting clear. .There was another popular dem mstration in the evening when Lady Dunlo's sister, " Miss Flo Bilton," appeared on the stage to do her "tarn" at the Trocadero Music Hall. Lady Dunlo occu- pied a private box. Lady Dunlo stated in the course of an interview on , Thursday that she intended going back to her profession, I while her relations with 111. d Dunlo would depend on : what action he tock. In the course of the interview she. complained bitterly of Lord Clancarty's action, and expressed great indignation at the attempt to disparage. her family by describing her father as "an old recruit-.. lug sergeant in the Royal Engineers," the fact being that her mother was a Miss Penrice, of Kfiverough Castle Glamorganshire, while her auat married a colonel in the Guards.

liNihvay Tux Railway Servants. of St,. seavants,' Helens and, district are,to be emir Demonstration gratulatod, upon the large demon:- straXen. which they held„ on Sunday afternoon,in supßort oi the national, programme for bettering their condition. Mr.. SuoN-Kans, aameirther.fer th,e.borough, was invitted to attend ;;buthet seat a letter of apology which; was anything but sails- factory. He said he. did not wish ‘fas,a rule to I attend Sunday monlings ;" but nobody desired him to make it "a rule;;"'for the occaaionwas,altogother exceptional, seeing: that, according to. his own admission, Sunday, was the only day Upia which such a meeting of. railway semnts could be held. He seems to him yet to lean that it, is, lawful to do good on the Sabbath, andthat the, Sabbath was made for man) and not man for the Sabbath. He professed, WO,, not to know sufficient of the merits of the resolutions; and yet he could refer to the., "reasonable demands and requiremeAts of the way servants." He stsmds condeuvaedin any case.. If ignorant, he should have sought enlightenment, by attending the meeting; if convinced that the. deniands are reasonable, he should have attended to give them his support. The railway workers had a good opportunity of noting a strong point of difference between Toryism and Liberalism, for Mr. KENNEDY, Q.C., the Liberal candidate for St. Helens, not only attended the demonstration, but delivered a thoughtful, earnest, and practical ad- dress. Incidentally, he made light of Mr. SETON- KARR'S squeamishness by saying he felt sure that he could not spend a Sunday afternoon more as Sunday afternoon ought to be spent than in listen. ing to the discussion of a question of great human interest.

attendance. Why should they not go forward, and complete the freeing of the schools, seeing that the money was available for that purpose? The answer to that question is that Tories are not in favour of Free Education—except as an election cry. But they are being found out; they have been corn- Polled to show their hand. They have done those things which they ought not to have done, and left undone those things which they ought to have -done, and there is no health in them.

Warrington THE majority of the members of the police force of Warrington are Police. like their metropolitan brethren in thinking the time has arrived when an attempt should be made to improve their position. They do not ask for higher wages, but for that which they will doubtless regard as an equivalent, namely, shorter hours and somewhat lighter ' duties. They are quite entitled of course to agitate for these things; but, as a matter of f' tactics, they made a false move in not sending their petition to the Watch Committee through the Chief Constable, in the usual way; and it was certainly ill-advised to permit of their memorial being made public before it had ' been considered by the Committee. However, as tO offence was intended in these matters, it is to be hoped that no offence will be taken, and that tile application will be dealt with purely on its ' Merits. If it can be shown that the police of War- lington are in worse position as to their hours and duties than the police of other towns similar to Warrington, it can hardly be doubted that the Watch Committee will make such changes , as will remove the grounds of complaint. • Information on the subject has been obtained, and is being tabulated with a view to guiding the Watch Committee at their next meeting. Speak- , log as outsiders, who cannot be supposed to be iarailar with the "ins and outs" of police adminis- tration, we may remark that it does not seem too Mach to provide, if it can be conveniently done, for each constable being allowed one day's leave of absence per month. All work and no play is bad for "bobbies" as well as boys. Then as to allowing tkae off when attending ;Police Court—that surely • is not an unreasonable thing. Indeed, we must

confess to a feeling of surprise at hearing that attending Court with a view to giving evidence, Say, against a," drunk and disorderly" is treated, ao far as the time is concerned, as if the con- Stable were not on duty. Such an arrange- 'bent is sure to give rise to a feeling of injustice; but it is objectionable, further, as a matter of Public policy, in that it puts a premium on Policemen winking at minor offences. It is "a toss up" in some instances whether to set the 114, in motion; and the police officer my well be • cliBPosed to hesitate when he knows that taking • action may mean spending time at the Police Court which properly belongs to himself. The Watch Committee will, we are sure, take these Points into consideration; and we have hopes that they will see their way, under the advice of ' the Chief Constable, to make the policeman's lot, ' uot a happy one, a little less irksome, at any sate, than it is at the present moment.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

"Speech ' Day" at the Warrington Grammar School has become a popular institution since the public Hall was used for the proceedings. Scholars and teachers have alike "done well" again; and the able, amiable and energetic headmaster has every reason to be proud of the work of the year.

There is to be a " Beamont Scholarship," after all, at the Warrington Grammar School, The pro- vision for it in the shape of £5O per annum is ng made by Mrs. Beamont in memory of her 44te husband. All honour to her; but how the gift shames Warrington which set about providing a 13eamont Memorial, and allowed the movement to Collapse!

The Sultan of Zanzibar lives in fear and tremb- ,4, pg, for he believes his brother has designs upon 'll3 Crown, and he has doubled his guards. Poor f ellow I ''uneasy lies the head when someone has ,4esigns on the "crown." But what about the -unglish protectorate of Zanzibar? Is it a protec- tion which doesn't protect?

Mr. Thomas Beecham remarked, whilst address- Tg the Journalists on a visit to St. Helens, on iaturday, that last year he spent £9,000 in a'arertising, and that this year the amount would not he less than £lOO,OOO. There now! That's a Wrinkle for everybody in trade. The advertising ;which pays is that which is unceasing and creasing.

"It has now been ascertained that the exact esBt of the Parnell Commission case to the `Times' £150,000. This has proved such a heavy drain PO the resources of the establishment that economy 18 the order of the day." If we may make a sug- .leBtlen, we should say that economy in "lying and 'aildering" will be best alike for the reputation 44d exchequer of the "Times."

Dr. Byrne has, we understand, resigned his post S resident snrgeon at the Ship Canal Hospital at atchforcl. " Society" in Latchford is quite con- ,seerned at the event; and if he should leave this Art of the country, as is likely, there will be quite t flutter amongst the dovecotes, for the doctor . was regarded as a bachelor who might soon he- Collie benedict. "There 'a many a slip betwixt 'll and lip."

tillhe Government leave refused to give Mr. Dillon opportunity of moving for an inquiry into tho 4,llRllage of Judge Harrison, who talked about iYoch law" in Ireland as if he would like to see it Pplied to the Nationalists. There is nothing, to 15/e sure, the Government dread so much as in- quiry ;" and it is quite in keeping with their usual ttolicy that they should back up their backers in -Ireland—especially when they are in the wrong.

-- It is „ actually intimated that the House of Lords 1111 u give judgment in the Bell Cox ecclesiastical 'ase on Tuesday next. And yet there are people tull living who remember the commencement of :4141 trial. Really if the authorities in the eccles- iaatical courts hurry themselves in this way, they 11143' break down through over-exertion ; and then Ilbat would become of us all ?

ba:When George Stephenson was asked in Corn- tee of the House of Commons how it would be Cow got on tho line when hislocomotiye was ap- liTaching, he said, in his broad way, that it would ue a bad thing for the coo." On Monday after- a passenger train from Bourne to Sleaford ton into a flock of sheep near Bourne Station. The numbered 120, and a number of animals were th' to pieces. In this case it was a bad thing for sheep.

It isn't everybody who thinks that all outrages .rareland by " Moonlighters " have their origin 133-11 the National League. Speaking with refer- to a case heard the other day, at Cork tt,les, Mr. Justice Holmes said :—"Even taking O• greatest enemy or fiercest denouncer of the 4 atie.nal League—unless he was a person n a 011uatic i asylum, or fit to be there—was there any- olle living who thought for a moment that the go was promoted by the National League ? "e idea was perfectly absurd." The

the 0- world moves in cycles. Here is a list of • vh ceupations of certain noble French families Oh ave come down in the world :—" Game- r, carpenter's apprentice, house painter, cab-. vert miller's assistant, inn-keeper, conductor of

an omnibus, box opener at a theatre, gasman, bathing-man, maker of mouse-traps, chorus-singer at the opera, and woodman." Some of them may think the fates hard on them ; but they may console themselves with the reflection that as Workmen they have a better title to respect than they would have as Idlemen.

It is an ill-wind that blows nobody good. Whilst the Corporation of Warrington were lamenting the failure of the extension clauses in the Borough Bill the Guardians of the Runcorn Union were, on Tuesday, rejoicing thereat. We have heard of one lively Councillor who wondered how it was that the bill had been Whittled down; but if he will prose- cute his inquiries we are rather inclined to think it will be found that it suffered through Brooks pouring too much cold water on it. There is no denying, at any rate, that a "burgess" was on the job; that "money made the mayor to go," and that there has been "long din' about it.

Some of the ladies of Richmond have been con- verted, or transformed, or sublimated, into Prim- rose Dames, and yet they are not happy. There has been so much "friction" that the "Grand Council " laps "withdrawn the warrant "—which means that they have not even "a local habitation and a name." They have been suppressed—just as if they were a body of "Balfour's Criminals." Indeed, it may turn out that this I:ttle bit of "coercion " has been carried out under the direc- tion of the Irish Secretary, who was announced the other day as Marshal of the Gra-ad Star of the League; the Primrose League—not the National League.

The Bishop of Chester has been saying a sensible word about dancing in connection with:the Chester Girls' Friendly Society. It seems basket mak- ing has been substituted for dancing at one branch ; and the girls were said to have preferred it. But did they really, now? However, the Bishop doesn't think it wrong for them to dance under proper supervision and control. "Until," he said, "they were prepared to introduce basket making into London society as a substitute for dances and balls' he was not prepared to accept it as a substitute for balls amongst girls of other classes." Very well put ; the Bishop has, in this instance, taken Dr. Johnson's advice) and cleared his mind of cant.

Twenty thousand people joined in procession at Manchester, on Saturday, to accord a welcome to Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., and Mrs. O'Biien. The demonstration was in every way worthy of the city. Mr. O'Brien said:—" The last time he was surrounded by a rather different escort. He did not think that it was a very brilliant testimony to the success of Mr. Balfour's coercion policy in Ire- land that a man who was brought through the streets of Manchester as one of Mr. Balfour's criminals should find himself traversing the same streets now amongst signs of welcome and of en- thusiasm as marvellous as ever stirred the heart of a great English city." The Irish Secretary will of course sneer at this ; but his sneer will not obliter- ate the lesson which it teaches.

Lord Dunlo has not got a divorce from his music- hall wife; but he has assisted nature in making a fool of himself, and brought more discredit upon himself and the Clancarty family by going into court than he did by marrying a woman, who,what- ever her failings is in almost every way his superior. What a revelation is the trial of the ways of our young aristocracy! They ought to be set to work— on the treadmill—till they are equal to earning a living. As for Wertheimer,—well there is no say- ing what he is; for has not the jury decided that he was not guilty of adultery with Lady Dunlo, notwithstanding a score of elements of suspicion? His conduct, we are asked to believe, was, as Bryon has it, _
—just a little innocent flirtation; Not quite adultery, but adulteration.
LOCAL NEWS.
IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES-.

At the weekly meeting of this society, on Sunday after- noon, Mr. Howlin presiding, a resolution of sympathy with Mr. John Dillon, M.P., in the attack made upon upon him by Dr. O'Dwyer, Bishop of Limerick, was un- animously passed.

The annual services in aid of the choir fund were held on Sunday last, and good congregations assembled both morning and evening. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. John Simpson, the pastor, who in the evening delivered an eloquent discourse on "The Ministry of Music." An enjoyable feature of the services was the admirable singing of the choir, under the leadership of Mr. J. Clough, who also presided at the organ.

THE INCORPORATION QUESTION AT WIDNES. The. T. P. O'Connor Widnes Branch of the Irish National League have forwarded to Mr. F. H. Gossage (chairman of the Widnes Local Board) a resolution passed by them in favour of the incorporation of the town. Mr. Gossage, in a letter to the secretary acknowledging the receipt of the resolution, says it is his intention to bring the matter forward at the next meeting of the Local Board. The meeting will be held on Tuesday, the 12th inst. MAIL DARTS for ehildren.—Garland, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestovrn.—Advt. FOUND DROWNED AT WESTON POINT.

_ At Weston Point on Thursday, the body of a man Un- known was taken from the river Weaver by Charles Bowyer, a boatman in the employ of the contractor to the Ship Canal. There were no marks of violence on the body, which is that of a man about 25 years of age, with black hair. The face is clean shaved. His clothing con- sisted of dark striped trousers and vest, and he had no shoes or stockings on. In the pockets were is. aid., a knife, a pincushion and several visiting cards. BATHS. all kinds,—J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge Street, Warrington, Branch—Barleatown.—Advt,

MILTON CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES. The anniversary of the establishment of this school was celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev. C. Chandler, of Liverpool, preached two sermons to good congregations. In the afternoon the service of song entitled, " Little Maggie's Mission" was rendered by the choir and scholars under the conductorship of Mr. J. P. Streets. Mr. .1. T. Jones played the accompaniments on the har- monium. The narrative was read by Mr. T. S. Swale Collections were Made in aid of the school fund.

A WIDNESIAN FOR THE MINISTRY. Mr. John Peter Streets, son of Mr. William Streets, wheelwright, Birchfield-road, has received a unanimous call from the Congregational Union to enter its ministry. He was recently examined for a studentship, and passed with distinction, obtaining the highest number of marks possible. He will enter upon his four years training in October next. At present Mr. Streets, who has spent two years in Rorough-road Training College, London, is an assistant master at Simms Cross Board School. He passed toe matriculation examination Of the London University. WIDNES ST. MARY'S FOOTBALL CLUB. The annual meeting of tne members was held on Tuesday night at the Grosvenor Hotel. Mr. H. Single- ton presided, and presented the members of the team with the Lancashire Junior Cup medal.—The Secretary (Mr. E. Gould), presented the annual reports, which showed that the team had won 20 games, lost four, and three were drawn. There was a balance in hand of £4. 7s. id. Mr. E. C. Gould, was appointed secretary, and Mr. J. Hogan captain—The Secretary announced that Mr. James Kiddie, the lessee of the Alexandra Theatre, had offered to give two benefit performances for the club, and avote of thanks was accorded to him for his generous offer.

_ SCHOOL TREATS AT RUNCORN. The scholars attending the Mersey Missions to Sea- men had their annual treat on Monday, when about 250 were conveyed by boat along the Bridgewater Canal to Grappenhall. Canon Greenall had placed a large room at the disposal of the party, and here the wants of the inner man were attended to. Mr. R. A. Na.yler had also thrown open his grounds for the editicationof the young- sters, who spent a very pleasant day. The Rev. C. M. Woosnam, M.A., the chaplain, and the Rev. James Fell, I assistant-chaplain, and Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary, accompanied the excursion. On Wednesday the children attending St. Luke's Congregational School had their an- nual treat, about 400 scholars, teachers, and friends being conveyed to Moore by boat. The weather, for- tunately, continued fine, and a happy time was spent in a field lent by Mr. Foster. Ample provision had been made for the feeding of the large party. The Rev. J. Simpson, the pastor, was present throughout the day. The childrqn attending Camden Sunday School had their annual treat, on Wednesday, when about 600 were con- veyed by special train to Frodsham and speut a most enjoyable day on Overton Hills. The scholars were liber- ally provided with the requisite refreshments.

_ _ A BATCH OF THIEVES AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Margaret Well- burn, of Sandy-lane, Lymm, was charged with stealing an aprOn worth Md., the property of John Pearson, of Lugsdatt:road. The prisoner had been staying at the house of the prosecutor for two days and it was alleged that when she left she took away the apron.—The pri- soner contended that the apron was given her in exchange for other articles.—The prosecutrix admitted that she had exchanged several articles and that the pri- soner was wearing the apron in her house. The prisoner was discharged.—An elderly woman named Elizabeth Wilson of no fixed residence, was charged with stealing nibs of bacon from the shop of S. Sadler, grocer, Ann-st. She was seen to take the bacon from the counter and walk away. She was followed and the bacon was found under her shawl. She was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. —Catherine Fallow, a Victoria-st., pleaded guilty to stealing 51 lbs. of tinned beef from the shop of Mr. S. Sadler, and she was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.— Charles Hazlehurst, a youth, of Robert-st., was charged with stealing 5 pieces of cask heads, valued at is., the property of Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Co., where he was employed.—The prisoner said he was taking the wood home for firewood, and did not know there was a notice against it. He was fined ss. and costs.—John Fallow, and Michael Devereaux, boys, of Victoria-st., were charged with stealing a silver watch and chain, worth £4, the property of Thomas Egan, labourer, of Brown-st. The prisoners went to the house with a mes- sage and when they had gone the watch and chain was missed.—The prisoners pleaded guilty and Fallow was ordered to receive nine strokes, and Devereaux five strokes of the birch rod. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-it., Warrington.—Add. MODEL YACHT RACE AT RENCOILN.

A model yacht race took place on Saturday after- noon in the Weaver Canal at Rock Savage. The course was a distance of about 500 yards, and Mr. W. Iloxworth, of Lowland-road, supplied the first and second with Joey and Willie, whilst Mr. W. Cooper's Annie occupied the third place. Six yachts competed. The first prize was 10s. and the flag of the Runcorn Club and the second prize ss. Joey won by 25 yards. SUMMER SALE now on a* J, & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-A., Warrington.—.Advt. BRIDGET KILDARE AGAIN!

The notorious St. ilei;;;CI;;O:ci-e-ic Bridget Xil- dare, "comes and goes" between St. Helens and Walton gaol with a persistent regularity which is almost painful to the frequenters of the police court. Last week we recorded her 183rd appear- ance, when on the previous Saturday she was removed to Walton forseven days. Last Saturday she was again brought up for misconducting her- self and was committed to prison for 28 days. She informed the Benck that she wished they would send her for six or twelve months. _ _ _

_ The International Congress on Inland Naviga- tion, which was opened on Monday evening in Man- chester, was continued on Tuesday at the Town Hall. There were four sectional meetings. Many members of the Congress and delegates from foreign countries availed themselves in the afternoon of the of visiting the works of the Man- ch poestoeprsrthuity Ship Canal. Odle' s went to view the 'Weaver Navigation. There was also an excursion to Chester and Eaton Hall; the day's proceedings concluded with a reception by the Mayor and Cor- poration of Manchester in the Town Hall.

RETURNING FROM THE RACES. William Cousins Goodenough,a cab driver,of War- rington, was charged at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, with being drunk in charge of a horse and waggonette, and also with cruelty to the horse by beating it with a stick on the previous after- noon. The prisoner was in charge of a waggonette conveying people from the Newton Common Races, and the °fence was committed in Market-street. Earlestown. The case was proved by a witness named Boothroyd and Inspector Jowett, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs for the drunkenness, and 20s. and costs for the cruelty. WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The 48th annual show of this Society is to be held at Birkenhead on Wednesday an,l Thursday, the 3rd and 4th of September. An idea of the large scale on which the show is conducted may be had from the fact that nearly £1,500 are offered in prizes for competition. There are prizes offered for horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, pigeons, poultry, dogs, grain, roots, cheese, butter, eggs, and horticulture, so that there will be plenty of variety about the exhibition. The prizes for pigeons and poultry are especially numerous, and the exhibition of dogs promises to be of exceptional interest. The Lancashire and Cheshire Bee-keepers' Association will hold an exhi- , bition of bees, hives, and honey in connection with the show.

„, U iNPLEASANT RIP PROM SOUTHPORT. • On Wednesday about 90 persons had an unplea- sant experience when making an excursion from Southport to Llandudno, in the steamship Adela. The vessel started at eleven o'clock short of coals. and had to put into Liverpool for supplies, arriv- ing-at Llandudno at half-past five o'clock. After an hour's stay the return journey was made, the Adele getting off Southport before ten o'clock. The tide was at full, with a strong wind blowing, and as the Adela's engines are not disconnecting the pier officials did not consider it safe for her to be brought up to the pier, the consequence being that the passengers were not landed until about low water, at half-past three in the morning.

• SODDEN DEATII iv HEATLEY. Last evening week a young man named Herbert Smith, son of Mr. John Smith, of Brook House, Heatley, met with a painfully sudden death at Manchester. It appears that about a week ago the deceased accepted a position as commercial traveller to a firm in the city, be prior to that time having been learning the grocery and provision business with Mr. John Gandy, at Warrington. lie was returning home on Friday evening, by way ford-road to the station at Manchester, when he suddenly fell down dead. The deceased, who was only 19 years of age, was of a very genial disposi- tion, and greatly respected by all with whom busi- ness and friendship brought him in contact. The funeral took place at Stockton Heath on Tuesday, when the friends and relatives of the deceased were present. The coffin,which bore a simple inscription, was covered with beautiful wreathe. Is "PiTat AND TOW GAMING? - ^

--- At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Henry Long, John Cunliffe, W. Beckett, and H. Smith, col- liers, Haydock, appeared in answer to a sum mons ' charging them with playing pitch and toss, at Hay- dock, on the 19th July.—Mr. J. 0. Swift (St. Helens) who appeared for the defendants, took exception to the information, which, he said, was bad and upon which the magistrtdes could not convict. He knew of no Act of Parliament which made it an offence to play pitch and toss in any highway. The inform- ation was bad in, at least, three points. It must follow the wording of the Act, the material points of which laid down that the gaming must be by way of wagering; it must be by some coin, or in- strument of gaming; and must be a game of chance. Those were necessary ingredients of an offence, and the information could not be good or valid unless it enumerated them. The Bench upheld the objec- tion, and the case was accordingly dismissed. '

Warrington.—Adrot. ROBBERY OF A GOLD _WATCH AT WARGRAVE.

Before Col. McCorquodale and other magistrates, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Samuel Lapsley, a fitter at the Vulcan locomotive works, and residing at Vulcan cottages, was charged with stealing a gold watch and chain, together of the value of II" 10s., the property of Robert Heßderson, Wargrave. It appeared that on the night of the 25th ult. Lapsley and some friends who were going to Scotland were at Mr. Henderson's house. After the prisoner had left, the watch and chain were missed from a dresser. Lapsley appeared to be under the influence of drink, and when he was returning home in company with a man named Platt, Lapsley went .on one side of the road for a few moments. Next day when the theft of the watch was reported Platt remembered Lapsley's conduct on the way home, and the spot was searched with the result that the watch and chain were found hid among some cinders. The prisoner was subsequently apprehended by Police Constable Bowes, and on being charged with the offence he said he was very sorry. Prisoner, who acknow- ledged his guilt and said he was drunk when he committed the theft, was fined 40s. and costs. Annurierwa AT THE LAKES.

At the Windermere Petty Sessions, on Tuesday morning, Mr. Edward Darcy Curwen, J.P., and Mr. Alan Delaney Curwen, brothers, of Longholm, Win- dermere, were each tined 40s. and costs for damag- ing certain advertising boards, the property of Messrs. Beecham and Co., of St. Helens. It appears that Mr. Beecham secured a site at Bowness for advertising purposes, and gold letters were placed upon wirework setting forth the value of the pills. This was pulled down ti few nights since, and the letters consigned to a watery level. Then Mr. Beecham purchased a, small yacht, and 'had the advertist.ment painted upon the sails. This yacht was sunk, but the sails with the words appeared above the water. Mr. Beecham erected a new sign, and a constable was concealed to watch it. The young men, early on Tuesday morning week, were seen near the sign, ancLwhile, it is stated, in the very act of attempting its demolition they were arrested and taken to the police station. On being taken before the magistrates, a remand was granted until Tuesday, the 29th July, to allow time to com- municate with Mr.Beecham, who, however, declined to interfere, and the result last Tuesday was that they were each tined 40s. and costs.

At the St. Hele...; 'ounty Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Deputy-Judge Goldthorpe;EdwardJones, Weaverham, near Northwich, sued the Travellers' Rest Lodge of Orderof Druids to recover ..£lO, which he alleged to be due to him on the death of his wife, and lie also sought to attain from the court a declaration that he was still a member of that lodge. Mr. Riley was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Mearns for I the defendants. Before any evidence was called Mr. Mearns objected to the case being brought before the court, as the rules of the society provided that such disputes should be settled by arbitration. The Friendly Societies' act, 1875, having, been consulted, the contention of Mr. Mearns was sustained, and the Case was adjourned for a week in order that arbitration proceedings might be instituted. Warrington.—Advt. THE PROTECTION OF WILD BIRDS. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Samuel Ellis, Thomas English, and John Woodcock, residents of Earlestown were summoned under the Wild Birds Protection Act for illegally having wild birds in their possession.—Police Constable Cameron proved the cases. It appeared that. from informa- tion he received he visted the houses of each defend- ant. Ellis had one young blackbird, English, a blackbird and three young throstles, and Woodcock had one blackbird and two young throstles. Ellis said the bird had been given to his son, and he did not know he was doing wrong in keeping it. Wood- cock said his boy brought the birds home, un- conscious of the fact that he had no right to take them.—Each defendant was ordered to pay the costs. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. div.head: FIELD NA.TBRALISTS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FIELD NA.TBRALISTS AT RUNCORN.

On Saturday the members of the 'Manchester 1 Field Naturalists and Archteologists' Society, to the number of 79, spent a fileb.sant and instructive day in the district of Runcorn. Leaving Manchester between one and two o'clock, the party accom- panied by Alderman W. H. Bailey, as conductor, arrived at North wich in good time to proceed by steamer to the Anderton lift. The system applied in the lift was a source of much favourable com- ment, and later on the archwologists were con- veyed along the Weaver to Weston Point, where they inspected the works on the Ship Canal routo. The most manifest interest was taken in the gigan- tic works in course of operation, and after the Man- cunians had given a thorough inspection, an ad- journment was made to Wilson's Hotel, where Host and Hostess Cooper gave evidence of desiring to cater for the party. Everyone present was more than satisfied with the manner in which the cater- ing was accomplished, and there was an evident desire to renew the visit. Subsequently the party left the town with the impression that it was not as bad as it had been of late depicted, and in many Cases it was announced, of course as a matter of conversation, that Runcorn would again be the scene of an early visit. • WELLINGTON COLLEGE, WELLINGTON, SITROPSH/RE. div.head: ANOTHER MINING DISASTER. EIGHT MEN KILLED.
div.p: ANOTHER MINING DISASTER. EIGHT MEN KILLED.

BERLIN, Tnonsney.—A telegram from Gelsenkudien announces that an explosion of firedamp occurred last night in the Unter Fritz Pit at that place, by which eight miners were killed on the spot, while three others, one of whom has since succumbed, were seriously injured. The cause of the explosion remains unexplained.

ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH RUNCORN. INDUCTION SERVICES. In connection with the induction of the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, of Bala college, as pastor of the above chapel, special services were held on Sunday, when the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. John Williams, of Chester. There were good congrega- tions at each service, and the choir, led by Mr. War- burton, rendered special music. On Tuesday afternoon a meeting of the Presbytery was belie in the chapel, and in the evening the induc- tion of Mr. Pulford Williams into his pastorate took place. There was a large audience, which included many members of other denominations. The Rev. R. G. Jones, the moderator of the Presbytery presided, and he was supported by the Rev. John Thomas 8.A., Liverpool ; Rev. J. C. Thomas, Rev. John Williams. Chester; Rev. John Simpson (Congregational) and the Rev. J. Pulford Williams; Messrs. John Jones (Chester) and James Kirkham.—Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from the Revs. H. Burson, W. Kendrew and G. Thompson.—The Chairman opened the proceedings with a few appropriate remarks and then Mr. James Kirkham gave an historical sketch of St John's Chapel, which. he said, was erected in the year 1818, when the oversight was entrusted to the Rev. A. Hay, of Warrington. At this time the chapel was con- nected with the Countess of Huntingdon's Connection, and the services conducted were similar to those of the Church of England. For some years the cause was very flourishing, but ultimately it languished and died away. In the year 1848, the doors were Closed, and the chapel advertised for sale. At this juncture, the treasurer of the church urged the Rev. John Hughes and others, of Liverpool, to purchase the building, assuring them that if the Gospel were preached in its simplicity and power, as he had heard it in Wales, great good would be done. The Liverpool friends listened to the appeal, and in- structed Mr. Owen Elias and Mr. Davies, Mount Gar- dens, to attend the sale, end If possible to purchase. The charel was bought, and Was re-opened May 21st, 1849, by the Rev. E. Willliams, Penybont, Radnorshire, and Mr. Wm. Evans, Chester. The congregations were large, and the services very impressive. Shortly after- wards, the Rev. William Roberts, of Holyhead, undertook the pastorate, and his labours were eminently blessed; the chapel was filled to over- flowing and many souls were converted to God. A church was then formed and 70 united in Church fellow- ship. These were happy times—days of heaven upon earth, and some of the old Runcornians even now would rapturously speak of these refreshing times. But this was not to continue, for after a successful ministry of six years, the Welsh church at New York, gave Mr. Roberts a call, and he accepted the pastorate. In the ' year 1856 the Rev. John Davieseof Kinchester took the oversight of the church, and remained nearly three years. doing a good work. He was succeeded by the Rev. Win. Evans. 111.A..wh0 laboured with considerable success, and during his ministey a chapel house was built which had ever since been of great service. In 1867 the Rev. Evan Williams was called to labour amongst them, and continued with them for over 20 years,. "breaking the bread of life." Up to the year 1872 yearly grants were received for the support of the mihister hit since that date the cause had been self-eupperting. In that year the chapel was renovated and reseated at a cost of £345 ; and in the year 1881-82, two new class-rooms were hunt and ether improvements effected. In the autumn of 1887 dark clouds hovered. over the haver home of Mr. Evan Williams, the pastor, which necessitated his removal from the flock to Australia. In the summer of 1889, Mr. Pulford Williams spent his holidays a menest them; the friends all round fell in love with him ; he reciprocated the affection, and the result was that he was invited to take the oversight of the church. He accepted the invitation and they trusted the union would meet with divine approval, and that God's gracious blessing would ratify that service—the induction of Mr. Williams to the work of Jesus Christ and the Church, and that all the friends would pledge themselves to help him in every possible way. (Applause.) The Rev. John Thomas (deputation from the Presby- tery), congratulated bath the Church and the minister upon that happy occasion, and expressed a sincere wish that all success, prosperity and blessing, would rest upon the union they were celebrating. He then delivered an address upon the duties and obligations of the Church in regard to their pastor, in which he urged them to be prayerful, faithful, and united, and to love one another fervently with pure hearts. Mr. John Jones, of Chester, delivered a speech in which he gave a prescription to keep alive a flourishing church and the ingredientsthree P's—prayer, peace, and pence. The young man they had selected as their pastor had come to Runcorn to do his duty,but he would fail un- less he was supported by the officers and members of the church. The Ray. J. C. Thomas having delivered an earnest address, The Rev. J. Pulford Williams said he entered upon his ministry with diffidence, but still with some degree of confidence. Of his unfitness and unworthiness he was painfully conscious; nevertheless his confidence was in the living God his strength was in the pure Gospel of Christ, which he was determined to preach amongst them. He expected their co-operation, and he knew he should not expect in vain. (Applause.) Mr. James Pritchard on behalf of the officers of the church and on behalf of the congregation, heartily welcomed Mr. Williamal amongst them. (Applause). They received him in the Lord with all gladness and they would hold him in reputation and honour. (Applause.) They would extend to Mr. Williams prayerful sympathy, hearty co-operation, and they would cherish towards him sentiments of esteem and regard. (Applause.) They trusted that his coming amongst them would be the com- mencement of good work, and that his ministry would be made a blessing not only to that place, but amongst the community in which they moved. (Applause.) The Rev. John Williams (Chester), said he war proud to tell them that Mr. Pulford Williams was not a bigot ; he was not a sectarian young man ; he was full of the love of Christ and rejoiced in the success of every denomination that were engaged in doing good. (Applause.) The Rev. John Simpson (Congregational) said he was very sorry that there were no otherministers of the town present, but he was quite sure that there were pressing circumstances which had kept them away. He had much pleasure in their name in welcoming Mr. Williams to Runcorn. (Hear, hear.) He was very glad that their minister was a young man, and one in whom he could look for a friend. He understood that Bethesda and St. . John's had alwaysbeen bound together in close friendship, : and now that they had got a new minister he hoped the same friendship would continue. • (Hear, hear.) There was plenty of work for every minister and every denom- ination in the town; and they ought to be able to work

together without any feeling of jealousy or envy. He sincerely trusted that would be the case with the two 'ministers and congregations of Bethesda. On the motion of Mr. Hewitt, seconded by Mr. Baxter, a vote of thanks was accorded to the speakers and the , proceedings terminated.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting was beld at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. -Colonel Ashton presided; and there were present :Mesh's. Mclntyre, Bran- dreth, Heywood, J. W. Baguley, J. Whitlow, Hewitt, Pickering, Aaron, W. Whitlow, Bretherton, H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk). Mr. Farrington (the in- spector) reported a nuisance at Lunt's Row, Weston, and he was authorised to take the steps necessary to cause an abatement. No communication having been received from the Local Government Board with reference to the pollution of Rekewick Brook, and on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. J. Baguley, the Clerk was instructed to write to the Board and press upon them the necessity for imme- diate action in the matter.

div.head: RUNCORN BUILDERS AND THE TOWN BYE-
div.p: RUNCORN BUILDERS AND THE TOWN BYE-
LAWS.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. C. Reynolds, and Major Ilazlehurst, John Thomason, builder, Norman-road,was summoned to answer the information of the Runeorn Board of Commis sion- era, that on the 12th July he did construct certain buildings in Norman-road,otherwlse than in accord- ance with the plans deposited and without the approve of the Commissioners to such deviation of the plans.— The defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. F. A. Lake prose- cuted and stated tint the defendant had erected houseg in Norman-road, and on the plans the scullery was shown adjacent to the main building. The defendant had, however, altered the plans, leaving out the scullery, and he had instead erected a wash- house in the yard. There was no objection to the alteration so far as construction went, but it was an alteration of the plans deposited, which should have been approved by the Commissioners before being car- out. He did not ask for more than a nominal penalty, because Mr. Thomason had not acted to thwart the Commissioners, but with the idea that he was in the right according to the bye-laws.—The defendant said he had done the same for twenty years, and Mr. Barker knew it.—Mr. Reynolds said any departure from the plans must be again submitted and approved.—The de- fendant said it was hard he should be summoned when it had been carried on for 20 years.—Mr. Reynolds: That does not make it right, when it is against the byelaws. The offence is a technical one, and we shall impose a fine of is. and costs.

div.head: SCENE AT THE CHESRIRE POLICE
div.p: A SCENE AT THE CHESRIRE POLICE

At the Cheshire Police Inquiry on Saturday, on resuming after luncheon, Mr. Peter Smith, of Runcorn, addressing the Chair- man, said it was reported in the local papers that at the last sitting of the inquiry, Mr. Lewis, in the course of his examination of Superintendent Hol- lingworth, asked if he thought he (Mr. Smith) was a suitable person to be on friendly terms with. He would like to ask Mr. Lewis to explain what he meant by suitability to speak to a citizen, police- man, or anyone else. The Chairman: I said before that your position in Runcorn is sufficient to take care of you. Your neigh- bours should know most about you.
Mr. Smith: It is not a very pleasant thing to have this thing poked under your nose and have your attea- tion drawn to it.
The Chairman: If you ask me the whole thing is un- pleasant. Mr. Smith: My character will bear as good an explan- ation as Mr. Lewis's.
Mr. Slater Lewis : You must not throw mud at me in such a manner.
Mr. Smith: You will have to have it if you insult me.

Mr. Slater Lewis : But I won't have it. My character will bear investigatkin and yours won't. You have been convicted of assaulting the police. Mr. Smith: I consider myself quite as good as you. Mr. Slater Lewis: You must not throw your insults at me.
Mr. Smith : But you have no business to make such remarlei.
Mr. Slater Lewis: Keep your hands off the police then.
The Chairman: Come, come; we must bave no more of this.
