PRESBYTERY CONFERENCE AT RUNCORN.

A conference in connection with the Lancashire, Sec. Presbytery was held on Tuesday, at St. John's Runcorn. The Moderator presided. The mission- aries were the Revs. R. R. Roberts. J. Davies, E. Salisbury, 0 B. Jones, R. G. Jones, W. H. Williams, G. E. Rogers, E. Jerman, J. Meredith, R. L. Roose, W. R. Evans, and T. Phennah. Delegates were appoint- ed to take the vote of Broughton Church in the election of deacons, and permission was given to Messrs. R. R. Roberts and J. P. Williams to attend the next synodical examination. The following reports were discussed and accepted :—Messages from the general assembly and association, and statistical report. The Sunday school examination was appointed to take place in April next, the subject being the three last chapters of St. Luke's Gospel. The examiners are to be the Revs. W. Robley, Buckley, and 0. Williams (Flint.) The report of the delegates to Salop-street Church was confirmed ,and Messrs. E. Jones, W. Wilcocks, and W. Evans, J.P. were , appointed to visit the church on behalf of the presbytery. A letter was read from Mrs. Jones, Little Mancott, in answer to a letter of condolence sent to her by the Secre- tary, and the Secretary was appointed to send a letter of sympathy to the bereaved family of Mr. David Davies, J.P., of Llandinam. It was announced that at Holywell a strong church was formed.

div.head: NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE NEW BRIGHTON TRAGEDY.
VERDICT AND SENTENCE. _ _. _ _ _ .

The trial of Felix Spicer for the murder of his two young sons, William and Henry, and the attempted mur- der of their mother, Mary Palin, was commenced at Chester Assizes, on Thursday,beforeMr. Justice Stephen. On being arraigned on the previous day, Spicer pleaded not guilty. He is defended by Mr. Edmund Burke Wood. Miss Palin, the mother of the children, was at times strongly affected during her examination, in the course of which she detailed a long course of suffering at the prisoner's hands. The trial was adjourned. The trial was concluded at the Chester Assizes yester- day. Prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to death.

div.head: RIVAL TO "TOMMY BURNS."
div.p: A RIVAL TO "TOMMY BURNS."

Tommy Burns, the champion diver, has his imitators like greater men, and a labourer at the evidences Alkali Works his attempting to emulate Burns' feats from Run- corn Bridge. This new seeker for fame is a man about 30 years of age, about Sit. 9inches, high and pmportion- ately built. He goes by the name of John Mack but his proper appellation is John McNamara. On Thursday about half-past eleven,Mack might have been seen dang- ling from the end of a rope attached to the foot walk of ' Runcorn Bridge. After a brief pause, he dropped into the water beneath, and on reappearing on the surface he de- clined the services of the boat in attendance and swam to the shore.—He declares his intention to dive from the Bridge a la Burns in a few days

div.head: ACTION AGAINST THE LANCASHIRE
div.p: ACTION AGAINST THE LANCASHIRE
WATCH COMPANY.

At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Judge Goldthorpe, James Morton, a watch move- ment maker, in the employ of the Lancashire Watch Company. Prescot, sued the company to recover five weeks' wages, £lO 10s., and £2 2s. for wages retained during his holidays. The defendants had paid into court £8 13s. Bd., and had put in a counter claim against the plaintiff claimingfrom the £lO los. a sum of £2 13s. 4d., and they also claimed the same sum as damages, for that the plaintiff being a workman employed under contract with the defendant, wrongfully absented himself from his employment during portions of days on and between those dates that the defendants factory was working. They did not dispute the plaintiff's claim in respect to the sum £7 16s. Bd. Mr. J. P. Mearns appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. The Deputy- Judge, having heard the case on both sides, gave judgment for the defendants with oosts. A similar action brought by John Wareing, also a watch movement ' maker, for a like claim under similar circumstinces a against the company was dealt with in a like manner.
THLNGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY AN OCCASIONAL COIMESPONDENT.
That the subject of the incorporation of Widnes will probably be discussed at the next meeting of the Local Board. ... . ... .

That several of the members while failing to see any great advantage in converting the town into a borough, are quite willing to vote for a charter of incorporation should the ratepayers wish it, and it is very likely that steps will be taken for ascertain- ing the views of the ratepayers on the question. • That from what one sees and hears there will be a great majority in favour of incorporation, and the Ratepayer's Association and the local Irish National League are doing their utmost to foster this favour- able felling. That Mr. Brunner has interested himself to some purpose with regard to the election for Guardians for Runcorn and the question he addressed to the Local Government Board last week, embodied a very real grievance. That the alleged irregularities at the last election might have been remedied had the voters had an opportunity of obtaining papers from the overseers office, instead of having to make a journey to Frod- sham for that purpose, and it is to be hoped that,: before another contest takes place, arrangements will have been made for the much needed improve- ment. . .

That it'is very rare indeed that there is a con- tested election in any township except Runcorn; and, as Mr. Brunner suggested, the counting of the votes might with advantage be done at Runcorn. That the carrying out of these improvements depends upon Mr. U. Linaker. the returning officer, who,with his usual desire to act for the pablic weal. will see the advisability of making the suggested change.

NORTIIWICH LIBERAL CLUB. SPEECHES BY MIL BRUNNER AND MR. STANSFELD. The new premises of the Northwich Gladstone Club were opened by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., on Tnursday afternoon. The building is one of the handsomest ip the main street of the town, and Mr. Brunner'a supporters were warmly congratulated on their new possession by the Right Hon. J.Stans- feld, M.P., who was present at the opening ceremony. Mr. Stansfeld also referred to the possibilities which such a club presented as a help to the future success of the Liberal party in the division. North- wich, he said, was strong and loyal in its Liberalism, and there might be little to fear from opposition, but it was best to make assurance doubly sure.—ln the evening a public meeting was held in the Cen- tral Hall. There was a large attendance. Mr. Brunner presided, and amongst those present were Mr. Stansfeld, M.P., Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., the Rev. F. Minton (vicar of Mialdlewich), Mr. R. Pratt, Mr. A. Fletcher, Mr. J. F. L. Brunner, Mr. King. There were present from Runcorn Messrs. S. Taylor, J. J. Howitt, W. Handley, T. Clegg, T. Spender, R. Morris, B. Kniveton, and S. Walton. Mr. Brunner, M.P., who was received with loud cheers. said he and his colleagues in the House of Commons had done precious little good during the last session, but it had taken a great deal of hard work to do that very little good. The Liberal party had been " whipped ' day by day and night by night, but through the perverse- ness of the Government their time had been wasted. Personally he was ready for a fight in his constituency as soon as possible. He hoped that at the next election there would be a contest in that division, because when an election took place without a contest the member did not come into contact with his friends nor with his enemies, and learned from neither. A free interchange of opinion between a member and his constituents was one of the things which John Bright believed was neces- sary to the good government of the country,imd, apart ' from his delight in battle, it was in the hope that he and his constituents might have the advantage of such an interchange that he wanted a contest in the Northwich division at the next election. If the electors of the country did their duty they would get rid of a set of politicians who were readtionaries. They had had before the public three great popular movements—Home Rule for Ireland, the disestablishment of the English Church in Wales, and the promotion of temperance. With regard to those movements what had the Tories done? Instead of giving Ireland Home Rule they had continued in that country to enforce a mean and cowardly system of oppression. All the power of the Governmerit had been extended to aid the rich and th timg, anti all their honours were reserved as A rea ward for subservience. They opprcsed the poorest of the poor. On the Ponsonby estate they had had a glaring example of their one-sided policy. The police Were con- tinually aiding and abetting the landlords in their struggle with the tenants. It was a remarkable fact that most of the landlords who had already sold their estates under the Ashbourne Acts appeared to be personal friends of the members of the present Administration, and the thought was impressed upon his mind that the latter gentlemen wanted their friends to get out before the arash. (Heardiear.) They wanted, to use a Stock Ex- change phrase, to unload and sell their estates, at the risk of the ratepayers for more money than they were likely to get in the open market. If for no other reason, the country ought to get rid of those men in order to raise the character of the country for commercial honesty. (Cheers.) Mr. Stansfeld, M.P., was also received with great cor- diality. He remarked that he was happy to announce to 1 the meeting that the session was drawing to a close, and he was happy to add that it was coming to an ignomini- ous close. (Laughter.) The ignominy would not rest with the House of Commons' but with the Government, which the Chairman and he hoped soon to see displaced. The Government had promised a measure of local self- ! government for Ireland. They introduced a Land Pur- chase Bill and a Tithes Bill. Those were the three prin- cipal measures promised or introduced. The promised measure of local government for Ireland had not even been brought in, and the other two main measures of the Government were dismal and absolute and admitted 1 failures (Cheers.) The Government had the presump- tion to talk of obstruction. Which of their measures had been obstructed? Not the Irish Land Purchase Bill; a very moderate number of nights was spent on discussing the second reading of that measore. Nor the Tithes Bill, for hardly any time at all had been spent on that mea- sure; and no time could be spent on the Irish Local Government Bill, the great pet embryo scheme of the Liberal Dissentients, because that measure was never in- troduced. (Laughter and cheers.) If the Government had stuck to their original programme, if they had not introduced any other measures, if they had concentrated all their force and employed all the time at their disposal, taking the time of private members as they had done— even then, ab initio, they made an absurd miscalculation of their power and of the time of the House, and those measures could not have been passed unless the Liberal party had not only not ob- structed but been content to abdicate their functions of legitimate criticism, and after a mere per- functory, short, and meaningless debate to record the votes of the majority of the composite party—the cabal which now ruled the country. But in the midst of all their difficulties, which had become more than apparent to most men, their confusion was intensified by the intro- duction of the Public-house Endowment Bill. (Laughter.) He asked if they could conceive a sane man introducing such a measure, which, right or wrong, was absolutely certain to meet the strongest, the most deep-rooted, and honest opposition, under the belief, too, that it would facilitate the progress of the other measures of the Government and the business of the House? He looked for an explanation of the fatuity of the Government in this direction. The Tithes Bill was the favourite project of the Prime Minister—the uncle of his nephew— (laughter)—and the land scheme was the favourite project of the nephew of his uncle. (Laughter.) Those bills were brought in. The Dissentient Liberals looked in vain for the Local Government Bill. But they knew what it was by this time to be dragged at the heels of the Tory car. They had sold their souls. They had no individuality; they had no future. (Cheers.) They lived upon the help which they hoped to receive from a party which used but which despised them. The schemes of both nephew and uncle, how- ever, were, destroyed by another extremely ambitious and very clever leader in the Government. a man who, who was only clever, a deserter from the Liberal camp, a traitor to Liberal principles—the present Chancellor of ' the Exchequer.—(Groans.) He had heard him called a ' turncoat. He objected entirely to that appellation. He could never call a man a turncoat who was wearing his coat the right side out for the first time.—(Laughter and cheers.) In his opinion, and it was not a newly formed opinion, Mr. Goschen never belonged to the Liberal party. He was heartily glad to get rid of him, and he wished the Tories joy of him. He had landed them in the greatest mess they were ever in, and when he and the other members of the Government turned round and said that their failure was due to obstruction, he declared that that allegation was a total falsehood.— (Cheers.) Mr. T. E. Ellis moved the following resolution which was adopted : " That this meeting, convened to cele- brate the opening of the new Gladstone Club Buildings, declares its complete confidence in the veteran leader of the Liberal party, the Right Flom W. E. Gladstone, and offers him sincere congratulations on the evidence afforded by the recent by-elections that the flowing tide is with us." Votes of thanks concluded the meeting,

Alexandra Jacques has now beaten all previous per- formances in the fasting line, having completed his fortieth day at 4 p.m. on Thursday. He complained of great weariness and drowsiness on Thursday, having had very little sleep. Dr. Robins, at noon, reported that Jacques had gained 12 oz. in weight since Wednesday, in consequence of the large quantity of water he had taken, within the present 2 hours.
THE BABY ON THE BATTLE-FIELD;

On the night after the battle of Waterloo, in the blood- stained mire of a ploughed field, lay an English efficer, dead where he fell. At his side, lay the body of his wife, who had followed him from England, and perhaps ar- rived in time to receive his lastsigh. On his breast was their baby, sound asleep, and smiling amid that dread- ful scene as though angels were inspiring its dreams. Ah. God, what a thing is childhood ! touching heaven in its innocence and earth in its agony. When we have the children how large the places they fill! When we lose them how great the vacancies they leave! Read the story of an escape, as told by a parent. My daughter, Lilian Kate, now eleven years old, bad always been delicate. She was pale and thin, and it seemed as though a breath of cold air would destroy her. She was now better, now worse, but never well. In the summer of 11385, she complained of a sense of weight in the chest and side. Her abdomen was distended as though she had over-eaten, when in fact she ate scarcely more than a bird. She spoke of a bad taste in the mouth, and would always be holding her sides, or plac- ing her hands against her temples, as if to relieve the pressure there. • She also had pains between the shoulders, and her breath was very offensive.—She was always tired and languid, and, though naturally a bright, intelligent child, would lie for hours in a listless condition. She grew weaker and weaker until she could scarcely stand. We thought her to be in a decline. Then came a sign even more alarming—a short, dry, deep-sounding cough. 3ly wife and I feared it was consumption. In our anxiety we consulted the doctors, who said "Yes your daughter has consumption." Wbat a sad prospect for us!
About Christmas, 1885, I removed my family from Huntingdon to Manchester. Poor Lillian was too weak

to take- the journey with us; she remained with her grandmother, Mrs. Lock, at Thorp Farm, West Harling, Norfolk. Still the dear child sank from week to week. What was our surprise, some time afterwards, to receive a letter from Grandmother Lock, reading like this—

!.• Lillian is very much better. She is eating teell and sleeping well; and the roses are coming into her thin cheeks." What could have happened? In another month we had the haupiness of welcoming our daughter in our new home in Manchester. How great was our joy when we saw the wonderful change which had taken place in her. She is now a fine, healthy child and never ails anything more than any girl may. _ . _ .

- Now, what wrought this change? What gave us back our daughter, seemingly almost from the brink of the grave? I will answer frankly, for there is nothing to conceal :—Seeing her deplorable state, and that none of the medicines she had taken proved appro- priate to her strange malady, Mrs. Lock one day said to herself, "I think I will give Lillian a dose out of my bottle of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup." She (Mrs. Lock) had received immense benefit from this medicine herself for a complicated disease. It was given to Lil- lian, and the good effect was Immediate. She at once rested more tranquilly and had something of an appetite, and a little later Mrs. Lock was justified in writing to us as I have already stated. (Signed) Frede- rick Butcher, 6, Birch-road, Crumpsall, near Manches- ter.

Mr. and Mrs. Butcher are people of the highest res- pectability and well educated. For some years Mr. Butcber was an assistant at the great shop of the Messrs. Lewis, Market-st., Manchester, and an impartial acquaintance writes that Miss Lillian Kate Butcher is one of the brightest young girls to be met with any- where—quick, precocious and full of vivacity and wit. Speaking of the daughter's recovery, her mother says: "I do not care what any one may say, there is no medi- cine so good as Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. Many years ago I lost my poor darling Hilda, who was taken off suddenly with an affection of the brain, and I really think if we had given her Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, instead of trusting to something else, she would have been spared to us." The proprietors of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup desire to make no false irrpressions. The young girl did not have consumption :—She suffered from indigestion and dyspepsia, and from poverty of the blood, like myriads of her sex. The hollow cough, which sounded so consumptive, was one of the symptoms, not the disease. She needed life and strength from her food, but how could she get it with 'her stomach torpid arid dead? Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup corrected the ailment at its root, and recovery quickly followed. We repeat once more the fact that is taught by this interesting case: —When in doubt treat any and all complaints as symp- toms of indigestion and dyspepsia, and in nine instances out of ten you will see just such a wonder as narrated above. We wish long life and happy days to this young lady and her good parents and friends.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A SHOCKING CASs OF CHILD ASSAULT. On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, John Peers, jun., a joiner, was charged with having on the previous day committed an aggravated assault on his daughter Jane, nine years of age. On Tuesday Mrs. Peers went in the house and found that her husband had committed an indescribable assault on the little girl, and consequently she had him locked up. The Chief Con- stable said it was one of the worst cases ho had ever heard of. Prisoner, in reply to the charge, said, " I admit I was very drunk, but I did not touch her." The bench committed him to prison for three months, with hard labour.

div.head: ASSAULT ON THE POLICH.
div.p: ASSAULT ON THE POLICH.

A stonemason, named William Brookes was summoned to the Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st., on Saturday night. He was also charged with assaulting Constable Rowbotham. That officer told the magistrates that he had received complaints about the conduct of the prisoner, who refused to go home and struck the witness, knocking him down. Another constable, who witnessed the assault, gave evidence in corroboration, and stated that when he came on the scene he found that Rowbot- ham's face was covered with blood. The magistrates decided to fine the defendant 10s. and costs for the assault, and ss. and costs for having been drunk.

A MAGISTRATE!! SPEAKS OUT AGAINST TRIVIAL PROSE- CUTIONS. William Carter, a Ship Canal workman, appeared be- fore the Daresbury Bench on Tuesday, on a made by Mr. Broady, the landlord of the public house at Higher Walton' of having stolen a towel which was valued at Is. Mr. P. Davies, of Warrington, defended. . A witness named Wright said he saw Carter going out of the public house with something under his coat' and he told Mr. Broady. The latter shouted after Carter, who ran some distance, but fell among some rows of potatoes at the back of Broady's house, and he was then collared and detained till a constable was sought. It
charge

was alleged that whilst struggling with Mr. Broady the prisoner pulled a knife out, baCthis the defence con- tended was to cut a muffler which Broady twisted so tight that it almost choked Carter. Mr. Davies ridi- culed the allegation that there was any intention of stealing the towel, which was shown to be in rather a dilapidated condition, as Carter had told the police- man he was only having a "bit game" on. Evidence having been given as to Carter's good character, the case was dismissed, and Mr. R. Pierpoint, one of the magis- trates, said it was a most absurd thing to take up the time of the magistrates and everyone concerned with so trumpery a charge. A charge of felony was a very seri- ous thing, and before anyone made it he should seriously consider whether it was worth while running the risk of ruining a man's character for life. A SCHOOLMASTER CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING A SCHOLAR.

John Wright, the master of Daresbury schools, was charged at Daresbury Sessions, on Tuesday, with having assaulted a scholar, named Thomas Dobson, on the 23rd of June. Mr. Jenkins, of Warrington, defended on ha- half of the National Union of Elementary School Teachers. The lad Dobson's evidence did not amount to much more than that he Wks thrashed on the back by Mr. Wright, and he admittted that this took place after Miss Kelly, his teacher, had sent for the master to take him in hand. Mrs. Dobson, the mother of the boy, said his skin was marked with the blows he had received, and P.C. Dutton, who had been called in by the mother, said he found five marks across the lnft arm and one on the right arm. The officer confessed that he had himself received worse punishments when at school than what the lad seemed to have got. In defence it was stated that Miss Kelly had to send for the master because the lad would not do his sums. lle was, she said, a notoriously bad boy, and the punishment begot was not half enough. It was further stated that Dobson had attempted to strike the master with a slate, and that his parents had been summoned for not sending him regularly to school. The Chairman said the Bench were of oranien that the school- master had acted quite rightly in punishing the boy, and his (the Chairman's; opinion was that the lad would have been better if he had got more. The case would be dismissed, and the complainant's would have to pay the costs of both sides.
FRACAS ON A BOWLING GRIM. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, two rnen uansed James Rows on and William Turner answered

charges of having disturbed the peace by fignUng in Liverpool-road on the 21st ult. Thomas lurner... summoned for a similar offence, did not put in ati appearance. From a statement made by the rJhlSf Constable it appeared that on the date in questior there was a match at bowls contested on the Bar ,k Quay .lkington, Green, for £lO aside, between a man named PI from St. Helens, and another named Gleave,, 'of Warring- ton. During the process of the game a 'quarrel took place between Howson and Thomas Turne'z, in which the other Turner,took part. The landlor6, as soon as he could, hurried the combatants off the, green, on to the highway, where the disturbance wr.,s continued for a quarter of an hour. In conseqvience the road was thoroughly blocked. It was a most disgraceful sight. He (Mr. Hunt) had received complaints from respectable persons who could not got through the crowd with their vehicles. These proceedings should be stopped, and it would be a question that he might bring before the Licensing Magistrates. He did not know that there was any law to prohibit the game of bowls, because it was a game of skill, but in cases where sums of money were played for there was a good ideal of gambling. Two or three men who were present, the Chief Constable added, tried to stop the fight, and succeeded in parting the combatants. Wherever this gambling took place there was bound to be disorder and disruption. The defendants were each bound over to be of good behaviour, themselves in £5 each, and one surety of £5 each. Yesterday, Thomas Turner was charged with disturbing the peace by being concerned in the fracas. The Chief Constable said that this defendant seemed to have been the instigator of the affair, and he was ordered to be bound over, himself in £lO and two sureties in £5 each, and to pay the costs.

WARRINGTON v. BOOTLE.—The first match between these clubs took place at Bootle. A poor wicket had been prepared, and the Bootle captain on winning the toss, took first innings, Johnson and Bate facing Smith and Jolley. In Smith's first over Johnson was leg before wicket (one for 1.) Williams and Bate put on 13 runs, when the former was leg before wicket to Jolley. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CUICKET.

Two or three weeks ago Lancashire were robbed of a I pretty certain victory over Yorkshire by the bad weather but on Saturday they were recouped to some extent by being saved from a probable overthrow by Gloucester- shire by the downfall of rain. The match was full of in- terest. Dr. W. G. Grace came down fresh from his splendid display in the match against Australians,and his runs were made in a manner worthy of his reputation. We are told that some cavil was raised at one of the umpires for not giving the champion out, caught at the wicket, when a confident appeal was made very early in the inning,s,but the umpire thought the batsman was not out, and very properly said so.

Whether his decision was erroneous or not, the result was that the spectators saw precisely what they came to see—namely the champion hitting :first-rate bowling to all parts of the field. There is a tradition about the champion that on one occasion in playing against a Twenty-two he went in first and was obviously out "lbw" to the first ball; but that umpire gave him "not out," and the great batsman thereupon began to hit in a style which amply rewarded the umpire for his leniency. Grace hit, indeed, so heavily and so long that his score was counted by hundreds, and the third day lfound him still at the wicket. The umpire is said to ,have excused himself on the ground that he "wanted to see him play" —and he had enough of it before the stumps were drawn

A writer says that the downfall of the Lancashire team on Friday morning was not to be altogether ac- counted for by the state of the 'wicket; some allowance must surely be made for Woof and Roberts's bowling and the excellence of the fielding. In the second innings the display was extremely creditable t) the batsmen, with two notable exceptions. Mr. Hornby set his men a splen- did example, and did all that a captain and great cricke- ter could do to atone for the shortcomings of the first innings ; but the ground that had been lost couid not be regained, and Gloucestershire went away with a "moral victory."

Kent, on Tuesday, suffered defeat at the hands of the Australians, who had nine wickets in band when the end arrived. The Australians have now brought their num- ber of successes even with the defeata, viz., nine, whilst six matches have been drawn. From start to finish the visitors had the whip hand of their opponents, and the result was in great measure due to the splendid bowling of Turner and Ferris, who performed wonders with the ball. Beautiful weather again favoured the contest. Taken altogether it was a busy days' cricket, as in four hours and ten minutes 15 wickets fell for an aggregate of 260 runs. When stumps were drawn on Monday the Australians had completed an innings for 189 runs, and Kent had lost six wickets for 53 runs. The County thus wanted 55 to avoid following on, but the task was altogether too formidable for the four remaining batsmen, who in thirty minutes were sent back for an addition to the score of only 22 notches. Being in a minority of 112, Kent had therefore to follow their innings, and at the second attempt they did much better than previously, more than one on their side playing sterling good cricket. ,The :venture lasted exactly three hours, and realised 174 runs, six bowlers being tried.

Yet another decisive defeat has to be added to the already long list of disasters sustained by Sussex this season; Surrey on Wednesday beating them by an in- nings and 165 runs. After Surrey's formidable score of 392 made on Monday, the visiting county could hardly hope to make a successful fight, and it was no surprise that they had to follow on in a minority of 301. The second innings was a better one than the first, being chiefly notable for a fine dashing score of 50 by Bean. Coming as it does after his fine innings of 101 against the Australians at Brighton, it shows that Sussex are by no means badly off for batsmen. He received minor support front Quaire, who contributed 21, whilst An- drews also hit out and soon put together 20. When stumps were drawn on Monday night Sussex in their first innings had lost two wickets for 28 runs. On resum- ing on Wednesday,Quaife and Bean were soon separated, whilst Lohmann and Sharpe,bowling unchanged through- out, dismissed the remaining batsmen in an hour for 91. Lohmann was wonderfully successful, taking seven wickets at a cost of 5 runs apiece. Sussex, who were 301 runs in arrear, had to follow on, and commenced their second innings at ten minutes past one. They were all got rid of by four o'clock, after batting rather over two hours. Surrey have now-twice beaten Sussex in a single innings.

The match between Notts and Derbyshire was brought to a conclusion at Derby on Tuesday afternoon, when Notts ware declared the winners of an uninteresting game with an innings and 71 runs to spare. On Monday evening Notts, with three wickets in hand, were 182 runs to the good, and on Tuesday morning the three wickets were captured for an addition of 40 runs. Notts held a commanding lead of 222, and although Derbyshire made a very much more creditable show with the bat at their second attempt than at their first, they never looked like wiping out the deficiency, and the venture closed , for 151.

When play ceased at Dewsbury on Tuesday night there seemed every prospect of a capital finish, as Yorkshire, with four wickets down in their second innings, required 140 runs to win. Some rain fell during the night, but on Wednesday the wicket was nevertheless in fairly good order. Woof arid Roberts, however, bowled splendidly, and in sixty-five minutes they got rid of the remaining batsmen foir the addition of 55 runs. The whole side were thus out for 120, and Glourester,hire were left vic- torious by 84 runs. After the ill-luck they have experi- enced this season Gloucestershire's success, the first this summer,will he welcome,to the supporters of the county. Woof was mainly responsible for the cheap dismissal of the Yorkshiremen, and his figures do him immense credit.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

The Brighto'n record has again been broken. One day last week S. F. Edge, covered the distance "out and home" in 7 hours 2min. 50sec., which is 10min. lOsec. faster than the time occupied by F. W. Shorland, and 47min. lOsec. less than the time occupied by Jim Selby, when he piloted the Old Times Coach in 1888. S. F. Edge is not related in any way to T. A. Edge, the well-known M.A.C. cyclist. though the latter rider, mounted on a tandem tricycle in company with F. Cooper (of Marriott and Cooper), rendered his 'famous namesaire very valu- able assistance in his great ride.

Mr. Charles Lucas, a member of the Sefton and Dingle Cycle Club, has just accomplished a smart distance re- cord from Liverpool to Edinburgh. He started from Liver- pool at midnight on Sunday, and though the roads were for the most part in bed condition, especially at Shap Fells,and the weather showery, he reached Edinburgh at 9.35 p.m. on Monday. Mr. Lucas thus rode the distance, which is 263 miles, in 21 hrs. 35 mins., beating the record made by M`Cann the other week. Mr. Lucas rode a safety with solid tyres, made by Winrow, of Ken- sington.

Six members of the Warrington Cycling Club turned out for the run to Cranage on Saturday last. This is one of the favourite runs, the road being the best in this district, the country exceptionally fine, and last but not least,the tea at the farm is always a treat,and is too well known among cyclists to need comment. No doubt the unsettled state of the weather had something 6) do with the small muster. The veterans, however, turned out as usual to uphold the honour of the club. It evidently takes something more than a cloudy sky and wet roads to k4p them at home.

The run to-day (Saturday) is to Sale Botanical Gardens, where a team has been entered for the two mile inter-club race, and, if reports may be relied on, they should give a good account of themselves. It is worth noting that lamps must be lit this evening at 8.45.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

We seem to have borrowed still another idea frcm our American coasins, for baseball is now fast becoming a most popular game, and especially in the North, where a league (with, we expect, the inevitable Challenge Cup) has been formed, and the famous Preston north End football tearrf, amongst others, are keepirig themselves in condition by a constant practice of this comparatively new amusement. As is well-known, it is the premier sport of its sort in the United States, and prominent pro- fessionals at the game can earn incomes which would make even our leading cricket professors envious. Five or six hundred a year is a by-no-means extraordinary or out-of-the-way salary for a first-rate " pitcher." I fancy there is just one thing necessary 05 make the Warrington F.C. sports on Monday a great success, and that is fine weather. The entries for the different events are more numerous this time than they have ever been before, and include the names of many noted athletes. The committee have taken great pains to make a good track, and, as I have said, all that is now wanted iz favourable consideration from the weather god.

TO THE DEAF.—A person cured of Deafness and noises in the heed of 23 years standing by a simple remedy, Will send a deserintion of it FREE to any Person who applies to NICHOLSON, 21, Bedford Bquate, London, W.C.-4det.

COLLIERY DISASTER IN FRANCE. 120 LIVES LOST. ST. ETIENNE, TUESDAY EVENING.—A terrible explosion of fire damp occurred this evening in the Pelissier Coal Mine, in the Jardin des Plantes district. The miners on the night shift had just reached the bottom of the mine, and it is calculated that 141 workmen were in the pit at the time of the explosion. ST. ETIENNE, TUESDAY, 10 P.M.—The authorities at the Pelissier Mine state that 165 lamps were given out this evening to the night shift men. Ten of those in the pit have been brought up in safety, while thirty-five injured miners have been rescued, thus making the number of the dead about 120.

ST. ETIENNE, WEDNESDAY.—TiIe work of rescue in the Pelisser coal mine has been concluded. Eighty-four dead bodies have been recovered, while of seventy-three miners who have been brought to the pit mouth fourteen have since succumbed to their injuries. A naked lamp,which has been found in the workings, appears to have been the cause of the catastrophe. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIMS. Sr. ETIENNE, THURSDAY.—The funeral of the unhappy victims of the recent terrible mining disaster here took place this morning. There were seventy-five coffins, many of which were covered with garlands and on some of these were inscribed the words, "To die martyrs of labour."

div.head: WIFE BEATING AND SUICIDE.
div.p: WIFE BEATING AND SUICIDE.

At Wincanton, Somerset, on Sunday, Thomas Parsons, after having dinner with his wife and a young woman lodger, attacked his wife and beat her with a hammer. The young woman rescued her, whereupon Parsons went out, and, after ineffectually trying to drown himself,' returned home and hanged himself. The woman may ' recover.

The Conservatives and Unionists of the Brightside Divi- sion of Sheffield,on Thursday night adopted Mr. Bargrave Deane, M.A., Recorder of Margate, as their candidate to oppose Mr. Mundella, at the next election.

div.head: CLOSE OF BISLEY DIEETINU.
div.p: CLOSE OF BISLEY DIEETINU.

The Bisley meeting closed on Saturday. The Royal Cambridge Challenge Shield was competed for by four troopers representing regiments of cavalry, and was won by the 14th Hussars, who scored 115 points in Bmin. 58sec. The Evelyn Wood competition took up the whole of the afternoon, and was carried on in the presence of the General from whom it derives its name. The highest percentage of hits to the rounds fired was made by the Ist Battalion Royal West Surrey, with 26.73. The deci- sion of the Council against a formal distribution of prizes caused some disappointment. Sergeant Bates, the winner of the . Queen's Prize at Bisley, returned to Birmingham on Saturday night, and there was a great demonstration in his honour. He was met at the Great Western station by about 1,200 meq of the Volunteer battalion to which he belongs, and in a carriage and pair was driven through the principal streets ,of the town, followed by thousands of people. At the 'headquarters the Volunteers were supplied with beer, with which they drank Bates's health, and subsequently he was entertained at the officers' mess. In the neigh- bourhood of Bates's house the streets were illuminated with Chinese lanterns.

div.head: DOUBLE MURDER .IN LOI.OON. --- ATTEMPT TO LYNCH THE MURDERER.
div.p: DOUBLE MURDER .IN LOI.OON. --- ATTEMPT TO LYNCH THE MURDERER.

A double murder was committed in Kingsland, London, on Wednesday evening, under startling circumstances. The murderer is a discharged soldier named Hargan, and his victims were two carmen, Walter Wheeler, aged about 35, residing at 85, Hertford-road, Kingsland • and William Lambert, aged about 60, residing at 25, Felton. street, Hoxton. The tragedy is said to be the outcome of a quarrel in a local public-house, but on this point the evidence is conflicting. There appears, however, to be no doulA about the circumstances of the crime. Wheeler, Lambert, and a man named Martin were stand- ing at the corner of Downham and Harford-roads, when Hargan' who was the stronger, passed the remark that lie had a revolver, and some one shouted out "Hi," whereupon he turned, levelled a six-chambered Colt's revolver at the trio, and fired three shots in quick suc- cession. Wheeler and Lambert fell dead, both shot through the head, but Martin escaped. A desperate struggle with the mtirderer ensued. A crowd attacked him, but he avoided capture for some minutes, and then William Knifton, brother of the pugilist of that name, and a man named Newman secured him, the former being injured in the struggle for the weapon, three chambers being discharged. For about eight minutes the murderer struggled with his captors on the ground, the crowd meanwhile kicking and stoning him. A rope was put round his neck, but Knifton relegsed it, and with diffi- culty he was put into apassing cart, his captors having to secure him by sitting upon him. When charged at the Police Station he was minus, it is stated, a leg of his trousers, and his head and face were cut, bruised, and bloodstained. He was recently discharged from the Surrey Regiment, but declines to give any particulars about himself or his motive for the tragedy. Another r.port says : About half-past four o'clock on Wednesday afternoon a double murder was committed in Hertford-road, Kingsland, London. Three men— Walter Alfred Hargan, Wm. Lambert, and John Wheeler —quarrelled in a public house, and on leaving continued wrangling as they walked up Hertford-road. When they reached Downhain-road Hargan drew a revolver and shot the other two men, who both expired almost im- mediately. The bodies were removed to Hackney mortuary. Hargan on being arrested was roughly treated by the crowd. He is said to be a discharged soldier from the P.nd West Surrey Regiment.

div.head: PRISONER IN COURT.
div.p: THE PRISONER IN COURT.

_ . On Thursday, at the North London Police Court, Walter Alfred Hargan, 27, deseribed as a clerk, of Southgate- road, Islington, was charged with " feloniously killing and slaying, on the 30th July, 1890, William Lambert, 45, and John Wheeler, 40, by shooting them with a revolver at Hertford-r)ad, Kingsland." The prisoner's face bore marks of the ill-treament he had received at the hands of the crowd after the murders, and he had been supplied with a decent suit of clothes in exchange f‘r the rags which the crowd had left him with. Evidence hav- ing been given as to the circumstances under which the crime was committed, a remand was granted. It was transpired that the prisoner, who has been in the West Surrey Regiment, was to have gone to America last June, but unaccountably remained at home.

THE BEHRING SEA DIFFICULTY. BRITISH SHIP BOARDED.

NEW Y 012%, THIIRSDAY.—A despatch from Victoria, Vancouver, states that information has been received from the captain of the British sealing ship Ariel, to the effect that, while at sea within the disputed limits, his vessel was boarded by an officer of the United States ship Rush, who tillowed him a copy of President Harrison's proclamation, expressing the intention to enforce American rights in the Behring Sea seal fishery. The officer, who behaved in a friendly spirit, strongly advised the captain to leave to the Behring Sea in order to avoid unpleasantness, as the American warships would follow this season the same drastic procedure as last year.

div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP

CANAL RAILWAY COLLISION NEAR ELT.F.SMERE PORT. LOSS OF THREE LIVES. An accident of a terrible character took place on Monday morning at the -Manchester Ship Canal works, near Ellesmere Port, resulting in the death of a man and two youths, who were in the employ of the company. It has been customary to start two workmen's "mail" trains from Ellesmere Port every morning, one at 5.30, and the other at 5.40, in order to convey the navvies and other employees to the scene of their labours on different parts of the canal works, extending over what is known as the Ince section. The first mail, it should be explained, runs through Ince to Frodsham Marsh, a distance of about seven miles; and the second proceeds to Ince only, which is some three and a half miles up the line from Ellesmere Port. On Monday morning, the 5.30 engine, ' called the Rhymney (which is usually despatched from Ince to Ellesmere to take the men to their work) had not arrived at Ellesmere Port as usual, and accordingly it was decided that the 5.40 engine (the Deal) should not only convey all her ordinary trucks but those which are usually relegated to the Rhymney. The Deal had in all ten trucks, containing four hundred men, when she left Ellesmere Port at 5.40. After proceeding a mile along the line the driver George Copeland, perceived the Rhymney coming towards Ellesmere with four empty trucks in front. At this part of the permanent way, there are two loops or sidings, and between them there is a stretch of single line, for a distance of about two hundred yards. It would appear to have been the business of thedriver of the Rhymney, Thomas Dunbebbin to have run his engine into one of these sidings, until the other passed He adhered to the rule on reaching the first loop, but he went in again on the main line, expecting it is said, to be able to get into the other siding before the Deal came up. He, however, must have miscalculated his distance, and ere he arrived at the place of safety (the second loop) the 'Ellesmere Port train was on him, although Copeland did his very best to avert the accident by let- ting off steam and applying the brakes. The fact that he was coming down ar . incline with a heavy train made it impossible to pull up in time, and both trains ran into each other on the single line with considerable velocity. The Deal and the whole of the ten trucks behind kept the metals, but the force of the collision knocked the Rhymney and the four cmpty trucks off the line. One of them mounted against the engine of the workmen's train, and broke the footplate off the Deal, on which James Henstock, an errand boy, aged fourteen; John Pilliam, deputy timekeeper, aged twenty-two ; and Wal- ter pennett, fireman, aged seventeen, were standing. Immediately before the impact the driver Copeland jumped from his engine and escaped unhurt, but the other three were not so lucky. Both Williams and Henstock were instantaneously killed, the former having been crushed to death and the latter fatally jammed between part of the broken truck and the fire-box of the engine Deal. Bennett, human, was found to be suffering from rvere scalds and his ribs were fractured. He was removed to the Ellesmere Port Hospital, where he received every attention at the hands of Dr. Entrican, but he succumbed to his injuries at half-past five o'clock in the afternoon the immediate cause of death being due to shock. Neither Henstock or Williams had any right to be riding on the engine, and they should have been in the trucks with the rest of the workmen, mine of whom were hurt, though they no doubt felt the effects of the collision, and were a little shaken. The driver of the Rhymney, Thomas Dunbeb- bin, and his fireman, sustained no injuries, each having jumped from their engine when they saw that the col- lision was inevitable. Mr. E. D. Jones, the agent of the contractors, was speedily on the spot, and the line was cleared in the space of an hour. The disaster caused the most intense excitement amongst the workmen, and all sorts of wild rumours were flying about. . .

The engine " Rhymney " was -at work again in the Ince section of the canal very shortly after the accident happened, and remained sin duty throughout the day and evening, being driven by a fresh driver. The Deal is. it is said, damaged in such a manner as to render it unfit for further use. THE KILLED. '

John Williams, twenty-two years of age, deputy time- keeper, whose parents reside in Chester. James Hensteck, fourteen years of age, errand boy, Niho lived at Ellesmere Port. Walter Bennett, seventeen years of age, fireman on the Deal. He was a native of Hally well, and lodged in the village of Ince. ARREST OF ONE OF TFIE ENGINE DRIVERS.

Thomas Dunbebbin, driver of the Rhymney engine, was on Monday detained in custody in the bridewell at Ellesmere Fort. Dunbebbin was visited on Wednesday evening in his cell at the bridewell by several of his fellow workmen on the Ship Canal, with whom he appears to be a favourite. He is a married man and has five children. His wife lives in Salford. For the past fortnight he has lodged at bite. He has been in the employ of Mr. T. A. Walker, the contrictor for the Ship Canal, since 1871. ENGINE-DRIVER CHARGED WITH MAN- SLAUGHTER.

On Tuesday, morning, Thomas Dunbebbin, engine driver, was brought up before Mr. Johs Thomson, magistrate, at the offices of Mr. W. H. Churton, clerk to the county magistrates, Chester, charged with, having caused the death of John Williams, James Benstock, and Walter Bennett, on Monday morning, on the Ship Canal works at Great Stanney, near Ellesmere Port. The pri- soner was brought from Ellesmere Port Bridewell in the custody of a police-constable. Evidence as to the arrest and the charging of the prisoner having been given by Constable Proctor, Frederick Dixon was examined. He stated that he was a ganger on the Manchestet Ship Canal. On Mon- day, at about five minutes to six o'clock, he was standing against the tool box, close to where the accident took place, which happened on the main route from'Ellesmeie Port to Ice. The railway was private property belong- ing to the contractor, and was used for the purpose of ,aiding in the construction ot the Canal. It was a single line with several sidings, loop lines, and branches at- tached to it at various places. Close to where the acci- dent took place there was a signal post with two arms, one for the up and the other for the down signal. The signals were worked by youths. There was a system of shifts practised by the employes, but there was always somebody at the signal spots. At ten minutes to six o'cllta he saw the engine Deal coming up from 'the dire6tion of Ellesmere Port with.the mail train, consisting of about eleven trucks, having on them about 400 men. These nen were going to their work and would be put off at various points along the line of route. Witness heard the Deal engine whistling. She was whistling loudly. He looked along the line, and saw the engine Rhymney coming in an opposite direction to the Deal. The driver of the Rhymney was Thomas Dunbebbin, the prisonerr Witness could not say what speed the Rhymney was being driven at, but Dunbebbin was driving it very fast. There were four empty trucks attached to the front of the Rhymney. Dunbebbin was making for the siding evidently for the purpose of getting out of the way of the Deal. He did not, however, succeed in getting to the siding. Witness did not see Dunbebbin attempting to stop the engine when the whistle of the Deal was blown. The prisoner (interrupting.)—Yes, your worship, I reversed the engine and shut off the steam. Witness (continuing.)—The Rhyriuley ran into the Deal. One of the trucks attached to the Rhymney mounted on the top of the Deal, and the others were knocked off the line. The Rhymney was also knocked off the line. Williams and Benstock, who were on the Deal, were instantly killed. The Magistrates Clerk: If the Rhymney had stopped when she heard the Deal's whistle, would there have been an 'accident P—No, sir. The Magistrate.—Could she have stopped when she heard the whistle P—No, sir. The Magistrate.—You had better not say anything now. An opportunity will be given you afterwards to say what you have to say. Witness (continuing his evidence),—About 300 yards separated the two engines when he heard the whistling. The engines could have been easily stopped within that distance before coming into collision. It was closeagainst the points where the accident took place. The empty trucks in front of the Rhymney- collided with the Deal. The Rhymney did not get into the siding, the signal was towards the other end of Ellesmere Port. There was a person working the signal at the time of the accident. The signal was down for the Deal and up for the Rhym- ney.

The Prisoner.—Your Worship, there was nobody work- ing the signals. The signals were down. In reply to a question from the magistrate, the pri- soner said he lived in the huts at Ince. His home was at Manchester: Dunbebbin was then remanded till to-day (Saturday), when he will be brought up at the Petty Sessions for the Chester Castle Division. In the meantime he will re- main in custody in the lock-up at Hoole, Chester. THE INQUEST.

Dr. Churton, district coroner, opened an inquest on Monday- evening at the Grosvenor Hotel, Ellesmere Port, on the bodies of Williams, Henstock, and Bennett. After the jury had viewed the bodies at the hospital, evidence as to identification was given, and the inquest was then adjourned till Wednesday morning, when Thomas Dunbabbin, engine driver, was again present in custody. The Coroner expressed his satistaction that the officials, contrary to their usual practice, had brought the prisoner there to make a statement or cross-examine witnesses. Mr. Yates, barrister, represented the Ship Canal contractors,and expressed their regret at the disas- ter. Copeland, the driver of the Deal engine, said he had seven men on the locomative with him, and was drawing 400 men in eleven trucks. When he saw the Rhymney engine coming he opened his whistle and reversed his en- gine, but the other train ran into him. He saved himself by jumping off, and tour others got off in safety, but the three persons named were killed. He was descending an incline when the other train was approaching, which rendered it difficult to pull up. The other engine was coming up, and as it was drawing only four empty trucks it was very easy to stop it. The driver of the Rhytnney engine had been there a fortnight. It was a rule that witness's train should have the whole line to go forward to put down the men. Had Dunbabin reversed his engine when witness ',blew his whistle the accident could not have happened, but the Rhymney engine was going finger than tow. PA.OIIIX alleged that he was

THE DEATH AT A WARRINGTON FORGE.

On Monday Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an in- quest at the Police Parade Room relative to the death of Joseph Hall, a foreman puddler at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company's Works, who died suddenly whilst at work under circumstances narrated last week. After the inquest had been opened, Mr. Lowdon Wells, undertaker, said that before the jury had inspected.the body it had been screwed down in the coffin, and in his opinion it would be danger- ous to health to again open the coffin.—lnspector Spinks said that'was the first intimation the 'police had received of the matter, and the Coroner added that the undertaker should have informed the police so that the jury might have had a view of the body. —Mr. Wells stated that the family of the deceased were so annoyed by the smell from the body that they had asked him to screw the lid down and he had not had time to tell the police.—The Coroner re- marked that, as the undertaker was of opinion that it would be dangerous to health to open the coffin, he should excuse the jury from viewing the body. The law re- quired them to view the body, and in not doing so they were acting illegally,but he would take the responsibility for that. His view of the question of inspecting bodies was that, in very many cases, the inspection was un- necessary, and if the law allowed any opening he should excuse the juries from making inspections in many cases. The inspection was, however, in some instances abso- lutely necessary, as, for example, in the case of murder. Evidence was then taken and showed that deceased, who was deemed a healthy man, went to work as usual on the morning of the Thursday previous. He afterwards complained of feeling ill, and after sitting down for a few minutes, fell to the ground and expired before a doctor arrived. A verdict of death from natural cawes was returned.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Warrington, on Wednesday night. Alderman Harrison presided, and there were also present, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton; Messrs. Dobson, T. Jones, Davies, W. Houghton, Balharry, smith, Eddowes, Heaton, Humphreys, J. Houghton, Auk- land, Hood-Wright, Gill, Jolley, Hibbert •' J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superin- tendent of Padgate schools.
SCROOL, FEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 62 cases.
THE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE 00 IN FORA CONVEYANCE.

The Schools Committee, in their minutes, recommended that a conveyance be provided for the purpose of bring- ing the Committee to and from Padgate on the occasion of their fortnightly meeting.—The CLERK said that recom- mendation could not be allowed in that form. He should suggest that in lieu of that, an arrangement be made for either a cab or a bus proceeding from the clerk's office, or from the Central station, at a certain hour on the meeting days. The minute would rather imply that they were to have a horse and carriage constantly.— The CHAIRMAN: Do you propose to go with postilions? (Laughter.)—Mr. ATYKLAND : We dont want to go shabby. —Mr. W. Hounlrrow said he had not agreed with the minute at the Committee meeting but the rest of the Committee seemed to be unanimous. He was rather unwilling to go on with the matter without, a little notice, as he thought it was rather premature.—The CLERK recommended that the minute be withdrawn for the present. He thought the Committee meetings as a rule fit in with the trains to and from Padgate, and if they took a conveyance it would have to stop at the schools the whole of the time of the meeting. It was only reasonable that gentlemen going to a place like Padgate Schools should be provided with means of conveyance, and the only question was whether the more expensive provision would be more convenient than the provision already made. He sup- posed that the railway fare to Padgate was so small that the members had not cared to ask for it.—ln answer to the Chairman, it was stated that the distance from Pad- gate Station to the schools was about half-a-mile.—Mr. W. FIOUGHTON moved that the minutes of the Committee be passed with the exception of that referring to the con- veyance.—Mr. HEATON moved that the minutes be passed as they stood. He pointed out that Mr. Houghton and other Guardians living in the neighbourhocd of the schools were very little affected by the incenvenience of getting too and from the schools, but if the Board had seen the steeplechases he (Mr. Heaton) had seen to get from the schools to the station in time to catch a train they would at once adopt the recommendation, which, he thought, was a very reasonable one.—Mr. Aukland said he believ- ' ed other Unions did the same thing.—The CLemt thought that, after the explanations that had been made the request was a reasonable one, and he suggested that an arrangement be made with the bus proprietors.—Mr. HEATON said he thought the cost would only be aboutes. or Bs. a journey.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON pointed out that only a portion of the Committee would be convemenced by the proposed arrangement, and added that the pro- posal when made before had been rejected on those grounds.—Mr. HEATON said eleven out of fifteen members travelled from Warrington.—The proposal of the Com- mittee was then adopted. acttrrs to tin Clutor. -;-,r HE SUNDAY OPENING OP WARRINGTON
LIBRARY.

Sir,—l should like to endorse the plea you put forward in a leading article last week for the Sunday opening of 'Warrington Library and Museum. It-seems to me that there is one question above all others which 9u,glit to be considered in a matter of this kind, and that is, whether the public are disposed to avail themselves to any con- siderable extent of the opportunities for visiting the library and museum afforded by Sunday opening. As you point out, that question has, by the experience of other towns, been answered in the affirmative most emphatically. I suppose it may be taken for granted that the people of Warrington are,pretty much like these -of Stockport, and at Stockport the Sunday attendance is very nearly equal to the total attendance of the other six days of the week. The returns-from other towns which ' have tried the experiment of Sunday opening appear to be very much like those of Stockport, and, therefore, it is most conclusively proven that Sunday opening is a much appreciated public benefit. What more aught to be said to ensure that benefitbeing extended to the people of Warrington? I can only think of one ,argurnent that should have any weight against Sunday opening, and that is, that it may deprive the librarian and his assistants of their day of rest in the week. I coOfess I should consider that a .very strong arg,niment if there were no way of meeting it. There is a wholesome feeling abroad that the leisure of the workers should be increased and not diminished, and it might well -be regretted if public Coporations set a bad example in this respect. But, as you say, this is a matter of detail for the Library Committee to arrange. It may mean a little additional expense, but is it not one of the chief functions of the Committee to spend public money in order to make the institutions in Bold-st. as useful and attractive to the public as pos.sitriel—Yours truly, A. B.

div.head: GRENADIERIGUAr.DS AND THEIR COLONEL.
div.p: THE GRENADIERIGUAr.DS AND THEIR COLONEL.

Sir,—The Guards have been sent to Bermuda to suffer penal servitude for three years. What their . crime has been has not been told. It seems rather strange to con- demn men to penal servitude when those ,who sit in judgment and pass sentence refuse to state the crime or crimes for which the men are sentenced—some to two years, eighteen months, and one year's imprisonment at home, with personal degradation at the -expiry of the sentences. And what for? It must not be told. Why? Because it would involve the personal disgrace of "officers and gentlemen." Insubordination is spoken of on the part of the men— mutiny, a refusal todo duty, disobedience, disrespect to officers, ,tc. These are some of the charges rumour assigns to the men. I maintain that tyranny on the part of the-officers and petty officers, from colonels to corporals, is often carried to such an extent that disobe- dience becomes a virtue rather than a crime. There are bounds to human endurance even in the army, and there are mean spirits who overstep these bounds. We gather indirectly from the severe reprimand of the 'Duke of Cambridge to the men, and his request to Colonel Eaton to "be good to the men," that they had been treated in some form until they could no longer bear it, and the effect was mutiny—followed by expatriation, penal servitude, imprisonment at home and degradation, with the severe condemnation of the Commander-in- Chief. He says they have disgraced themselves, and that he is ashamed of them.! What next? His Royal High- ness has been their Colonel since 1881,`for which service, or supposed service, he draws £2,132 ,a • year and has drawn it for Z 9 years.; in all £61,828. 'What has he done for it? As Colonei of the Regiment, it was his duty to personally devote his time to the welfare of the service and the men underhiscommand ; but, being a Royal Duke, he followed the example of Royalty in general and did nothing of the kind. He with others of his rank monopolise a number of fat-paying offices, simply for the pay, for which they do nothing until.a crisis comes, and then they talk of shame and disgrace. Where now, in this case, as between the Guards and their Colonel, does the onus of shame and disgrace, rest? The men have struck against unnecessary, irritating, vexatious, and harrassing orders and commands borne long and patiently. The Duke,who should be.well and thoroughly acquainted with all that goes on in .his regiment, knows nothing of this until it comes as a surprise to him. This is the outcome of his neglect, the shirking of the duty for which he is paid £BOO a month, and then he says he is ashamed of the rnen. He should be ashamed of himself. .' You have disgraced yourselves,' he -says, and how truly could they answer "and so have you." Conduct like the Duke's would, in the commercial world, be punished, for when it is laid bare it is something like obtaining money ender false pretences. The fault does not so much rest with the Duke as with Parliament and the wretched system-under which we are governed, which creates and perpetuates such a fraudu- lent system of robbery by Royalty. In addition to his many military posts, the Duke of Cambridge is and has been since 1852 Ranger of St. Jamas, --the Green, and Hyde Parks, and, since 1857, Ranger of Richmond Park. The income of the Rangershi,ps at a low estimate will be £2,000 a year, with Gloucester "House, -rent, rates, and taxes free, and this is the man who tells men - who are goaded by tyranny to desperation that he is ashamed a them They may be very thankful that" the cat" is dead, or some of their backs would have been well scratched by this. I hope good may come out of the evil done, and that the administration•of the army and the position of the men may be improyed,by more rational and humane treatment than has frequently been the case in the past.-1 am, sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, July 28th, 1190.

div.head: INSTITUTE OF JOURNALISTS
div.p: INSTITUTE OF JOURNALISTS

PRESSMEN AND PILLS. BUSINESS AND PLEASURE COMBINED. BY Ko-Ko. As a rule journalists, more commonly called pressmen in these peculiar parts, are a deuced hard-working set, but on occasions they can fling a loose leg, so to speak. with the best. "Guiding public opinion," and making good speeches for bad speakers, is all very well in its way, but it becomes monotonous sometimes, andthe humble quill-pusher feels that he must spread himself a bit or burst.
The journalists of the 'United Kingdom, late in the day, it must be conceded, have organised themselves, _ _ .

and now have the distinction of forming a chartered Institute, and about four times a year they meet in different towns to transact business, and, where opportunity permits, to enjoy themselves a little Pressmen are considerably scattered. They labour night and day, and penetrate to the uttermost ends of the earth. They toil, also do they spin, and it is very seildom that they get the chance to fore- gather in a friendly way. If the " G.0.M.," or some other big spouter is a-spouting, the reportorial section nod to each other over the table, but as the insatiable "comp," is always waiting for "copy," and the wires have to be kept in agitation, the nod is about all that happens in the way of hob-nobbino% You can't ask Jones, of the "Post," to go out an% , " see a man"; he is too busy with the " flimsies " ; and if you put the question to Robinson, of the "Examiner," he snarls because you cause him to miss the tag end of a sentence involving the fate of the Empire—and goodness knows what besides. And thus it comes to pass that the quarterly meetings of the Institute of Journalists are in the , nature of a good thing; not only in the way of business, which, by the bye, is never neglected, but because they bring together in friendly intercourse the festive jokers who combine to turn the lever that controls the world, and keeps it in a state of due respectability. The Liverpool district of 'the Institute takes the cake in point of strength of num- bers, and, as it is with the Liverpool district that this article deals, it may be pertinent to point out that it follows the lead of Lancashire in thinking a good deal of itself. It embraces a wide area, and', even runs over into Wales on the one hand and the Isle of Man on the other; so that you will under- stand that a meeting of the said district is,, vulgarly speaking, no small beer. The District has held many a pleasant meeting,' but the one that came off on Saturday was, to put it in that way, " Worth a guinea a box." Ali ; that makes you think of Beecham, does it'? •And straight-' way your internal works are set a fluttering. "What are the wild waves saying ?" as Beecham puts it, hasn't very much to do with the matter in 'hand.' Instead of babbling about luxurious pills, the wild waves aforesaid are for this occasion only singing of the pleasures of the journalists who met at. St. Helens on Saturday. All of which means to convey that the quarterly meeting of the before mentioned district, was held on the date in question, in the said town of St. Helens—which may incidentally be described as a go-ahead place, with a fine Town. Hall, pills, steam-trams,and newspaper men thrown in to make weight. Somewhere about forty of the faithful, of all shapes and sizes, turned up. The London & North-Western Railway had the responsi- bility of conveying to the gay and festive scene Mr. R. M. Read, Mr. H. Ridgway. and Mr. Haigh. of the "Guardian ;" Mr." Koko," of the " Examiner ;" Mr. W. Gill and Mr. IL Isherwood. of the " Warrington Observer ;" and Mr. Law, of the " Widnes Weekly News." Other delegates came from Liverpool, Wrexham, Southport, Wigan, and Chester, but the names mentioned are a sufficient, guarantee of the genuineness of the article. The St. Helens journa- lists extended the right hand of fellowship in a. real lively fashion, and it was well shaken. make the entertainment of the guests doubly sure, they had the hospitable assistance of the greatest advertiser in the world—to wit, Beecham—who, on the occasion in question was, if repetition will be excused, worth considerably more than "a guinea a box." As a matter of fact, Mr. Thomas Beecham, and his I wide-awake manager, Mr. Rowed, had a very large finger in the pie of welcome, and did the thing handsomely in the • way of greeting the pressmen. The first "item on • the programme " was a visit to the famous "pillatial" factory, where the visitors completely lost themselves—in wonder. It was, indeed, an important function. Well ;it was sur- prising. Such a large place ; such fine rooms; such civility. And all out of pills! Electric light, velvet carpets, pictures, statues, and yet again, civility. And all out of 'Tis passing strange, but when you learn and digest the fact that these little "health restorer" of Beecham's are turned out of a wonderful 'machine at the rate of I-5,000 per one minute of sixty seconds, and are boxed, stamped, labelled, packed, and despatched all over the civilised world in the twinkling of an eye, as the saying goes, it is not so strange after all that the controllers of this unique enterprise find their paths to lie in pleasant places. The representa- tives of the press spread themselves all over the place, and everything was fully explained, with the exception of trade secrets, in regard to which "Mum's the word:" McGinty, who was a very decent fellow, enjoyed • the 'matter thoroughly. It is a pity he was absent-minded. He was watching the pills come tumbling gaily out of the machine, and if he hadn't been so abstracted he wouldn't have kept swallowing an odd one every minute or two. Alas, poor McGinty. we knew him well. He has gone hence, and the "Daily So-and-So" laments his loss. His name had been heard in the land, and fame was at his feet. Nothing now remains of him but the outer dross of his ready-made suit, and a wail of lamentation follows him to whatever parti- cular place he may have arrived. His was a sad fate ; but gluttony in pills never did pay. However, perhapelleGinty is happier hence. The gloom his disappearance caused was soon removed, again by the powerful hand of Beecham. This came about in the ,way of an equally powerful luncheon,served up. or down;if you like that better. at the sign of the -Fleece. Mr. Beecham occupied the chair. He looked happy, • and everybody else felt so. The waiters wondered if pressmen were always so hungry, and the pressmen didn't care a pill what the waiters 'thought. They broke bread with a man who spends nearly a hundred thousand pounds a year in advertising, and what else could be desired? Surely-nothing. They gave him three hearty cheers at the finish, and made a rush for a collection of brakes and waggonettes that were in waiting to carry tolinowsley Hall such an intellec- tual weight as has never-before inflicted itself on St. Helens. The visit was a pleasant one, and when all returned to the Town Hall to discuss matters of business weight. which do not need 'to be particu- larised here, it was in such a happy frame of mind as the poor pressman-very-seldom experiences. Tea followed and home again, and all was well. It has just occurred to me that the Editor may • think I have been working an "ad" for Beecham. That is not so ; he works his own "ads," and his •pills work—wonders.

div.head: PLEURO-PNEUMONIA.
div.p: PLEURO-PNEUMONIA.

PROSECUTION AND HEAVY PENALTY. Before Colonel George McCorquodale and other .matzistrates,at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Satur- day, Stephen Dean, a farmer, at Orford, near War- rington, was summoned for an offence under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) ket of 1878 by having in his possession a cow suffering from pleura-pneu- monia and not reporting it to the authorities, as _required by the Act. It was stated that extracts from the Act relating to the matter had been freely 'posted throughout the district, and Superintendent .Weir stated that on Wednesday, the 16th of July,he visited the defendant's premises and was accom- panied by Messrs. Hewitt and Darwell, veterinary surgeons for the county. He there f ound a cow suffering from pleuro-pneumonia, andan order was obtained for-its destruction. The cow was accord- ingly slaughtered. The defendant gave himself ' out as a " cow doctor" and he (Mr. Weir) told him; that lie had been trafficking in the disease and had spread it. There bad been 21 outbreaks of the disease in the district, and the compensation that had been paid was enormous. In his (Mr. Weir's) •district Otteut £6.000 had been paid. The defendant, be added, had been going about from place to place with a medicine chest pretending that he could cure the disease.—Mr. Hewitt (veterinary surgeon) gave evidence in corroboration, and said there were three other cows in the shippon besides the one suffering from the disease when the place was visited.—The defendant said lie had bad plenty of experience in dealing with the disease, but had treated the animal for quinsey. He was daily expecting the animal to die from that complaint, and he did not suspect pletiro-pneumonia until after the beast was slaugh- tered.--The Chairman said the Bench thougitt the case was a very serious one, and said they would signify their disapprobation of defendant's reclaf:iii cooduct by inflicting a fine of LW and Costa. •
