div.head: EARLESTOWN.
div.p: EARLESTOWN.

A great deal of excitement was occasioned at Earlestown on Saturday, by the report that there had been a terrible attempted murder at the old Sankey Paper Mill, near the old waste heaps known as the Vitriol Mountains. It was currently reported that an old man named Kay had received some dangerous injuries to his head from an axe, and that a man named Mercer, commonly called " Gold- seeker " had been apprehended on a charge of attempting to murder Kay. Inquiries elicited that there was some foundation for toe reports. It ap- pears that Messrs. Kellett and Barker, builders and contractors, Earlestown, as the agents of Messrs. Hicks, Hargreaves and Co., Bolton, owners of the property were engaged demolishing the works. An old man, named Thomas Kay,was employed by them and on Saturday forenoon he was "chipping "bricks with a hatchet on a part of the premises, when Thos. Mercer, a labourer of unsettled residence, and at present out of work, visited him. They had sonic

- conversation and a few minutes later Kay was heard moaning. Mercer was seen running away, and Kay was found to have received terrible injuries to his head. He was lying unconscious at the spot, and after Dr. Valentine had bandaged the wounds Kay was removed in a critical condition to the Warring- ton Infirmary. Mercer was subsequently appre- hended, on a charge of unlawfully wounding Ray. MAGISTERIAL PROCEEDINGS.

At the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday morning, be- fore Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Thomas Mercer, 28 vearsof age, of unsettled residence and described as a labourer, was charged with unlawfully wounding Thomas Kay, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm, by striking him five times on the head with a hatchet, on the the 25th ult. Police Sergeant Longworth stated that about quarter to eleven o'clock on Saturday forenodn Kay, who was engaged by Mr. Kellett in demolishing the old Paper Mill, was sitting down "chipping "bricks with a hatchet. At that time the prisoner Mercer came up and was seen talking, to Kay by a man named Thomas Singleton, who was loading some bricks in a cart. Shortly afterwards Sing,loton, who was about 20 yards away., heard Kay call out "Oh I" and on looking round Singleton saw prisoner standing behind Kay with a. hatchet in his hand. He saw him delibera- tely strike Kay on the head, and Singleton then ran for assistance. He and others saw Mercer run-

'cling, away and found Kay lying on his side 'unconscious, and bleeding profusely from severe wounds on the head. Dr. Valentine was sent for, and on that gentleman's arrival he bandaged his head and ordered his removal to an Infirmary. The prisoner was found hiding.below the Vitriol Mountains among some nettles and other bushes. He was taken into custody by Police Constable Hughes, and on being charged with the offence he replied: "It was his own fault I hit him. I was I going to ask Kellett for a job this morning and Kay said "A d— thing like you ask for a job that has been knocking about so long." Kay was removed on the ambulance litter by the police and was conveyed to the Infirmary at Warrington, where, on being examined, lie was found to be suffering, from a compound fracture of the skull. He had five different wounds on the head. He (Police Sergeant Long,worth) applied for the prisoner to be remanded until Friday morning.—The magistrates accordingly remanded the prisoner.

div.head: DEATH OF KAY.
div.p: DEATH OF KAY.

The announcement of the deat-171--oi- the old man Kay, which took place at Warrington Infirmary, on Thursday morning, occasioned renewed excitemont in Earlestown where both men are well-known. Somewhat tingularly neither the deceased nor the prisoner have ever had any I settled residence, nor any definite means of employment for some years past. The deceased had no relatives in the neighbourhood, and used to earn a few coppers from , tradesmen and others who could find him any little job to do. Where he slept or stayed at nights was often a mystery and it is said he used to sleep in outhouses, barns, stables, or even under hedges when the atmos- nherical conditions were favourable. It is statod that he has a sister and a brother residing in the neighbourhood of Shrewsbury. The prisoner, Mercer, is a native of Earlestown, but, like the man, whose life he is now charged with taking, he has not followed any trade or consistent occupation. A few years ago his aged mother was killed by accidentally falling down stairs, and this fact, coupled with his long idleness seems to have preyed on his mind. It is said he has latterly been somewhat strange in his behaviour and was easiiy excited. THE PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATE. A PLEA OF INSANITY.

At the Earlestown Police Station, yesterday morning, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Thos. Mercer, a labourer, 29 years of age, was charged with the wilful murder of Thomas Kay, an old man, by striking- him on the head with a hatzhet at the Sankey paper-mills, on Saturday last. Outside the police-station a crowd had gathered, and people residing in the vicinity were on the look out to catch a glimpse of the murderer *ho, it was expected, would be taken for trial at the Newton Town Hall. Their expectations, however, were not realised. Superin- tendent Weir said that it was hisduty now to prefer a more serious charge against the prisoner, who, on Monday last, had only been charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm on Thomas Kay. This man had, however, succumbed to his injuries, and hence the graver charge. The deceased man was engaged chipping or clearing mortar Off old bricks down at the Sankey paper works on Saturday morning, and the prisoner was seen to go up and join in conversation with him. A man named Singleton, who was lading his cart a short distance away, heard the deceased cry out apparently from pain, and looking round saw the prisoner strike deceased with an axe on the head. Mercer then threw away the axe and ran off. Singleton called for help, and the deceased was found lying on the plank where he had been chipping bricks; he was unconscious. The police were sent for and also a doctor. Mr. Valentine, who seeing Kay was in ahopeless state, ordered his removal to Warrington Infirmary. Mercer was sub3equently found concealing himself in some long grass, and was given into custody. When charged with the offende of unlawfully wounding, the prisoner replied, "Well, I hit him, but it was his own fault. I was looking for a job of work from Kellett this morning, and Kay said, 'How can a—thing like von be asking for a job that has been knocking about so long 2" Prisoner had since been charged with the graver offence, and be replied. "Did he die this afternoon 2" Singleton was called as a witness. He said he was a carter in the employ of William Long,ton. Ile corrobo- rated the statement of the superintendent, and said that the axe produced was that with which Mercer struck Kay. Police Constable Hughes also gave corroborative evi- dence and Superintendent Weir asked that the prisoner be remanded until Tuesday next. Prisoner was asked by the magistrate whether he had anything to say against a remand, but he made no reply. On the question being repeated by the Stiperintendent he merely shook his head. He was then removed in custody. It is said that Mercer is not in his right mind, and he certainly did not appear to be so at the trial. The axe with which the crime was committed is an old one, and the edge is somewhat broken.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

A sitting of this Court was held on Thursday, before His Honour Judge Foulkes. The cause ,list comprised one default summons, tthree adjourned. plain ts,66original plaints, and 30judgment summ ons PADGATE NEIGHBOI7RS.—WiIIiam Pilkington, brick- maker, Pad gate, sued Peter Philips, .of the same place, a file cutter, for 18s. Defendant disputed the debt. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the plaintiff and explained that 10s. had been lent to make up defendant's rent on the 12thof December last, followed by a loan of 2s. to buy meat with. A further sum or6sowas lent on 19th December last, to redeem out of pledge a watch which defendant had been entrusted with for sale, but which he had •pledged. Plaintiff and his wife corroborated the above, but Philips, though he admitted pledging the watch, flatly denied having borrowed any money. Ulti- mately his Honour said that perjury had been committed on one side or the other, but he was satisfied as to the 12s. having been lent, and gave judgment for that amount. There being some doubt about the remaining 6s. he would not -allow that part of the claim. —William Pilkington, plaintiff in the last named case, sued Mary Hindley, a lodging, house keeper, of l'adgate, for 10s. balance of money lent.—Mr. Longton again appeared for the plaintiff, and stated that on New Year's Day, 1689, 'Mrs. Hindley, with whom plaintiff had tor- merly lodged, asked him for a loan to .enable her to pay her quarters vent. Plaintiff said he was expecting some money neXt day and promised her Mg. She called, but plainiiff had not received his m Dney. However, he gave his wife a SICW suit of clothes and told her to pawn them, and give Mrs. Elindley the money, which Mrs. Pilkington did. The defendant had paid ss. on account. leaving 10s. owing.—The 'defendant disputed ever having, borrowed the money. and denied the truth of the wholeof plaintiff's case, except that she admitted having once had a pair of plaintiff's trousers to pawn.—Mr. Longton offered to ad- journ the case for the attendance of the pawnbroker, but his Honour said he would give judgment for the plaintiff fcgr the amount claimed. A CASE FROM HoLLINg GREEN. -- Richard Lazenbi beerhouse keeper, Hollins +Green, sued Thos. Pemberton, army pensioner, for £3 95.., money lent.—Mr. Browne, for the defence, contended that the money was borrowed to pay for drink, and under the County Court Act. 1288, could not be recovered. The Act stated that "no action shall be brought or maintainable in any county or otber courtto recover any debt or stur of money alleged to be due in respect of the sale of any ate, porter, beer, cider, or perry which was consumed on the premises where sold .or supplied,"—Judgment was given for defendant.

VARIANCE. CLAIM FOR DAMAGES FOR ASSAULT. Last evening, in the Nisi Prius Court at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Smith and a special jury, a case was commenced in which Christian Bower, butcher, Church-st., and Market Hall, Warrington, claimed damages for personal injuries caused by assault from John Cross, also a butcher, of Corporation-st., Warring- ton. The case caused a good deal of interest' amongst Warrington people, of whom there were a good many in Court. Mr. Addison, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw, War- rington), were for the plaintiff, and Mr. Bigham, Q.C. and Mr. A. G. ' Steele (instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, Warrington), appeared for the defendant. Mr. Mulholland informed his lordship that the action was brought to recover damages for an assault, which the defendant denied, and contended that if he did com- mit an assault, it was to preserve the peace. Mr. Addison, Q.C., M.P., in opening the case, said that althougt it was a very serious one—serious as to the conduct of the defendant and as to the consequences that ensued to the plaintiff—it was a very simple one, and would be considered very shortly. Plaintiff com- plained of an assault. He was a Warrington butcher in a large way of business, with a turnover of £lO,OOO or £12,000 a year. On the 3rd of February last he was attending a sate of beasts at the Eagle and Child Inn at Warrington, where there were a number of butchers as- sembled. Amongst them was the defendant John Cross, also a butcher in a large way of business in the town. During the afternoon, while the sale was going on, a little chaff occurred between the son of the defendant, and the plaintiff, on the latter asking Cross, junior, for a light. He (Cross) said—" Do you want it for that stump of a cigar," and then knocked the cigar out of the plaintiff's hand. Plaintiff, in a jocular way, gave Cross a tap on the face. Defendant, whohad beenon theother side of the yard, saw what had occurred, and came towards the two. His son, who seemed to be frightened said that it was only 'in fun, hnt the defendant taking I hold of a stick with both hands, brought it heavily down on the plaintiff's head and literally cracked his skull. He did it with so much violence that the blow sounded all over the yard—it seemed to strike awe ititc the butcher's about—and stopped the progress of the sale for about ten miputes. Subsequently, plaintiff had brain fever, and his life was despaired of for some time. He, however, gotbetter ()Übe fever, but it was found by the doctor that there were eye symptoms and brain symptoms that were very serious. Prefe,ssor Hare, of Owen's University. was called in, and found that the plaintiff's aye was affected. One of the nerves was paralysed, and plaintiff still suffered from headaches caused by condi- tion of the membrane of the brain. The most serious and permanent effects werethose to the eye. The plain- tiff did not claim for loss of business, but his out of pocket expenses were serious, and included the payment for some time of £4 a week paid to a relative in connec- tion with the management of his business. There were , also expenses at the seaside, and for extra nourishment, &c., which made a total of £142 as actual expenses out lof pocket. The most serious matter, however, was that for the rest of his life plaintiff might suffer from the injuries to his left eye, and the injury to the nervous system of the brain. '1 Plaintiff, in the course of his evidence, said, that dur- ing the sale mentioned by Counsel the defendant's son, in reply to arequest for a light made by witness, said "What do you want it for, to light that stump ?" Wit- ness replied " yes," and Cross then tried to knock the cigar out of his hand. Shortly afterwards defendant's son said " Have you got that stump yet," and knocked it out of his hand. Witness picked it up, and a short time afterwards young Cross said—" Throw it away; it will burn your moustache "and-again knocked the cigar out of his hand. Witness was then about to knock young Cross on the shoulders with his stick, but inadvertently hit his head. Defendant came up,and said " Who has done that?? —Cross's son said "Never mind father, it has all been done in fun ; there's no harm in it. It is nothing." Witness got to the son and told him he was very sorry it had hap- pened,and he tried to shake hands, but the father came acrbss and hit witness on the head a heavy blow with the stick. He felt at the moment all right, but excited. He however, fainted a few moments afterwards. He went to Dr. Cannel, but as he was out he went to the Infirmary:where his wounds were dressed by Dr. Smith. He could not sleep at all that night, and in the morning he sent for Dr. Cannell, his regular medical attendant, who attended him two or three times a day. for three weeks, and VMS still attending him. He was in bed three weeks. He suffered from brain fever. Witness had been examined by Prof. Hare and Dr. Glascqt of Manchester. He had to make an arrangement for his brother-in- law to look after his business, and in payment to him he had put £55 in his statement of claim. Witness's busi- wss was a large one. He had a turn over of about £lO,OOO or £12,000. Dr. Cannell's bill was £l2 125., 1 Prof. Hare's £9 95., and Dr. Glascott's £4 45., travelling expenses came to £1 Bs., extra nourishment £25, ex- ' penses at seaside and elsewhere £35. He was away al- together five weeks. His health had not improved. He had had a good deal of pain in his eye, and still suffered. IHe suffered from headache now, and was very restless at night. Cross-examined by Mr. Bigham, witness said he bought and sold cattle, and his brother-in-law who looked after his business had been a butcher but had retired now. And only comes out when he is to get £4 a week ? No. plenty of butcher's managers got £4 a week. He had received that amount from his brother-in-law. When at the seaside witness went into lodgings. He paid 30s. for lodgings. Witness when asked what he paid for meat and drink said that he had to pay more when away from home than he did at home. He had kept no bills He had paid £24 a year as rent for his own house. Cross-examined as to the assault, witness said he could not say -whether or not he had early in the morning been to Stanley cattle market. He had had no drink. witness and defendant had always been good friends before this, but when witness commenced business in the beef trade defendant became very spiteful. It was mot true that witness etruck young Cross across the leg and then on the head with a stick. He did not hit him twice: He struck him once with the butt end of a stick. When the father saw 'blood running from his son's head he said" Who the done this ? Witness became excited. Defendant's son had not brought an action against witness for the blow he struck him. After the assault witness stopped at the sale, and he hid for cattle but he could not remember that he bought any: He had no drink at the Eagle and Child, nor did ne remember going to the Central Hotel at night. His lordship : You can't tell where you were before the fight nor after the fight; really you must pull yourself together. In further cross-examination, witness said Ben. Coss and John Hatton took him away from the sale when he fainted. He didn't lose consciousness but felt weak. Re-examined by Mr. Addison : I was perfectly sober at the sale. Witness did not intend to hit young Cross. By a juryman :1 was in the habit of killing four or five bullocks a week or 20 or 30 sheep. His Lordship : He ;night get up to the value with that.

The Juror They would have to be very valuable. Plaintiff said he also sold ten or twelve pigs. William Hawksworth, butcher, Liverpool, said he at- tended the sale at the Eagle and Child on the 3rd Febru- ary. Plaintiff was sober to all appearance. He saw some play between plaintiff and young Cross, and plain- tiff hit Cross on the head, but it was all in joke. Cross's head bled. Cross-examined by Mr. Bigham He was astonished at defendant being angry when the plaintiff struck his son, as it was all in play—mere child's play. sohn Mainwaring, auctioneer, who conducted the sale at the Eagle and Child 'Hotel, mentioned on being sworn that he attended on subpoenas from both sides. He saw young Cross bleeding from the head. He told his father not to interfere, but the defendant struck plaintiff on the head, causing blood to flow freely. Cross-examined by Mr. Bigham : Defendant was at- tempting to strike plaintiff, when his son said, "Don't interfere." It was all done in a minute. Thomas Unsworth, butcher, John Smith, town crier, Thomas Jackson, butcher, gave corroborative evidence. Other witnesses were, beinv called, when his lordship interfered With the remark "For goodness sake, don't call any more witnesses—you'll call all Warrington." (Laughter.) Counsel, however, called John Coggins, who also de- posed as to the assault. Dr. Cannell•said he was called to attend plaintiff, and found him inta dazed condition. His left eye was blood- shot, and there was great congestion about the veins of the left side of the head. Plaintiff complained of great pain. In The evening plaintiff seemed delirious, and after that he had %rain fever. His life was in danger from inflammation of the membranes and the substance of the brain. Plgirrtiff was not now the same man he was, nor ever would be Cross-examined by Mr. Iligham : He was present when plaintiff was dehrions. Professor Hare said he was called in to seethe plaintiff. He found him suffering from very considerable dulness. He was able to stand, but not without assistance. On the top of the head was a wound, nearly healed, and he ,concluded that he was suffering fromthe result of a blow on the head. There was no doubt that there was inflam- mation of the lining membrane of the skull, and of the brain in its neighbourhood, 'The eyes were bloodshot, and he did not at that titne particularly noticethe symp- toms of the left eye. Witness SaNr plaintiff again on the 9th of April, when his condition had considerably ho- proved. He complained of reduced strength and a diffi- culty in sustaining his attention to mental work. Wit- ness. considered that plaintiff was permanently iej.ured in the respect that the damage he had sustained would not disappear for a considerable time, and that he was liable to have lnflammation in the parts affected. Cross-examined by Mr. Bighatn. Plaintiff was suffer- ing from Intellectual dulness. He was also inclined to take an exceedingly low view of his position, and his Prospects in life. The general tendency of the plaintiff's remarks was distinctly of a pessimistic character. Dr. Glenn% surgeon of the Royal Eye Hospital, Man- chester, deposed to examining plaintiff's left eye, on the 9th of April. ciiie of the muscles was paralysed, and the action of the muscle that lifts the upper lid was weakened. There was considerable intolerance of light, and the left pupil WAS dilated awl fixed. .

div.head: WARItINGTON EXTENSION, &c.
div.p: THE WARItINGTON EXTENSION, &c.
BILL

This Bill came on Thursday before the Earl of Morley, chairman of committees of the House of Lords, as an unopposed measure. A clause had been inserted at the instance of the Lancashire County Council referring to arbitration any ques- tion of compensation for loss of rateable value con- sequent upon this alteration of boundaries. The Local Government Board now Suggested that the arbitration should be left to them instead of to an arbitrator appointed by the parties themselves, or as an alternative that the powers of the arbitrator should be limited. The clauses were gone throngh and approved as they stood in the bill, but Lord Morley said he would defer making the report for a few days in order to give the Lancashire County 1 Council time to consider the suggestions of the ' Local Government Board. One of the conditions of the Bill is thattlhe part of the township of Warrington added to the boidugh be placed 1 upon a differential rating for 5 years. ONE INSTALMEN'f OF COSTS. _

At a meeting of the Warrington Town Council, next Tuesday,the General Purposes Committee will recommend that the sum of £660 be paid to the Parliamentary agents further on account of out-of-pocket expenses in connec- tion with the Warrington Extension and Water Bill.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT RUNCORN BONE WORKS, A shocking accident occurred at Runcorn Bone Works, Sutton, on Wednesday. A young men named Charles Edwin Houghton, and a man named William Wild, were employed in unloading a cargo of bones from a flat, by means of a crane and buck- ets. The two men were in the hold, filling the buckets with bone, which were then hoisted up by the crane. After about ten bucketsful had been removed, the chain of the crane snapped, and a full bucket fell back into the hold of the flat, and alighting upon Hough- ton, smashed his head in dreadful fashion, and also broke one of his arms and legs. He died immediately. On Thursday, at the Aston Arms, Frodsham Bridge, Mr. R. Dobson, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body. —Chas. Eloughton, labourer, of Seven Houses, Frodsham Bridge, said the deceased was his son. He was 22 years of age.—Wm. Wild, of Rocksavage, said he had worked for Mr. Riley at the bone Works for three months. The deceased had been longer in the employ. On Wednes- day morning he and the deceased were engaged in empty- ing a flat laden With bone. They were in the flat, and George Rulse was the crane driver. There were two buckets in use and bone was filled into these and after- wards drawn up by the crane. They had sent up nine or ten buckets when the accident happened. An empty bucket was sent down and the full one dropped. He did not hear the chain snap, nor see the bucket fall, and he was quite startled when he saw the bucket roll over and the deceased lay dead at his feet. The chain was .brokeu and part of it fell with the bucket. He did not know how long the chain had been in use.—George Hulse, Frodsham the crane driver, said he heard the chain snap and he called out "Hey up" and then saw the bucket fall straight upon the back of the deceased, who was stooping at the time.—By the Coroner: He had several times , warned the men against standing under the buckets. Houghton 'had frequently done this kind of work, and he had warned him. It was a link of the chain which snapped. It was not a new chain and there was nothing to tell him the chain was wrong. About a week ago he examined, the chain and it appeared all right then.—The bucket was half way up when the chain snapped. He had known the chain to break three times previously, but there had not been any accident. It was over six years since it last broke.—Mr. T. Nicholas said the chain was examined every month or six weeks.—The deputy Coroner said it appeared from the evidence that the deceased met his death by accident and that there was no neglect or de- fault on the part of any person. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.

div.head: RAINEORD MURDER.
div.p: THE RAINEORD MURDER.
TRUE BILLS AGAINST THE PRISONERS,

- At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, true Bills were presented by the grand jury against John Duckworth Pickavance (28), shoemaker, and Mary Jane Pickavance (20), for the wilful murder of Mr. Henry Granger Foster, at Rainford, on the 7th July. On the application of Mr. M'Keand, whp defends the male prisoner, the hearing of the charge of Murder against both prisoners was fixed for Friday. Mr. M'Keand, added that he understood that Mr. Shea would defend the female prisoner, while Mr. Watson would conduct the case for the Crown. His Lordship observed that from what hesaw on perusing the depositions the case would not last more than two days. He was anxious that the case should not be so fixed that it would necessitate the jury being required to stay over Sunday. He considered that Friday morning would be the best time to name for the commencement of the trial. Mr. M'Keand con- curred in his Lordship's view. TRIAL AT THE ASSIZES.

At the Liverpool Assizes, Crown Court, yesterday, the trial was commenced, before Mr. Justice Vaughan Williams, of John Duckworth Pickavance, twenty-eight, shoemaker, and Mary Jane Pickavance, his wife, who were indicted for having at Rainford on the 7th July last feloniously, wilfully, and of their malice afore- thought, killed and murdered Mr. Henry Granger Foster, colliery proprietor, of Brook Lodge, Rainford. : The trial drew together the usual crowd of sightseers, and; admittance to the court was eagerly sought, but the police took the greatest precaution that the precincts should not be over-crowded. The weather was dull and miserabla, and proba,bly on this account and the early hour at which the hearing was fixed to commence--viz,, 9.30, the neighbourhood of St. George's Hall was less frequented than is customary upon the occasion of great trials such as that of Mrs. Maybrick and other noted criminals. The prisoners had been brought to the cells beneath the hall at an early hour in the morning, so that there was no opportunity, except lay a few early birds, of even having a glimpse at the vehicle in which they were conveyed for trial. Counsel for the prosecution were' Mr. Watson and Mr. coiling wood Hope; Mr. M'Keand was for the male prisoner, and Mr. Shee for Mrs. Pickavancee. Mr. T. Swift was also with Mr. Shee for Mrs. Pickavance. The Judge took his seat promptly on the bench at 9.30, just after the flourish of trumpets announcing his arrival had died away in the remotest corners of the h.Lll. An ap- palling silence ensued, and all eyes were turned in the direction of the dock. Several routine matters having been arranged, the Clerk of AfkeiZe called, "Put up Jchn Duckworth Pickavance and Mary Pickavance." The female prisoner, who was well-dressed, with a black hat, came first, and was crying bitterly: the male prisoner was placid and collected, and had his hands clasped as usual. The female prisoner is understood to be enciente. Mr. Watson having opened for the prosecution, the first witnesscalled was James Baron, a surveyor practising at Rainford, whb produced a tracing double the size of the ordnance man of the county, embracing the district from Ecclestnn to Four Lane Ends, about six and a half miles by road. Evidence, similar to that previously made public, was next given bv Alice Lee„ deceased's hone- keeper: Mrs. Morris, of the Old Saddle Inn, Rainford: J. Macbeth, grocer, Rainford; Clara Macbeth ; Thomas Dyke, gardener. Ormskirk. Several other witnesses were called for the prosecution. Aftec an adjournment, Dr. Wiglesworth was put in the witness box, snd, in reply to Mr. M'Keand, said he was superintendent a Rainhill Lunatic Asylum. He had a large experience in the study ot mental disease. He was lecturer of Univer- sity College. Livernool, on that subject. He was instructed by the Director of Public Prosecutions to examine the male prisoner. He had several interviews, one which lasted an hour and a half, and which took place on the 28th July, 1890. Witness was struck with his peculiar manner, the expression of his face, his demeanour and character. There was not sufficient evidence to justify the can- elusion that the prisoner was actually insane, but he had an insane temperament, that was to say that his brain was badly organised, that his modes of thought and feeling, his ways of looking at things dif- fered from ordinary people. and his feelings were more readily overthrown. He had another interview which enabled him to better determine the condition of tip prisoner's mind. He was still disposed to think that the prisoner occupied the borderland between sanity and in- sanity, and he went further now and stated that the prisoner showed a nearer approach to insanity than sanity.—Elizabeth Preston, a sister of the male prisoner, and other witnesses, were called to show that he had al- ways been strange in his conduct.—Mr. McKeand after- wards made the opening'speech for the defence in which he dwelt upon the evidence of insanity in the male prisoner.

FATAL FLOODS. IN AUSTRIA.

VIENNA, (filiD-N—E—SDA.Y.—Last night, owing to the flood- ing of the river Salza, consequent on torrential rains, the -village of Bisettofshoten, which is well known to tourists in the Salzburg Alps as a railway junction, was almost completely inundated. Bridges over the Salza were car- ried away by the flood, houses were destroyed, and the railway Was damaged, Several lives were lost, either by drowning or injury through destruction of houses, and many head of rattle perished.

div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY, Z. 45 P.M.— This market is not In a state that pleases everybody, and it has become somewhat difficult to get business put through in quantity. Cotton is somewhat different. In yarns there is considerably more strength than business, but spinners of good marks are content to quote high and wait for opportunities. Common yarns are more plentiful, and sellers are careful not to turn offers away without due consideration when they get them, but at the moment offers are not too plentiful. Bundles are firm at quotations, but merchants are acting with consider- able caution and not much goes through. In cloth, the mar ket is slow all round. _ .

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY.— Beef meets a fair demand at the quotations. In Pork a quiet trade is passing. There is no change to report in the Bacon market, which continues firm at unchanged rates. div.head: IMPENDING STRIKE IN WALES.
div.p: THE IMPENDING STRIKE IN WALES.

The Welsh labour crisis is now assuming a m3st serious aspect. The dockers have posted up notices for an imme- diate advance in wages, ranging from 25 to 50 per cent.; while the loaders of coke demand an advance equal to 100 per cent. Many of the notices terminate to-day (Satur- day), and great excitement prevails in the Principality.

div.head: ARGENTINE REVOLUTION,
div.p: THE ARGENTINE REVOLUTION,

A " s telegram, published yester- day afternoon, says a manifesto from President Celman appeared on Thursday evening. It attributes as the sole cause of the revolution the insensate ambition of local parties in Buenos Ayres. Members of Dr. Celman's own party are aghast at the callousness and incomprehensible, vain ignorance of the real gravity of the situation which the President displays. NEWS OF EMIN PASHA. SEVERE FIGHTING.—GREAT SLAUGHTER.

A Zanzibar telegram says authentic news has been received of Emin Pasha. He had some severe fighting with the Masai in Ugogo,and killed many of them, using a Maxim gun with destructive effect. His soldiers,artned with the new German rifle, fired an immense quantity of ammunition, of which the Pasha now needs a fresh supply. Emin seized 1,200 head of cattle, fighting with the Ugogo natives, whom he defeated with great slaughter.

div.head: TRIAL OF LAERNIANN.
div.p: THE TRIAL OF LAERNIANN.

At the Central Criminal Court, London, yesterday, Albert Laermann, 34, a Belgian, described as a surgeon. was indicted for the wilful murder of Grace Ethel Hall, by using illegal means to procure miscarriage. Mr. C. Matthews prosecuted, and detailed the circumstances under which the charge was preferred, as deposed to at the magisterial, investigation. Hermione Grandt was called, and deposed that in May last she accompanied Mrs. Hall to the residence of the prisoner. Deceased handed £l5 in bank notes to the accused. Witness des- cribed what was done to the deceased by the accused, and said the deceased was caused great pain. Prisoner told witness she would be well paid, and handed her a cheque.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOU:
OF LORDS, FRIDAY.

The House met at four o'clock. LONDON GATES AND BARs.—Lord MomovrELT., moved the third reading of the Bill for the removal of gates and bars in London.—Lord BRAMWELL moved its rejection. The third reading of the Bill was carried after a division of 38 for to 29 against. THE RUSSIAN JEWS.—Lord SALISBURY, replyino. to Earl Meath, said the Government had no information of fresh edicts having been passed by the Russian Govern- ment against Russian Jews. The House adjourned at 7.30 o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. ZANZIBAR.—Mr. FERGUSON informed Mr. Buchannan that the date was not fixed for the assumption of the Zanzibar protectorate. The Government would provide for effective working of the Brussels Act respecting slavery. TRADE UNIONS FUNDS.—Mr. GOSCITEN, replying to Mr. Howell and Mr. Gladstone, said £110,000,000 was in savings banks at the call of Trades Unions, and seeing the possible withdrawal in times of strikes the treasury deemed that some limitation was necessary. The question was being carefully considered. BRITISH SUGAR —Mr. CITAPLIN in f -irmed Mr. Farquhar- son that he was inquiring as to the conditions of suc- cessful cultivation of sugar beet in southern parts of England and Ireland.

TEMPORISING WITH SLAVERY.—Regarding slaveti Zanzibar, Mr. FERGUSSON said it would be unjust air unpolitic to demand confiscation of domestic slaves In Mohammedan country. As soon as placed under British protection the Brussels Act, would, however, ensure the gradual extinction of slavery. rLEFT SITTING.]

As it is impossible to thank yon individually for your services so successfully put forth in our behalf on Wednes- day. we beg you to accept this public expression of our Indebtedness to you as a token that we appreciate the honour you have conferred upon us by electing us as your Representatives on the Newton Board of Commissioners. Act. James Massey (who did not appear) was sum- moned for driving the cattle from Wfolsbon on the day in question.—The defendant Hepherd, Who pleaded guilty, was fined L 1 for each anima/ rerdated. THE ALLEGED THEFT BY A FARM LABOVRER.—A' farm labourer, named Patrick Crow, was brought up on re- mand charged with stealing the sum of £2 55., the money of John Welsh. Two other farm labourers, named John Burke and Michael Connor, were charged with receiving part of thc money knowing it to have been stolen. Mr. P. Davies defended.—Welsh said that he and the prisoners had been, for about a fortnight, em- ployed by Mr. Percival, at Whitley Inferior. On Friday the 11th July, he (witness) received his wages, and he then had a ss. in hispcssession. He and Burke decided to hide their money under a bush in Mr. Gough's field, but Crow subsequently was seen to go in the direction of the hiding place, and take the money. P.C. Bratt also gave evidence, and said that the priioner when charged admitted that Crow had taken Lne money, and they had agreed to divide it.—The prisoners were com- mitted for one days' imprisonment each, they having already been in gaol for 18 days, it being understood that prosecutor was to receive his money back.
